sources.title: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng says hackers used fake job interviews, AI tool to steal $6.3 billion in crypto - CNBC
passages: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct.
29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.

The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.
As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets.
Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added.
The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges.
Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.

Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.

extraction.body: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop. "In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction." He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets. Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group. Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker." As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance. Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack. The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges. As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street." "We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. sources.title: Fake job interviews helped hackers pull off Binance’s record crypto heist - Yahoo Finance
passages: "It's been a pretty hectic process," Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance in an interview that aired Tuesday morning .
"But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the system's back to normal.
People are free to use the platform without any issues now.
The fake job interview was just one stage of the hackers' multistep attack.

Binance said the campaign began in June, when another engineer downloaded a "popular AI coding tool." Additional employee devices were later compromised before the hackers gained access to systems involved in authorizing wallet transactions.

Hackers behind the record-breaking Binance heist spent weeks masquerading as recruiters and fake executives, eventually convincing an engineer to download malicious software onto a work computer as part of a larger-scale ruse, the company said Tuesday.
20, hackers used the engineer's laptop, which had been compromised during the fake interview process, to infiltrate two other employees' computers.
Days later, they used stolen credentials to launch the malware responsible for the unauthorized transfers.
Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but a broader review revealed a wider series of security breaches.
The company temporarily suspended withdrawals late last week before reopening them Sunday.
Binance says it has since replenished 98% of the affected assets.
"This was a complex attack," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on social media Monday.
"The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers."
Hours after the hack, Binance said it would cover all customer losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users .
Stablecoin issuers including Tether and Circle ( CRCL ) were able to freeze a little less than half of the stolen assets.
Binance attributed the attack to North Korea, following a similar finding by the Federal Bureau of Investigation over the weekend and by outside investigators.
Binance added that it has fended off 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats so far this year.

extraction.body: Hackers behind the record-breaking Binance heist spent weeks masquerading as recruiters and fake executives, eventually convincing an engineer to download malicious software onto a work computer as part of a larger-scale ruse, the company said Tuesday. Binance said the ploy included two rounds of interviews, with a supposed human resources representative conducting the first interview and sharing social media information to gain the programmer's trust. A second person, posing as the CEO of a fake company, later persuaded the engineer to download a file containing malware under the guise of an interview assessment. "This was a complex attack," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on social media Monday. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers." The company emphasized that there was no single breach or mistake behind the hack, which is by far the largest crypto theft in history . Instead, the campaign unfolded over several months. The fake job interview was just one stage of the hackers' multistep attack. Binance said the campaign began in June, when another engineer downloaded a "popular AI coding tool." Additional employee devices were later compromised before the hackers gained access to systems involved in authorizing wallet transactions. On Oct. 20, hackers used the engineer's laptop, which had been compromised during the fake interview process, to infiltrate two other employees' computers. Binance said the attackers also used an internal AI tool, though it did not provide further details on how the tool was used. Days later, they used stolen credentials to launch the malware responsible for the unauthorized transfers. Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but a broader review revealed a wider series of security breaches. The company temporarily suspended withdrawals late last week before reopening them Sunday. Hours after the hack, Binance said it would cover all customer losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users . Stablecoin issuers including Tether and Circle ( CRCL ) were able to freeze a little less than half of the stolen assets. By late Sunday night ET, the company said it had processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and roughly $1.01 billion in deposits. Binance says it has since replenished 98% of the affected assets. "It's been a pretty hectic process," Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance in an interview that aired Tuesday morning . "But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the system's back to normal. People are free to use the platform without any issues now. And then all user funds are covered. The users did not suffer any loss." Binance attributed the attack to North Korea, following a similar finding by the Federal Bureau of Investigation over the weekend and by outside investigators. North Korea denied the allegations Monday. Binance added that it has fended off 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats so far this year.

passages: The postmortem also goes into why Binance wasn’t able to stop the transactions that occurred nearly two hours after the first unauthorized transfers, saying that “Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations.” Binance says that it has prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases, and CEO Richard Teng writes that no user is bearing the loss, with about $2.85 billion in stolen assets frozen or intercepted: “At this moment, 98% of impacted tokens had been replenished; we’re completing the remaining 2%.

By October 20th, the story goes, the attackers, whom the FBI has identified as a North Korean unit dubbed “TraderTraitor,” used Binance’s own internal AI tool to gain control over wallets for the first engineer compromised in June, as well as a third employee, before logging into the third employee’s computer on October 29th and launching their attack.
The largest crypto theft to date was pulled off by combining some well-known hacking techniques over the course of a few months, according to Binance.

Binance claims that its security teams did detect the first installation of malware in June, and replaced the worker’s device, but that its security tools didn’t detect the second attack that deleted the pyenv executable and replaced it with a malicious version that gave them backdoor access: > The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server.

Then, in September, another engineer was targeted by someone pretending to be interested in hiring them; that person set up a series of calls and multiple rounds of interviews, shared social media pages to build trust, and eventually prompted them to download a fake interview assignment that was actually malware.

extraction.body: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop. "In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction." He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets. Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group. Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker." As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance. Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack. The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges. As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street." "We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. passages: The postmortem also goes into why Binance wasn’t able to stop the transactions that occurred nearly two hours after the first unauthorized transfers, saying that “Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations.” Binance says that it has prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases, and CEO Richard Teng writes that no user is bearing the loss, with about $2.85 billion in stolen assets frozen or intercepted: “At this moment, 98% of impacted tokens had been replenished; we’re completing the remaining 2%.

By October 20th, the story goes, the attackers, whom the FBI has identified as a North Korean unit dubbed “TraderTraitor,” used Binance’s own internal AI tool to gain control over wallets for the first engineer compromised in June, as well as a third employee, before logging into the third employee’s computer on October 29th and launching their attack.
The largest crypto theft to date was pulled off by combining some well-known hacking techniques over the course of a few months, according to Binance.

Binance claims that its security teams did detect the first installation of malware in June, and replaced the worker’s device, but that its security tools didn’t detect the second attack that deleted the pyenv executable and replaced it with a malicious version that gave them backdoor access: > The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server.

Then, in September, another engineer was targeted by someone pretending to be interested in hiring them; that person set up a series of calls and multiple rounds of interviews, shared social media pages to build trust, and eventually prompted them to download a fake interview assignment that was actually malware.

Google’s new overarching approach to AI in K-12 classrooms sounds good on the surface. After consulting educators, researchers, and lawmakers, Google has decided that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default. It will be up to administrators to manually enable them when these changes roll out in the coming months. When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear. The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search . Google’s new overarching approach to AI in K-12 classrooms sounds good on the surface. After consulting educators, researchers, and lawmakers, Google has decided that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default. It will be up to administrators to manually enable them when these changes roll out in the coming months.

When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear. The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search . There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.

This is actually consistent with Google’s approach in the consumer space. Google executives have said in no uncertain terms that Google Search is AI search . Most searches now provide an AI Overview at the top, and the company is constantly coming up with new ways to nudge people toward the conversational AI Mode chatbot function. Google sees this as the future.

In a statement to The New York Times , Google education VP Chris Phillips reiterated this approach to web search. “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” he said, adding that if a school chooses not to enable AI, the students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Google could make a version of search for schools that doesn’t have AI tools, but it’s not doing that. Instead, it’s creating two different versions of AI in search. When schools enable AI for student accounts, they’ll have two options: the standard Gemini-based AI and the new “Guided Learning” version. The latter, available in Classroom as well as search, is supposed to provide one-on-one tutoring and assistance without giving away all the answers. Google notes all of its generative AI products can make “mistakes,” though, so it may not be difficult to talk the chatbot into doing your homework.

Google is betting that schools won’t want to give up Google Search and will therefore accept AI tools. This will expose students to AI early and often, possibly changing the way they interact with technology. Schools that don’t like Google’s approach could switch to alternatives like DuckDuckGo, which lets you disable AI features. But will Google’s new Guided Learning be enough to assuage their concerns?

sources.title: Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search
passages: Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on.
The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers.
As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable.
Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector.
Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools.
The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers.
The launch comes amid concerns that AI chatbots undermine the learning process because they spit out direct answers.

Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials.

sources.title: Google Requires AI Features in Schools or Risk Losing Search Access in ‘Guided Learning’ Rollout
passages: Google is making a significant structural change to how its products work in schools, and the announcement has implications well beyond a simple feature update.The company is shifting from a default-on model for AI tools in education to one where access is fully controlled by school administrators, with AI turned off by default until someone explicitly switches it on.Google Requires AI Features in SchoolsGoogle announced earlier today that it is updating its approach to school controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search for K-12 student accounts.

In Google Classroom, Guided Learning is now globally available, allowing teachers to assign it as a 1-on-1 study tool anchored to class material, with real-time insights for teachers to track where students may need extra support.In Google Search, Guided Learning is rolling out to select US schools through a pilot program starting later in November, with broader school district expansion planned for the coming months.

In recent years, Google has significantly expanded what Search can do beyond returning a list of links, introducing AI Overviews that synthesize information from across the web into a conversational summary at the top of the results page.The addition of Guided Learning to Search for school accounts represents the most education-specific customization Google has applied to Search to date, turning a general information tool into one that can respond differently depending on whether the user is a student working on homework.How Can Guided Learning Help Schools?Guided Learning helps schools by giving teachers and students access to an AI-powered coaching tool that complements classroom instruction rather than replacing it.

The feature is designed to activate when Google's systems detect that a student is seeking homework help, at which point Search will walk the student through the topic step by step rather than surfacing a direct answer.If a student pastes a complex physics problem into Search or asks for help with a book report, they will see prompts guiding them to think critically about the concepts rather than receiving the completed work outright.The philosophy behind Guided Learning, which Google calls "productive struggle," is to keep students actively challenged at a level that promotes learning without pushing them to the point of frustration.

For districts that want the full AI-enhanced experience, school IT administrators will need to actively configure their Google Workspace for Education settings to unlock it.Google's AI in 'Guided Learning'The centerpiece of the announcement is Guided Learning, a framework Google has been developing that is now expanding into two additional products.

The core idea is that AI should function as a learning scaffold rather than a shortcut, helping students work through problems and develop critical thinking skills rather than simply giving them answers.Google has been building and testing these tools over the past two years, conducting research studies in countries including the United Kingdom, Italy, and Japan to measure whether Guided Learning actually improves outcomes.

The new opt-in framework reverses that dynamic completely, putting the initial decision to enable AI tools entirely in the hands of school IT administrators rather than making access the default state.Google: No AI, No Search AccessThe implications of the new default-off policy extend to Google Search itself, which is a central tool for student research in many schools.

"Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit," Phillips wrote in the company's official blog post.Google said it will notify schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out, giving administrators time to prepare and configure access before the new defaults take effect.The shift represents a meaningful change in posture.

The AI-guided assistance that helps students work through problems step by step will simply not appear for school-managed accounts in districts where administrators have not turned the features on.9to5Google noted that the change essentially creates a two-tier Search experience, where the same query entered by a student on a school account versus a personal account may receive very different types of responses.

coreStoryFacts.text: Google is betting that schools won’t want to give up Google Search and will therefore accept AI tools.
This will expose students to AI early and often, possibly changing the way they interact with technology.
Schools that don’t like Google’s approach could switch to alternatives like DuckDuckGo, which lets you disable AI features.
But will Google’s new Guided Learning be enough to assuage their concerns?
Google will offer schools AI tools that purportedly don’t give away the answers.
While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks , the ubiquity of these devices has made the company’s education products huge in schools.
Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom.
However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision.
Google could make a version of search for schools that doesn’t have AI tools, but it’s not doing that.
Instead, it’s creating two different versions of AI in search.
The latter, available in Classroom as well as search, is supposed to provide one-on-one tutoring and assistance without giving away all the answers.
Google notes all of its generative AI products can make “mistakes,” though, so it may not be difficult to talk the chatbot into doing your homework.
In a statement to The New York Times , Google education VP Chris Phillips reiterated this approach to web search.
Google executives have said in no uncertain terms that Google Search is AI search .
Most searches now provide an AI Overview at the top, and the company is constantly coming up with new ways to nudge people toward the conversational AI Mode chatbot function.
Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years.
With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information.
After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.
When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear.
The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search .
There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post that Search, along with Google's Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Google Classroom, will be set off by default for K-12 student accounts until school administrators turn them on.

The company said it would share more specifics with schools "in the coming months" ahead of the rollout and that the decision followed conversations with schools, teachers, researchers and policymakers.

(Bloomberg) -- Schools that want their K-12 students to have access to Google Search will soon have to turn it on themselves, and the AI features built into Search will come with it, under changes the Alphabet Inc. company announced Tuesday.

(Bloomberg) -- Schools that want their K-12 students to have access to Google Search will soon have to turn it on themselves, and the AI features built into Search will come with it, under changes the Alphabet Inc. company announced Tuesday.
The company also said Guided Learning, a study mode Google first released in its Gemini app, would be extended into Search.
When Google's systems detect a student is looking for certain types of homework help, Search will walk them through a problem one step at a time.
A student who pastes in a physics problem or asks for help with a book report, for example, will get prompts meant to make them work through the concepts instead of skipping to the answer.
The change comes as Google, whose Chromebooks are the most widely used laptops in American classrooms, faces growing resistance to AI from parents and school districts.
Google will pilot Guided Learning within Google Search in select US schools later this month and plans to expand it to other districts after collecting feedback from teachers.
Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on.
The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers.
As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable.
Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector.
Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools.
The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers.
The launch comes amid concerns that AI chatbots undermine the learning process because they spit out direct answers.

Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials.

sources.title: Google Requires AI Features in Schools or Risk Losing Search Access in ‘Guided Learning’ Rollout
passages: Google is making a significant structural change to how its products work in schools, and the announcement has implications well beyond a simple feature update.The company is shifting from a default-on model for AI tools in education to one where access is fully controlled by school administrators, with AI turned off by default until someone explicitly switches it on.Google Requires AI Features in SchoolsGoogle announced earlier today that it is updating its approach to school controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search for K-12 student accounts.

In Google Classroom, Guided Learning is now globally available, allowing teachers to assign it as a 1-on-1 study tool anchored to class material, with real-time insights for teachers to track where students may need extra support.In Google Search, Guided Learning is rolling out to select US schools through a pilot program starting later in November, with broader school district expansion planned for the coming months.

In recent years, Google has significantly expanded what Search can do beyond returning a list of links, introducing AI Overviews that synthesize information from across the web into a conversational summary at the top of the results page.The addition of Guided Learning to Search for school accounts represents the most education-specific customization Google has applied to Search to date, turning a general information tool into one that can respond differently depending on whether the user is a student working on homework.How Can Guided Learning Help Schools?Guided Learning helps schools by giving teachers and students access to an AI-powered coaching tool that complements classroom instruction rather than replacing it.

The feature is designed to activate when Google's systems detect that a student is seeking homework help, at which point Search will walk the student through the topic step by step rather than surfacing a direct answer.If a student pastes a complex physics problem into Search or asks for help with a book report, they will see prompts guiding them to think critically about the concepts rather than receiving the completed work outright.The philosophy behind Guided Learning, which Google calls "productive struggle," is to keep students actively challenged at a level that promotes learning without pushing them to the point of frustration.

For districts that want the full AI-enhanced experience, school IT administrators will need to actively configure their Google Workspace for Education settings to unlock it.Google's AI in 'Guided Learning'The centerpiece of the announcement is Guided Learning, a framework Google has been developing that is now expanding into two additional products.

The core idea is that AI should function as a learning scaffold rather than a shortcut, helping students work through problems and develop critical thinking skills rather than simply giving them answers.Google has been building and testing these tools over the past two years, conducting research studies in countries including the United Kingdom, Italy, and Japan to measure whether Guided Learning actually improves outcomes.

The new opt-in framework reverses that dynamic completely, putting the initial decision to enable AI tools entirely in the hands of school IT administrators rather than making access the default state.Google: No AI, No Search AccessThe implications of the new default-off policy extend to Google Search itself, which is a central tool for student research in many schools.

"Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit," Phillips wrote in the company's official blog post.Google said it will notify schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out, giving administrators time to prepare and configure access before the new defaults take effect.The shift represents a meaningful change in posture.

The AI-guided assistance that helps students work through problems step by step will simply not appear for school-managed accounts in districts where administrators have not turned the features on.9to5Google noted that the change essentially creates a two-tier Search experience, where the same query entered by a student on a school account versus a personal account may receive very different types of responses.

Under the new framework, access to all of those products will be entirely off by default for student accounts until school administrators explicitly enable them.The announcement was made by Chris Phillips, VP and General Manager of Education at Google, who framed the change as a direct response to feedback from schools, teachers, researchers, and policymakers. "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit," Phillips wrote in the company's official blog post.Google said it will notify schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out, giving administrators time to prepare and configure access before the new defaults take effect.The shift represents a meaningful change in posture. Previously, Google's AI tools in education followed an opt-out model where features were often available by default and administrators had to actively disable them. The new opt-in framework reverses that dynamic completely, putting the initial decision to enable AI tools entirely in the hands of school IT administrators rather than making access the default state.Google: No AI, No Search AccessThe implications of the new default-off policy extend to Google Search itself, which is a central tool for student research in many schools. When students use Google accounts managed by their schools, Search will now have its AI features, including AI Overviews and the new Guided Learning capabilities, turned off until an administrator enables them.This is a nuanced but significant point: students can still use Google Search without AI features enabled, but the experience they receive will be qualitatively different from what general users access on the same platform. The AI-guided assistance that helps students work through problems step by step will simply not appear for school-managed accounts in districts where administrators have not turned the features on.9to5Google noted that the change essentially creates a two-tier Search experience, where the same query entered by a student on a school account versus a personal account may receive very different types of responses. For districts that want the full AI-enhanced experience, school IT administrators will need to actively configure their Google Workspace for Education settings to unlock it.Google's AI in 'Guided Learning'The centerpiece of the announcement is Guided Learning, a framework Google has been developing that is now expanding into two additional products. In Google Classroom, Guided Learning is now globally available, allowing teachers to assign it as a 1-on-1 study tool anchored to class material, with real-time insights for teachers to track where students may need extra support.In Google Search, Guided Learning is rolling out to select US schools through a pilot program starting later in November, with broader school district expansion planned for the coming months. The feature is designed to activate when Google's systems detect that a student is seeking homework help, at which point Search will walk the student through the topic step by step rather than surfacing a direct answer.If a student pastes a complex physics problem into Search or asks for help with a book report, they will see prompts guiding them to think critically about the concepts rather than receiving the completed work outright.The philosophy behind Guided Learning, which Google calls "productive struggle," is to keep students actively challenged at a level that promotes learning without pushing them to the point of frustration. Research Google has conducted and cited in its announcement showed that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students.The feature already operates in a similar coaching mode within the Gemini app and is now being extended to Classroom and Search to reach students across more of the tools they use daily.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat Is Google's AI Push?Google's AI push in education is a broad initiative to integrate its Gemini-powered AI tools into the products that students and teachers use most, including Google Search, Google Classroom, and Gemini Notebook. The core idea is that AI should function as a learning scaffold rather than a shortcut, helping students work through problems and develop critical thinking skills rather than simply giving them answers.Google has been building and testing these tools over the past two years, conducting research studies in countries including the United Kingdom, Italy, and Japan to measure whether Guided Learning actually improves outcomes. The November 2026 announcement extends that work by bringing Guided Learning into Search for the first time and shifting all AI features to an opt-in model for school-managed accounts, giving educators more control over how and when AI enters the classroom.What Is Google Search?Google Search is the company's flagship internet search engine, used by billions of people globally every day. For students in particular, it has long been one of the primary tools for academic research, project work, and general curiosity-driven learning. In recent years, Google has significantly expanded what Search can do beyond returning a list of links, introducing AI Overviews that synthesize information from across the web into a conversational summary at the top of the results page.The addition of Guided Learning to Search for school accounts represents the most education-specific customization Google has applied to Search to date, turning a general information tool into one that can respond differently depending on whether the user is a student working on homework.How Can Guided Learning Help Schools?Guided Learning helps schools by giving teachers and students access to an AI-powered coaching tool that complements classroom instruction rather than replacing it. For students, it provides a structured way to get help without the AI doing the work for them, which research suggests leads to stronger understanding and retention compared to simply receiving an answer.For teachers, the Classroom integration provides real-time data on where individual students or the class as a whole may be struggling, allowing educators to adjust their instruction without waiting for a test to surface those gaps.For administrators, the new opt-in control system means schools can roll out AI tools gradually, starting with specific grade levels or subjects, and can disable them entirely in contexts where the school has decided AI assistance is not appropriate.That level of control is what several school systems and advocacy groups had been requesting, making the November 2026 update a direct response to documented feedback from the education sector.

sources.title: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
passages: Google is betting that schools won’t want to give up Google Search and will therefore accept AI tools.
This will expose students to AI early and often, possibly changing the way they interact with technology.
Schools that don’t like Google’s approach could switch to alternatives like DuckDuckGo, which lets you disable AI features.
But will Google’s new Guided Learning be enough to assuage their concerns?
Google will offer schools AI tools that purportedly don’t give away the answers.
While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks , the ubiquity of these devices has made the company’s education products huge in schools.
Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom.
However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision.
Google could make a version of search for schools that doesn’t have AI tools, but it’s not doing that.
Instead, it’s creating two different versions of AI in search.
The latter, available in Classroom as well as search, is supposed to provide one-on-one tutoring and assistance without giving away all the answers.
Google notes all of its generative AI products can make “mistakes,” though, so it may not be difficult to talk the chatbot into doing your homework.
In a statement to The New York Times , Google education VP Chris Phillips reiterated this approach to web search.
Google executives have said in no uncertain terms that Google Search is AI search .
Most searches now provide an AI Overview at the top, and the company is constantly coming up with new ways to nudge people toward the conversational AI Mode chatbot function.
When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear.
The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search .
There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.

extraction.body: Google is changing how its artificial intelligence tools work in classrooms, and the move is drawing sharp criticism from teachers and parent advocates. The tech giant announced on Tuesday, Nov. 3, that it will switch off its AI products by default for students in schools that use its education software. But there’s a major catch. Schools that choose not to turn on Google’s AI services will also lose access to Google Search for their students. Until now, Google’s AI products, branded under the name Gemini, were automatically turned on for schools using Google Classroom. Under the new policy, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be completely turned off for student accounts in kindergarten through 12th grade. They will stay off until school administrators choose to turn them on. Google said Search is included in the change because AI is now deeply built into its search products. In a blog post announcing the update, Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said the company believes schools should have control over how AI is used in their classrooms. Some education and technology advocates quickly criticized the decision. They argue it punishes schools that don’t want to use Google’s AI tools. Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, said Google had put its business interests ahead of children’s education. She added that instead of working with teachers and parents to make its tools safe and protect privacy, the company chose to cut off access entirely. Josh Golin, executive director of the advocacy group Fairplay, accused Google of trying to pressure schools into using its AI products. He encouraged schools to help students find search alternatives that better protect their privacy and to explore deeper research methods. The move follows growing criticism from advocacy groups and senators about the spread of Google’s AI tools in classrooms. Earlier this year, Google turned on Gemini in its Classroom app, which allowed children of any age to use AI products unless their district turned them off. Parent groups and education technology experts pushed back. Many worried that students would rely on AI to do their schoolwork. In early October, 13 parent advocacy organizations signed an open letter urging school districts to turn off Gemini and YouTube, which Google also owns. Google has become a major player in education technology over the past 15 years. Most Chromebook laptops are bought by school districts for students. A 2023 report found that nearly 2 in 3 school assignments involve a Google product. This year, the company also began offering AI training sessions for educators lasting several days. Some sessions focused on how to address pushback from teachers who don’t want to use AI. Research has not yet shown a lasting benefit from AI in schools. According to researchers at the Stanford Graduate School of Education, there are no high quality studies showing cause and effect when students use AI. Experts have also warned that many existing studies didn’t measure whether AI improved learning or whether it worked better than other teaching methods. For schools that choose to enable Google’s AI tools, the company says its products will now detect when students try to use them just to get answers on assignments. In those cases, a redesigned version of Google Search will guide students through the topic or problem step by step, helping them understand the concepts instead of handing over the answer. This story was originally reported by NBC News. Tega Egwabor is a writer with RollingOut, covering diverse stories that span politics, health, fitness, finance, and more. Guided by a philosophical background, Tega approaches stories with depth, balance, and nuance. Passionate about connecting ideas with everyday life, her work seeks to spark curiosity, encourage reflection, and open up meaningful conversations.

Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector. Schools that want to continue to have access to Google Search will have to accept its AI features.

“We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition,” Phillips wrote in a blog post . “Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.”

sources.title: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
passages: Google is betting that schools won’t want to give up Google Search and will therefore accept AI tools.
This will expose students to AI early and often, possibly changing the way they interact with technology.
Schools that don’t like Google’s approach could switch to alternatives like DuckDuckGo, which lets you disable AI features.
But will Google’s new Guided Learning be enough to assuage their concerns?
Google will offer schools AI tools that purportedly don’t give away the answers.
While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks , the ubiquity of these devices has made the company’s education products huge in schools.
Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom.
However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision.
Google could make a version of search for schools that doesn’t have AI tools, but it’s not doing that.
Instead, it’s creating two different versions of AI in search.
The latter, available in Classroom as well as search, is supposed to provide one-on-one tutoring and assistance without giving away all the answers.
Google notes all of its generative AI products can make “mistakes,” though, so it may not be difficult to talk the chatbot into doing your homework.
In a statement to The New York Times , Google education VP Chris Phillips reiterated this approach to web search.
Google executives have said in no uncertain terms that Google Search is AI search .
Most searches now provide an AI Overview at the top, and the company is constantly coming up with new ways to nudge people toward the conversational AI Mode chatbot function.
When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear.
The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search .
There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.

Under the new policy, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be completely turned off for student accounts in kindergarten through 12th grade.
Josh Golin, executive director of the advocacy group Fairplay, accused Google of trying to pressure schools into using its AI products.
He encouraged schools to help students find search alternatives that better protect their privacy and to explore deeper research methods.
A 2023 report found that nearly 2 in 3 school assignments involve a Google product.

Google is changing how its artificial intelligence tools work in classrooms, and the move is drawing sharp criticism from teachers and parent advocates.

extraction.body: Google is changing how its artificial intelligence tools work in classrooms, and the move is drawing sharp criticism from teachers and parent advocates. The tech giant announced on Tuesday, Nov. 3, that it will switch off its AI products by default for students in schools that use its education software. But there’s a major catch. Schools that choose not to turn on Google’s AI services will also lose access to Google Search for their students. Until now, Google’s AI products, branded under the name Gemini, were automatically turned on for schools using Google Classroom. Under the new policy, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be completely turned off for student accounts in kindergarten through 12th grade. They will stay off until school administrators choose to turn them on. Google said Search is included in the change because AI is now deeply built into its search products. In a blog post announcing the update, Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said the company believes schools should have control over how AI is used in their classrooms. Some education and technology advocates quickly criticized the decision. They argue it punishes schools that don’t want to use Google’s AI tools. Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, said Google had put its business interests ahead of children’s education. She added that instead of working with teachers and parents to make its tools safe and protect privacy, the company chose to cut off access entirely. Josh Golin, executive director of the advocacy group Fairplay, accused Google of trying to pressure schools into using its AI products. He encouraged schools to help students find search alternatives that better protect their privacy and to explore deeper research methods. The move follows growing criticism from advocacy groups and senators about the spread of Google’s AI tools in classrooms. Earlier this year, Google turned on Gemini in its Classroom app, which allowed children of any age to use AI products unless their district turned them off. Parent groups and education technology experts pushed back. Many worried that students would rely on AI to do their schoolwork. In early October, 13 parent advocacy organizations signed an open letter urging school districts to turn off Gemini and YouTube, which Google also owns. Google has become a major player in education technology over the past 15 years. Most Chromebook laptops are bought by school districts for students. A 2023 report found that nearly 2 in 3 school assignments involve a Google product. This year, the company also began offering AI training sessions for educators lasting several days. Some sessions focused on how to address pushback from teachers who don’t want to use AI. Research has not yet shown a lasting benefit from AI in schools. According to researchers at the Stanford Graduate School of Education, there are no high quality studies showing cause and effect when students use AI. Experts have also warned that many existing studies didn’t measure whether AI improved learning or whether it worked better than other teaching methods. For schools that choose to enable Google’s AI tools, the company says its products will now detect when students try to use them just to get answers on assignments. In those cases, a redesigned version of Google Search will guide students through the topic or problem step by step, helping them understand the concepts instead of handing over the answer. Guided by a philosophical background, Tega approaches stories with depth, balance, and nuance. Passionate about connecting ideas with everyday life, her work seeks to spark curiosity, encourage reflection, and open up meaningful conversations.

Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg said in May 2024 that power will be one of the biggest factors that will constrain artificial intelligence , and, true enough, tech giants and hyperscalers have begun to hit power constraints.

According to SemiAnalysis , electricity loads of tens of gigawatts have been requested in the state of Texas alone, but only a little over a gigawatt has received approval, signalling that the power grid may be stretched thin.
Aside from these two, several other projects are going off-grid, with 62% of data centers considering on-site power generation, according to Data Center Knowledge .
Furthermore, Natural Gas Intel estimated that data centers will use 35GW of behind-the-meter power by 2030.
xAI contracted VoltaGrid to deliver power to its Memphis data center while it was waiting for a connection from the TVA.
This begs the question: should AI data centers rely entirely on their own power?
AI companies are turning to gas turbines to run their data centers without grid power.
So, even if the company fails to secure power from the grid, it can get the needed electricity from its own turbines.
While gas generators seem to be the silver bullet that will help solve the electricity supply puzzle many data centers face, it also comes with its own set of problems.
To achieve this, data centers cannot just purchase the generators that can deliver the load they need; they need to build in redundancy.
Elon Musk was the first to use gas turbine generators to power a data center at this scale and duration at xAI’s Memphis Supercluster.

This entails an extended power purchase agreement between the provider and the data center, wherein the former will deliver everything that the latter needs for their operation — from power capacity and day-to-day operations to maintenance and uptime reliability.

AI companies are turning to gas turbines to run their data centers without grid power. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg said in May 2024 that power will be one of the biggest factors that will constrain artificial intelligence , and, true enough, tech giants and hyperscalers have begun to hit power constraints. According to SemiAnalysis , electricity loads of tens of gigawatts have been requested in the state of Texas alone, but only a little over a gigawatt has received approval, signalling that the power grid may be stretched thin. However, this doesn’t mean that companies are ditching dreams of building massive AI data centers across the globe. Instead, they’re looking at alternative power sources to bring their projects online, regardless of the availability of power from the grid. This limitation has tech and power companies investing in small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) , which can potentially deliver large amounts of power in a relatively compact package. Microsoft has even recommissioned the old Three Mile Island nuclear power plant to deliver 819 MW of power for AI and cloud data center usage. These initiatives will take years to take off, though. The Three Mile Island plant is expected to be operational only by 2028, while the earliest SMRs won’t enter service until the 2030s. There has even been a proposal to use retired U.S. Navy reactors for data centers , but the project proponent hasn’t offered a timeline for how quickly it could potentially get up and running. Elon Musk was the first to use gas turbine generators to power a data center at this scale and duration at xAI’s Memphis Supercluster. In 2024, the AI startup signed a 50-MW deal with the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), which only became operational months after. Aside from the delay, this is nowhere near enough of the 155MW that the 100,000 H100 GPUs running on the site require. There was also a 150-MW substation under construction on the site, which also required additional setup. Waiting for these power sources to come online would have negated Musk’s historic 19-day setup of an AI data center , so he turned to VoltaGrid to deliver the power he needed to run the Colossus site. Just a few months later, OpenAI followed the billionaire’s lead and ordered 29 gas turbines capable of producing 34MW each for its Stargate data center in Abilene, Texas. All these turbines would output a total of 986MW of power, which should be enough to run up to half a million GB200 NVL72 chips. So, even if the company fails to secure power from the grid, it can get the needed electricity from its own turbines. Aside from these two, several other projects are going off-grid, with 62% of data centers considering on-site power generation, according to Data Center Knowledge . Furthermore, Natural Gas Intel estimated that data centers will use 35GW of behind-the-meter power by 2030. This technique is crucial for the U.S.’s AI infrastructure to stay ahead, which is especially true as experts warn that China is miles ahead when it comes to electricity generation . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang also reportedly commented that “China is going to win the AI race,” pointing directly toward power constraints as one of the reasons behind his statement. While gas generators seem to be the silver bullet that will help solve the electricity supply puzzle many data centers face, it also comes with its own set of problems. Uptime is the principal issue among them, since data centers require near constant uptime reliability. To achieve this, data centers cannot just purchase the generators that can deliver the load they need; they need to build in redundancy. AI data centers must have N+1 or N+1+1 redundancy to ensure continued operation, even if some fail. N+1 means that they must have a backup generator, which takes over should one fail during normal operations. Meanwhile, N+1+1 recommends having an additional power source on site as well as a backup, in case one of the generators in regular operation is in maintenance. As well as all of this, maintenance, spare parts, necessary personnel, and fuel also remain additional considerations. Despite these challenges, it’s estimated that AI data centers could generate $10 to $12 billion per gigawatt annually. Musk fired up the Colossus data center in July 2024 , while the 150MW substation only delivered power to the site in November 2024 . This meant that he could have made somewhere between $3 to $4 billion in revenue during that time, which likely would have offset the cost of running the entire site on natural gas turbines. Another issue that data centers face is permitting requirements, which can take as long as a year or more. The OpenAI/Oracle site at Abilene, Texas, is reportedly facing delays because of this. Musk’s Colossus 2 site mitigated the permit delay by building near the border of Tennessee and Mississippi , allowing him to hedge his bets by applying for permits from the two states and securing supply from both. Aside from that, communities around these data centers might complain about the power plants they’re putting up just to provide the power they need. xAI faced this exact issue , with residents complaining about the pollution generated by the gas turbines deployed around the Memphis site. Though investors could throw unlimited amounts of money at the problem, there's another factor they cannot escape — long equipment lead times. It takes about 12 to 36 months before any of the gas turbine manufacturers can deliver them, especially as these are intricate machines that use highly specialized materials and require specific processes to manufacture. These lead times could get longer, especially as more AI data centers are competing for the same amount of production capacity from these companies. xAI contracted VoltaGrid to deliver power to its Memphis data center while it was waiting for a connection from the TVA. But even as the utility company finally delivered the 150MW it needed, some turbine generators remained on site as a backup to the system. This begs the question: should AI data centers rely entirely on their own power? VoltaGrid and other firms seem to think so, even going as far as offering “energy-as-a-service,” or EaaS, to AI companies. This entails an extended power purchase agreement between the provider and the data center, wherein the former will deliver everything that the latter needs for their operation — from power capacity and day-to-day operations to maintenance and uptime reliability. However, even though this may be favorable in terms of deployment time, it will still get prohibitively expensive in the long run. At the moment, AI companies rent gas generators for bridge power, allowing them to get their data center operations up and running as soon as possible while waiting for approval from the local utility. But when they finally connect their site to the grid, it’s still often more economical to just keep these mobile generators as backup units in case their primary sources fail, not as their sole power source. EaaS could possibly work as a permanent solution when the national electric grid is maxed out. When there is no more extra capacity to be had for power-hungry AI infrastructure, AI companies might have no choice but to rely on services like this just to get their projects up and running. AI companies are turning to gas turbines to run their data centers without grid power.
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg said in May 2024 that power will be one of the biggest factors that will constrain artificial intelligence , and, true enough, tech giants and hyperscalers have begun to hit power constraints. According to SemiAnalysis , electricity loads of tens of gigawatts have been requested in the state of Texas alone, but only a little over a gigawatt has received approval, signalling that the power grid may be stretched thin.

However, this doesn’t mean that companies are ditching dreams of building massive AI data centers across the globe. Instead, they’re looking at alternative power sources to bring their projects online, regardless of the availability of power from the grid.

This limitation has tech and power companies investing in small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) , which can potentially deliver large amounts of power in a relatively compact package. Microsoft has even recommissioned the old Three Mile Island nuclear power plant to deliver 819 MW of power for AI and cloud data center usage.

These initiatives will take years to take off, though. The Three Mile Island plant is expected to be operational only by 2028, while the earliest SMRs won’t enter service until the 2030s. There has even been a proposal to use retired U.S. Navy reactors for data centers , but the project proponent hasn’t offered a timeline for how quickly it could potentially get up and running.

Elon Musk was the first to use gas turbine generators to power a data center at this scale and duration at xAI’s Memphis Supercluster. In 2024, the AI startup signed a 50-MW deal with the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), which only became operational months after.

Aside from the delay, this is nowhere near enough of the 155MW that the 100,000 H100 GPUs running on the site require. There was also a 150-MW substation under construction on the site, which also required additional setup. Waiting for these power sources to come online would have negated Musk’s historic 19-day setup of an AI data center , so he turned to VoltaGrid to deliver the power he needed to run the Colossus site.

Just a few months later, OpenAI followed the billionaire’s lead and ordered 29 gas turbines capable of producing 34MW each for its Stargate data center in Abilene, Texas. All these turbines would output a total of 986MW of power, which should be enough to run up to half a million GB200 NVL72 chips. So, even if the company fails to secure power from the grid, it can get the needed electricity from its own turbines.

Aside from these two, several other projects are going off-grid, with 62% of data centers considering on-site power generation, according to Data Center Knowledge . Furthermore, Natural Gas Intel estimated that data centers will use 35GW of behind-the-meter power by 2030.

This technique is crucial for the U.S.’s AI infrastructure to stay ahead, which is especially true as experts warn that China is miles ahead when it comes to electricity generation . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang also reportedly commented that “China is going to win the AI race,” pointing directly toward power constraints as one of the reasons behind his statement.

While gas generators seem to be the silver bullet that will help solve the electricity supply puzzle many data centers face, it also comes with its own set of problems. Uptime is the principal issue among them, since data centers require near constant uptime reliability. To achieve this, data centers cannot just purchase the generators that can deliver the load they need; they need to build in redundancy.

AI data centers must have N+1 or N+1+1 redundancy to ensure continued operation, even if some fail. N+1 means that they must have a backup generator, which takes over should one fail during normal operations. Meanwhile, N+1+1 recommends having an additional power source on site as well as a backup, in case one of the generators in regular operation is in maintenance. As well as all of this, maintenance, spare parts, necessary personnel, and fuel also remain additional considerations.

Despite these challenges, it’s estimated that AI data centers could generate $10 to $12 billion per gigawatt annually. Musk fired up the Colossus data center in July 2024 , while the 150MW substation only delivered power to the site in November 2024 . This meant that he could have made somewhere between $3 to $4 billion in revenue during that time, which likely would have offset the cost of running the entire site on natural gas turbines.

Another issue that data centers face is permitting requirements, which can take as long as a year or more. The OpenAI/Oracle site at Abilene, Texas, is reportedly facing delays because of this. Musk’s Colossus 2 site mitigated the permit delay by building near the border of Tennessee and Mississippi , allowing him to hedge his bets by applying for permits from the two states and securing supply from both.

Aside from that, communities around these data centers might complain about the power plants they’re putting up just to provide the power they need. xAI faced this exact issue , with residents complaining about the pollution generated by the gas turbines deployed around the Memphis site.

Though investors could throw unlimited amounts of money at the problem, there's another factor they cannot escape — long equipment lead times. It takes about 12 to 36 months before any of the gas turbine manufacturers can deliver them, especially as these are intricate machines that use highly specialized materials and require specific processes to manufacture.
These lead times could get longer, especially as more AI data centers are competing for the same amount of production capacity from these companies.

xAI contracted VoltaGrid to deliver power to its Memphis data center while it was waiting for a connection from the TVA. But even as the utility company finally delivered the 150MW it needed, some turbine generators remained on site as a backup to the system. This begs the question: should AI data centers rely entirely on their own power? VoltaGrid and other firms seem to think so, even going as far as offering “energy-as-a-service,” or EaaS, to AI companies.

This entails an extended power purchase agreement between the provider and the data center, wherein the former will deliver everything that the latter needs for their operation — from power capacity and day-to-day operations to maintenance and uptime reliability. However, even though this may be favorable in terms of deployment time, it will still get prohibitively expensive in the long run.

At the moment, AI companies rent gas generators for bridge power, allowing them to get their data center operations up and running as soon as possible while waiting for approval from the local utility. But when they finally connect their site to the grid, it’s still often more economical to just keep these mobile generators as backup units in case their primary sources fail, not as their sole power source.

EaaS could possibly work as a permanent solution when the national electric grid is maxed out. When there is no more extra capacity to be had for power-hungry AI infrastructure, AI companies might have no choice but to rely on services like this just to get their projects up and running.

The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout. For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said. Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week . In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s. Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets. In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April. In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines. Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity. Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two. sources.title: Data centers turn to old jet engines to power AI’s soaring energy demands
passages: Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new.

Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power.

Each refurbished unit can generate up to 48 megawatts (MW) of electricity, enough to power a small-to-medium data center or a town of 20,000 to 40,000 households.Landon Tessmer, Vice President of Commercial Operations at ProEnergy, told IEEE Spectrum that they have sold 21 gas turbines for two data-center projects, amounting to more than 1 gigawatt (GW).
For decades, companies like GE Vernova and Siemens Energy have converted aviation engines for stationary power generation.

These “aeroderivative” turbines are lighter, smaller, and easier to maintain than their heavy-frame industrial counterparts, making them ideal for temporary or mobile power setups.At the Data Center World Power show in San Antonio this October, Missouri-based energy firm ProEnergy showcased how it modernizes this approach.

Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power. Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new. The company buys and overhauls used CF6-80C2 engine cores used in GE’s LM6000 and refits them into natural gas turbines branded as PE6000 units. Each refurbished unit can generate up to 48 megawatts (MW) of electricity, enough to power a small-to-medium data center or a town of 20,000 to 40,000 households.Landon Tessmer, Vice President of Commercial Operations at ProEnergy, told IEEE Spectrum that they have sold 21 gas turbines for two data-center projects, amounting to more than 1 gigawatt (GW). According to Tessmer, some facilities use ProEnergy’s turbines to power construction activities and initial operations, after which the units are moved into backup roles or sold to local utilities.Beyond faster delivery times, ProEnergy can supply a unit as early as 2027. As the global turbine shortage deepens, their second act as power generators may prove vital in sustaining the momentum of the AI revolution.
