extraction.body: Welcome to Global Data Center Hub . Join investors, operators, and innovators reading to stay ahead of the latest trends in the data center sector in developed and emerging markets globally. Large power transformers, the equipment that converts the very high voltage carried by long-distance power lines into a voltage a building can actually use, now average 128 weeks from order to delivery , according to a Wood Mackenzie survey of utility and developer orders. The largest units, which connect power plants to the grid, average 144 weeks. A data center building takes roughly two years to construct. Developers now order power equipment years before a project has a customer or a final go-ahead. Chevron ordered seven large gas turbines from GE Vernova, the power equipment company spun out of General Electric in 2024, roughly two years before signing the twenty-year electricity agreement with Microsoft that those turbines will serve. The published order books of power equipment makers show whether an announced AI buildout is real. GE Vernova reported $2.4 billion of data center electrical equipment orders in the first quarter of 2026, more than the company booked in all of 2025, and those figures are filed with regulators every quarter while project announcements carry no such requirement. Somewhere near your house there is a grey drum on a wooden pole, or a green metal cabinet sitting on a concrete pad at the end of the street. That is a transformer. It takes the very high voltage that travels down long-distance power lines and turns it into the much lower voltage your kitchen can handle. Every building on earth has one of these standing between it and the grid. In June 2026, Chevron announced a deal with Microsoft. Chevron will build a power plant near Pecos, in West Texas, and sell all of its electricity directly to a Microsoft data center under a twenty-year agreement. The plant is designed for roughly 2.67 gigawatts, which is about the electricity used by two million American homes. First power is expected in 2028. Read as a headline, that is a story about an oil company walking into the AI business. A gas turbine is essentially a truck-sized jet engine that burns natural gas to spin a generator. Chevron ordered seven large ones from GE Vernova, the power equipment company spun out of General Electric in 2024. It placed that order before it had a signed customer, before its own board had given the project a final approval, and before the design was settled. The plant burns natural gas, and Microsoft has a standing pledge to remove more carbon from the atmosphere than it emits by 2030, a target this makes harder to reach. Chevron has said the plant will run separately from the regional grid so that local households are not competing with it for power. If you read that announcement as an oil company discovering technology, you missed the part that decided it, which is that the winner was whoever had joined the queue earliest. Here is the number that reorganizes everything. Wood Mackenzie, an energy research firm, surveyed actual utility and developer orders and found that standard large power transformers average 128 weeks between order and delivery. That is close to two and a half years. The largest units, the ones that connect a power plant to the grid, average 144 weeks. A large power transformer needs a specialized electrical steel that only a few mills in the world produce, plus copper, plus custom engineering, plus months of testing before it ships. Adding factory capacity takes years, because a transformer plant is itself a heavy industrial building. And three separate waves of demand arrived at those same factories at once. Data centers need them. Older grid equipment installed decades ago needs replacing. Factories and vehicle fleets switching from fuel to electricity need them too. None of those three has any reason to slow down for the others. The obvious response to a shortage is to build more factories, and that is happening. In South Boston, Virginia, Hitachi Energy has made transformers since 1968. In 2026, it began a $457 million expansion to make the site the largest power transformer factory in the U.S. The project adds around 825 jobs to a workforce of about 850, close to doubling the place. Relief may not arrive until the end of the decade. Virginia is a fitting place for it. Northern Virginia holds the largest concentration of data centers on earth. Data centers already account for roughly a quarter of the electricity sold by the state’s main utility. In the first quarter of 2026, GE Vernova’s electrification division, which makes transformers, switchgear, and the substations that connect large buildings to the grid, booked $2.4 billion of orders tied to data centers. That was more than the division booked from data centers in the whole of 2025. Total orders across the company reached $18.3 billion for the quarter, up 71 percent on the year before, and its order backlog, meaning work sold but not yet delivered, stood at $163 billion. Those numbers say something that a press release cannot. Somebody signed for the equipment, and somebody is paying for it. So, the next time a very large AI project is announced, the fastest way to know whether it is real is to wait a quarter and look at what the equipment makers say they sold.

This entails an extended power purchase agreement between the provider and the data center, wherein the former will deliver everything that the latter needs for their operation — from power capacity and day-to-day operations to maintenance and uptime reliability.

Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg said in May 2024 that power will be one of the biggest factors that will constrain artificial intelligence , and, true enough, tech giants and hyperscalers have begun to hit power constraints.

According to SemiAnalysis , electricity loads of tens of gigawatts have been requested in the state of Texas alone, but only a little over a gigawatt has received approval, signalling that the power grid may be stretched thin.
Aside from these two, several other projects are going off-grid, with 62% of data centers considering on-site power generation, according to Data Center Knowledge .
Furthermore, Natural Gas Intel estimated that data centers will use 35GW of behind-the-meter power by 2030.
xAI contracted VoltaGrid to deliver power to its Memphis data center while it was waiting for a connection from the TVA.
This begs the question: should AI data centers rely entirely on their own power?
AI companies are turning to gas turbines to run their data centers without grid power.
So, even if the company fails to secure power from the grid, it can get the needed electricity from its own turbines.
While gas generators seem to be the silver bullet that will help solve the electricity supply puzzle many data centers face, it also comes with its own set of problems.
To achieve this, data centers cannot just purchase the generators that can deliver the load they need; they need to build in redundancy.
Elon Musk was the first to use gas turbine generators to power a data center at this scale and duration at xAI’s Memphis Supercluster.

This entails an extended power purchase agreement between the provider and the data center, wherein the former will deliver everything that the latter needs for their operation — from power capacity and day-to-day operations to maintenance and uptime reliability.

For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times.
With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said.

In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers.
Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s.

Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new.

Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power.
For decades, companies like GE Vernova and Siemens Energy have converted aviation engines for stationary power generation.

These “aeroderivative” turbines are lighter, smaller, and easier to maintain than their heavy-frame industrial counterparts, making them ideal for temporary or mobile power setups.At the Data Center World Power show in San Antonio this October, Missouri-based energy firm ProEnergy showcased how it modernizes this approach.
Normally, developers would connect directly to the grid or build dedicated on-site power plants, but the surge in demand has exposed a deep supply shortage.
Join investors, operators, and innovators reading to stay ahead of the latest trends in the data center sector in developed and emerging markets globally.
Chevron will build a power plant near Pecos, in West Texas, and sell all of its electricity directly to a Microsoft data center under a twenty-year agreement.

In the first quarter of 2026, GE Vernova’s electrification division, which makes transformers, switchgear, and the substations that connect large buildings to the grid, booked $2.4 billion of orders tied to data centers.

AI companies are turning to gas turbines to run their data centers without grid power. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg said in May 2024 that power will be one of the biggest factors that will constrain artificial intelligence , and, true enough, tech giants and hyperscalers have begun to hit power constraints. According to SemiAnalysis , electricity loads of tens of gigawatts have been requested in the state of Texas alone, but only a little over a gigawatt has received approval, signalling that the power grid may be stretched thin. However, this doesn’t mean that companies are ditching dreams of building massive AI data centers across the globe. Instead, they’re looking at alternative power sources to bring their projects online, regardless of the availability of power from the grid. This limitation has tech and power companies investing in small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) , which can potentially deliver large amounts of power in a relatively compact package. Microsoft has even recommissioned the old Three Mile Island nuclear power plant to deliver 819 MW of power for AI and cloud data center usage. These initiatives will take years to take off, though. The Three Mile Island plant is expected to be operational only by 2028, while the earliest SMRs won’t enter service until the 2030s. There has even been a proposal to use retired U.S. Navy reactors for data centers , but the project proponent hasn’t offered a timeline for how quickly it could potentially get up and running. Elon Musk was the first to use gas turbine generators to power a data center at this scale and duration at xAI’s Memphis Supercluster. In 2024, the AI startup signed a 50-MW deal with the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), which only became operational months after. Aside from the delay, this is nowhere near enough of the 155MW that the 100,000 H100 GPUs running on the site require. There was also a 150-MW substation under construction on the site, which also required additional setup. Waiting for these power sources to come online would have negated Musk’s historic 19-day setup of an AI data center , so he turned to VoltaGrid to deliver the power he needed to run the Colossus site. Just a few months later, OpenAI followed the billionaire’s lead and ordered 29 gas turbines capable of producing 34MW each for its Stargate data center in Abilene, Texas. All these turbines would output a total of 986MW of power, which should be enough to run up to half a million GB200 NVL72 chips. So, even if the company fails to secure power from the grid, it can get the needed electricity from its own turbines. Aside from these two, several other projects are going off-grid, with 62% of data centers considering on-site power generation, according to Data Center Knowledge . Furthermore, Natural Gas Intel estimated that data centers will use 35GW of behind-the-meter power by 2030. This technique is crucial for the U.S.’s AI infrastructure to stay ahead, which is especially true as experts warn that China is miles ahead when it comes to electricity generation . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang also reportedly commented that “China is going to win the AI race,” pointing directly toward power constraints as one of the reasons behind his statement. While gas generators seem to be the silver bullet that will help solve the electricity supply puzzle many data centers face, it also comes with its own set of problems. Uptime is the principal issue among them, since data centers require near constant uptime reliability. To achieve this, data centers cannot just purchase the generators that can deliver the load they need; they need to build in redundancy. AI data centers must have N+1 or N+1+1 redundancy to ensure continued operation, even if some fail. N+1 means that they must have a backup generator, which takes over should one fail during normal operations. Meanwhile, N+1+1 recommends having an additional power source on site as well as a backup, in case one of the generators in regular operation is in maintenance. As well as all of this, maintenance, spare parts, necessary personnel, and fuel also remain additional considerations. Despite these challenges, it’s estimated that AI data centers could generate $10 to $12 billion per gigawatt annually. Musk fired up the Colossus data center in July 2024 , while the 150MW substation only delivered power to the site in November 2024 . This meant that he could have made somewhere between $3 to $4 billion in revenue during that time, which likely would have offset the cost of running the entire site on natural gas turbines. Another issue that data centers face is permitting requirements, which can take as long as a year or more. The OpenAI/Oracle site at Abilene, Texas, is reportedly facing delays because of this. Musk’s Colossus 2 site mitigated the permit delay by building near the border of Tennessee and Mississippi , allowing him to hedge his bets by applying for permits from the two states and securing supply from both. Aside from that, communities around these data centers might complain about the power plants they’re putting up just to provide the power they need. xAI faced this exact issue , with residents complaining about the pollution generated by the gas turbines deployed around the Memphis site. Though investors could throw unlimited amounts of money at the problem, there's another factor they cannot escape — long equipment lead times. It takes about 12 to 36 months before any of the gas turbine manufacturers can deliver them, especially as these are intricate machines that use highly specialized materials and require specific processes to manufacture. These lead times could get longer, especially as more AI data centers are competing for the same amount of production capacity from these companies. xAI contracted VoltaGrid to deliver power to its Memphis data center while it was waiting for a connection from the TVA. But even as the utility company finally delivered the 150MW it needed, some turbine generators remained on site as a backup to the system. This begs the question: should AI data centers rely entirely on their own power? VoltaGrid and other firms seem to think so, even going as far as offering “energy-as-a-service,” or EaaS, to AI companies. This entails an extended power purchase agreement between the provider and the data center, wherein the former will deliver everything that the latter needs for their operation — from power capacity and day-to-day operations to maintenance and uptime reliability. However, even though this may be favorable in terms of deployment time, it will still get prohibitively expensive in the long run. At the moment, AI companies rent gas generators for bridge power, allowing them to get their data center operations up and running as soon as possible while waiting for approval from the local utility. But when they finally connect their site to the grid, it’s still often more economical to just keep these mobile generators as backup units in case their primary sources fail, not as their sole power source. EaaS could possibly work as a permanent solution when the national electric grid is maxed out. When there is no more extra capacity to be had for power-hungry AI infrastructure, AI companies might have no choice but to rely on services like this just to get their projects up and running. Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg said in May 2024 that power will be one of the biggest factors that will constrain artificial intelligence , and, true enough, tech giants and hyperscalers have begun to hit power constraints.

According to SemiAnalysis , electricity loads of tens of gigawatts have been requested in the state of Texas alone, but only a little over a gigawatt has received approval, signalling that the power grid may be stretched thin.
Aside from these two, several other projects are going off-grid, with 62% of data centers considering on-site power generation, according to Data Center Knowledge .
Furthermore, Natural Gas Intel estimated that data centers will use 35GW of behind-the-meter power by 2030.
xAI contracted VoltaGrid to deliver power to its Memphis data center while it was waiting for a connection from the TVA.
This begs the question: should AI data centers rely entirely on their own power?
AI companies are turning to gas turbines to run their data centers without grid power.
So, even if the company fails to secure power from the grid, it can get the needed electricity from its own turbines.
While gas generators seem to be the silver bullet that will help solve the electricity supply puzzle many data centers face, it also comes with its own set of problems.
To achieve this, data centers cannot just purchase the generators that can deliver the load they need; they need to build in redundancy.
Elon Musk was the first to use gas turbine generators to power a data center at this scale and duration at xAI’s Memphis Supercluster.

This entails an extended power purchase agreement between the provider and the data center, wherein the former will deliver everything that the latter needs for their operation — from power capacity and day-to-day operations to maintenance and uptime reliability.

extraction.body: Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday. The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout. For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said. Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week . In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s. Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets. In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April. In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines. Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity. Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two. sources.title: Data centers turn to old jet engines to power AI’s soaring energy demands
passages: Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new.

Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power.

Each refurbished unit can generate up to 48 megawatts (MW) of electricity, enough to power a small-to-medium data center or a town of 20,000 to 40,000 households.Landon Tessmer, Vice President of Commercial Operations at ProEnergy, told IEEE Spectrum that they have sold 21 gas turbines for two data-center projects, amounting to more than 1 gigawatt (GW).
For decades, companies like GE Vernova and Siemens Energy have converted aviation engines for stationary power generation.

These “aeroderivative” turbines are lighter, smaller, and easier to maintain than their heavy-frame industrial counterparts, making them ideal for temporary or mobile power setups.At the Data Center World Power show in San Antonio this October, Missouri-based energy firm ProEnergy showcased how it modernizes this approach.

He adds, “Both projects are expected to provide bridging power for five to seven years, which is when they expect to have grid interconnection and no longer need permanent behind-the-meter generation.”Bridging power for the AI infra boomThese modified engines are an essential bridging technology.
Normally, developers would connect directly to the grid or build dedicated on-site power plants, but the surge in demand has exposed a deep supply shortage.

extraction.body: As the world races to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, data centers are hitting a critical energy roadblock. Across the U.S. and beyond, old airplane engines are being repurposed into power generators, keeping the AI boom from stalling.Data centers are expanding faster than utilities, with megawatt-hungry facilities waiting years to access grid power. Normally, developers would connect directly to the grid or build dedicated on-site power plants, but the surge in demand has exposed a deep supply shortage. Lead times for new gas turbines from manufacturers like GE, Vernova, and Siemens Energy now stretch from three to five years, sometimes even longer.“There just aren’t enough gas turbines to go around, and the problem is probably going to get worse,” says Paul Browning, CEO of Generative Power Solutions and former head of GE Power & Water and Mitsubishi Power, in an IEEE Spectrum report. Wood Mackenzie notes that lead times for new gas turbines are extending past 2029, while the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) reports backlogs of up to eight years for new plants in regions like Southeast Asia.This mismatch between demand and availability has created a new and flourishing market for refurbishing retired aircraft engines into fully functional power generators, known as aeroderivative gas turbines.A second life for jet enginesThough the demand is growing, the concept is not new. For decades, companies like GE Vernova and Siemens Energy have converted aviation engines for stationary power generation. These “aeroderivative” turbines are lighter, smaller, and easier to maintain than their heavy-frame industrial counterparts, making them ideal for temporary or mobile power setups.At the Data Center World Power show in San Antonio this October, Missouri-based energy firm ProEnergy showcased how it modernizes this approach. The company buys and overhauls used CF6-80C2 engine cores used in GE’s LM6000 and refits them into natural gas turbines branded as PE6000 units. Each refurbished unit can generate up to 48 megawatts (MW) of electricity, enough to power a small-to-medium data center or a town of 20,000 to 40,000 households.Landon Tessmer, Vice President of Commercial Operations at ProEnergy, told IEEE Spectrum that they have sold 21 gas turbines for two data-center projects, amounting to more than 1 gigawatt (GW). He adds, “Both projects are expected to provide bridging power for five to seven years, which is when they expect to have grid interconnection and no longer need permanent behind-the-meter generation.”Bridging power for the AI infra boomThese modified engines are an essential bridging technology. A stopgap between the construction of large-scale data centers and their eventual grid connection. According to Tessmer, some facilities use ProEnergy’s turbines to power construction activities and initial operations, after which the units are moved into backup roles or sold to local utilities.Beyond faster delivery times, ProEnergy can supply a unit as early as 2027. Their emissions, averaging 2.5 parts per million of nitrogen oxide, are well below Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) thresholds, typically ranging from 10 to 25 ppm.Each engine undergoes a painstaking overhaul, where thousands of components are disassembled, cleaned, inspected, and repaired or replaced. Originally aimed at helping utilities meet peak power demands, the technology has found a new and booming market in data centers. Tessmer has even seen permitting delays for new grid connections stretch to eight or even ten years in some cases.With AI infrastructure scaling at an unprecedented rate, these repurposed engines, once symbols of aviation’s golden age, quietly keep the digital world alive on the ground. As the global turbine shortage deepens, their second act as power generators may prove vital in sustaining the momentum of the AI revolution.

extraction.body: Welcome to Global Data Center Hub . Join investors, operators, and innovators reading to stay ahead of the latest trends in the data center sector in developed and emerging markets globally. Large power transformers, the equipment that converts the very high voltage carried by long-distance power lines into a voltage a building can actually use, now average 128 weeks from order to delivery , according to a Wood Mackenzie survey of utility and developer orders. The largest units, which connect power plants to the grid, average 144 weeks. A data center building takes roughly two years to construct. Developers now order power equipment years before a project has a customer or a final go-ahead. Chevron ordered seven large gas turbines from GE Vernova, the power equipment company spun out of General Electric in 2024, roughly two years before signing the twenty-year electricity agreement with Microsoft that those turbines will serve. The published order books of power equipment makers show whether an announced AI buildout is real. GE Vernova reported $2.4 billion of data center electrical equipment orders in the first quarter of 2026, more than the company booked in all of 2025, and those figures are filed with regulators every quarter while project announcements carry no such requirement. Somewhere near your house there is a grey drum on a wooden pole, or a green metal cabinet sitting on a concrete pad at the end of the street. That is a transformer. It takes the very high voltage that travels down long-distance power lines and turns it into the much lower voltage your kitchen can handle. Every building on earth has one of these standing between it and the grid. In June 2026, Chevron announced a deal with Microsoft. Chevron will build a power plant near Pecos, in West Texas, and sell all of its electricity directly to a Microsoft data center under a twenty-year agreement. The plant is designed for roughly 2.67 gigawatts, which is about the electricity used by two million American homes. First power is expected in 2028. Read as a headline, that is a story about an oil company walking into the AI business. A gas turbine is essentially a truck-sized jet engine that burns natural gas to spin a generator. Chevron ordered seven large ones from GE Vernova, the power equipment company spun out of General Electric in 2024. It placed that order before it had a signed customer, before its own board had given the project a final approval, and before the design was settled. The plant burns natural gas, and Microsoft has a standing pledge to remove more carbon from the atmosphere than it emits by 2030, a target this makes harder to reach. Chevron has said the plant will run separately from the regional grid so that local households are not competing with it for power. If you read that announcement as an oil company discovering technology, you missed the part that decided it, which is that the winner was whoever had joined the queue earliest. Here is the number that reorganizes everything. Wood Mackenzie, an energy research firm, surveyed actual utility and developer orders and found that standard large power transformers average 128 weeks between order and delivery. That is close to two and a half years. The largest units, the ones that connect a power plant to the grid, average 144 weeks. A large power transformer needs a specialized electrical steel that only a few mills in the world produce, plus copper, plus custom engineering, plus months of testing before it ships. Adding factory capacity takes years, because a transformer plant is itself a heavy industrial building. And three separate waves of demand arrived at those same factories at once. Data centers need them. Older grid equipment installed decades ago needs replacing. Factories and vehicle fleets switching from fuel to electricity need them too. None of those three has any reason to slow down for the others. The obvious response to a shortage is to build more factories, and that is happening. In South Boston, Virginia, Hitachi Energy has made transformers since 1968. In 2026, it began a $457 million expansion to make the site the largest power transformer factory in the U.S. The project adds around 825 jobs to a workforce of about 850, close to doubling the place. Relief may not arrive until the end of the decade. Virginia is a fitting place for it. Northern Virginia holds the largest concentration of data centers on earth. Data centers already account for roughly a quarter of the electricity sold by the state’s main utility. In the first quarter of 2026, GE Vernova’s electrification division, which makes transformers, switchgear, and the substations that connect large buildings to the grid, booked $2.4 billion of orders tied to data centers. That was more than the division booked from data centers in the whole of 2025. Total orders across the company reached $18.3 billion for the quarter, up 71 percent on the year before, and its order backlog, meaning work sold but not yet delivered, stood at $163 billion. Those numbers say something that a press release cannot. Somebody signed for the equipment, and somebody is paying for it. In a statement published by North Korean state media, Kim Yo Jong , the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, denied the country was responsible for carrying out last week's hack, thought to be the largest financial heist in history.
Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency was hacked from exchange company Binance, but who was behind the attack?
Ms Kim also warned the country had "issues to reconsider" over US hostility.

"The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," she said in the statement.
"But the US assertion is absurd rhetoric and nothing new.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds."
On Saturday, the FBI accused a North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor of carrying out the hack and stealing billions in crypto.
The FBI says North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor is behind the heist. ( Pexels: Tibe De Kort )
The US bureau said it had observed TraderTraitor converting stolen assets into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum and expected it to launder the assets further.

"The FBI maintains its commitment to protecting the virtual asset community by identifying, mitigating, and disrupting North Korea's illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities," a statement read.
Cybersecurity experts said North Korean hackers were among the world's most prolific crypto thieves, with the proceeds used to help fund the country's weapons programs.
North Korea has denied all allegations of its links to cryptocurrency theft and other cybercrimes.
Ms Kim said North Korea would reconsider unspecified issues in light of the "very unpleasant US hostile attitude".
It comes as Pyongyang remains silent on US President Donald Trump's offers to resume US-North Korea summit diplomacy.
Experts have indicated Pyongyang may be weighing its options.
Binance customers withdrew about $US4.64 billion ($6.6 billion) worth of assets after the company lifted its temporary suspension on Sunday.
Zhao Changpeng is the founder and CEO of Binance, which has moved to reassure its users following the hack. ( Reuters: Benoit Tessier )

"Between 06:00 and 15:30 UTC on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion," the company said on X.
"Our team continues testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets.
"Rest assured that market conditions are stable."
The company said it had recovered 90 per cent of the stolen assets by using company money.

North Korea has denied US allegations that it was behind the $US6.3 billion ($9 billion) heist of cryptocurrency exchange platform Binance as "absurd rhetoric" and proof that Washington remained hostile towards the country. In a statement published by North Korean state media, Kim Yo Jong , the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, denied the country was responsible for carrying out last week's hack, thought to be the largest financial heist in history. Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency was hacked from exchange company Binance, but who was behind the attack? Ms Kim also warned the country had "issues to reconsider" over US hostility. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," she said in the statement. "But the US assertion is absurd rhetoric and nothing new. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds." On Saturday, the FBI accused a North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor of carrying out the hack and stealing billions in crypto. The FBI says North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor is behind the heist. ( Pexels: Tibe De Kort ) The US bureau said it had observed TraderTraitor converting stolen assets into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum and expected it to launder the assets further. Markets Binance says customers pulled net $4.7 billion after hack as crypto world weighs risk North Korea is blamed for the $6.3 billion Binance hack, raising significant security concerns for the crypto market and institutional investors Published November 2, 2026 Updated November 2, 2026 05:10pm Save Saved 5 min Comments Photo: Reuters By Reuters Binance’s customers have withdrawn almost $5 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened after a hack that saw $6.3 billion of crypto stolen from the platform in what could be the largest financial heist in history.
Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, also sought to reassure customers.
The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
“After an initial spike, withdrawal volumes have declined and are stabilising,” Binance said on X.
A spokesperson said there had been $2.7 billion in inflows.
Binance said the net outflow amounted to about 2.8% of assets on the platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
Binance to resume withdrawals after recovering bulk of $6 billion in stolen funds
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
“Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds and Binance can resume operations,” Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X on Monday.

“I would not necessarily withdraw everything from Binance, because centralised exchanges continue to play an important role in liquidity, trading and market access,” said Jay Koh, vice president of the Asia Web3 AI Association, a blockchain advocacy group based in Singapore.

extraction.body: Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop. Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months. This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance's systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world's largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network. The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer's work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware. That foothold in Binance's network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer's laptop, the hackers used the engineer's stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto. Binance said the attack "should not have happened," and that it had improved its network security following the theft. The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime's repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems. These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters. By Binance's own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the "persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry." But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance's own network, will likely be the focus of investigators' attention. While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it's ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise. A Binance spokesperson referred to the company's public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch's questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees' laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance's network prior to the hack. The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident. The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history. Updated to remove name of Binance spokesperson in thirteenth paragraph.

extraction.body: Binance prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats during 2026, but a fraudulent recruitment scam still helped attackers steal USD 6.34 billion in cryptocurrency on October 29. The exchange's November 3 security report details how compromised developer computers and stolen permissions enabled the breach..Security Defenses Missed Recruitment Scam.Binance stated that its security team intercepted 57 suspected North Korean operations involving malicious software, fake interviews, and credential theft. Yi He, Binance's co-CEO, acknowledged the failure: “We intercepted many of them, but the cost of failing to stop even one was severe and this should never have happened.”The exchange has not specified how many blocked attempts involved recruitment fraud or whether they originated from the attackers responsible for October's theft..Attack Started with Compromised Software.In June, a wallet infrastructure engineer downloaded a modified Homebrew installer while installing an AI coding tool. Binance detected the intrusion, replaced the computer and reset credentials, but attackers obtained information about employee responsibilities.In September, another engineer encountered a supposed recruiter on an employment platform. After video interviews with individuals impersonating company executives, the employee downloaded a coding assignment containing malware.Binance said that the malicious repository bypassed endpoint protection and connected the computer to attacker-controlled infrastructure..Stolen Credentials Enabled October Theft.By October 20, attackers had exploited the infected computer and an internal AI tool to access two engineers' systems. extraction.body: Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop. Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months. This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance's systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world's largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network. The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer's work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware. That foothold in Binance's network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer's laptop, the hackers used the engineer's stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto. Binance said the attack "should not have happened," and that it had improved its network security following the theft. The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime's repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems. These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters. By Binance's own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the "persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry." But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance's own network, will likely be the focus of investigators' attention. While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it's ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise. A Binance spokesperson referred to the company's public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch's questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees' laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance's network prior to the hack. The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident. The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history. Updated to remove name of Binance spokesperson in thirteenth paragraph.

extraction.body: Connecting decision makers to a dynamic network of information, people and ideas, Bloomberg quickly and accurately delivers business and financial information, news and insight around the world Connecting decision makers to a dynamic network of information, people and ideas, Bloomberg quickly and accurately delivers business and financial information, news and insight around the world A New York judge likely will soon have to tackle some of the thorniest questions for regulators trying to police the cryptocurrency market. Richard Heart, who founded and marketed the crypto token Hex, is accused by the Securities and Exchange Commission of selling unregistered securities and illegally using investor funds to buy luxury goods, including a $1.38 million Rolex watch and a 555-carat black diamond known as “The Enigma.” Heart is asking a federal judge to dismiss the SEC’s case. The case is a test of law enforcement’s reach in policing borderless crypto transactions. It also underscores questions about liability and who—or what—can be named as defendants as the US government cracks down on decentralized finance platforms, and as currencies such as Bitcoin have once again surged in trading. The SEC has appointed itself the “global governor of blockchain technology,” lawyers for Heart, who lives in Finland, said in an April court filing . The SEC’s response is due in the coming weeks. Crypto users, including tens of thousands who have come to Heart’s defense, are raising concerns about the SEC naming Hex and a blockchain protocol as defendants in the suit, and the implications it could have down the road. In a filing last month, they argued those are technological innovations that can’t be sued. Legal scholars agree the SEC’s approach appears new. “This is a case of technology moving faster than the law,” said Michele Neitz, a professor at the University of San Francisco School of Law and the founder of the Blockchain Law for Social Good Center. Financial regulators have increasingly set their sights on decentralized finance, or DeFi. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought enforcement actions in September against three DeFi firms and signaled more may be coming. The SEC is also investigating Uniswap, the creator of the largest DeFi trading platform on Ethereum, for securities law violations. The nature of the technology poses tricky questions for regulators. The SEC alleges Hex, which trades at a fraction of 1 cent, is both a security and an entity. Heart and crypto users dispute both interpretations. “So much of it is the fact that it could be a security, it could be a currency, and then it could be an entity, that makes it confusing and hard to get your arms around,” said Carliss Chatman, a Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law professor who teaches business and commercial law. The SEC has also named as defendants, along with Heart and Hex, the PulseChain blockchain network and PulseX, a decentralized finance platform. The SEC alleges Hex and the other software are “unincorporated alter-ego entities” of Heart. Suing computer software is “bizarre,” and the SEC’s legal theories are “novel and unsupported,” PulseChain users said in a filing last month. “You can’t sue the sidewalk, or a piece of software,” users said in the brief , authored by Jenner & Block LLP partner Kayvan Sadeghi and Nick Morgan, a former SEC attorney and founder of the Investor Choice Advocates Network. The SEC’s reasons for including the token and network as defendants are unclear. But users fear it’s an attempt to effectively shut down PulseChain and Hex, which have amassed a significant following. Some blockchain attorneys say the agency’s approach could open the door to developers being held liable for the computer software they write. The SEC’s investigation of Uniswap has triggered similar concerns. Allowing the SEC to proceed with the case would create a “cloud of uncertainty about what conduct may or may not ultimately be deemed to violate the federal securities laws (and what inanimate technology might somehow be deemed liable for any violation),” the users’ brief said. The SEC isn’t the first regulator to advance what critics have called novel, and concerning, arguments in this area. The CFTC in 2022 won a ruling that a so-called decentralized autonomous organization, the Ooki DAO, could be sued as an unincorporated association. DAOs are blockchain-based groups controlled by their members. The CFTC had served the DAO with notice of the suit by posting a copy of the complaint in an online chat box and help forum, which various crypto groups argued was improper. In another case, a judge allowed crypto users to sue a related DAO as a general partnership. The ruling put thousands of members of the group at risk of being held personally responsible in the suit, which the parties later settled. These types of cases underscore lingering uncertainties about how the new technologies fit into traditional legal concepts, and the extent of potential legal risk for DeFi participants, attorneys say. “I think people starting crypto and DeFi were hoping that you’d have even greater protection because there’d be no entity at all,” said Stephen Rutenberg of Polsinelli PC, who focuses on cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. “But the nightmare scenario,” Rutenberg said, “is you lose even the corporate protection and you become basically a partnership where everyone is responsible for everything.” Another question in the case is whether Heart can be sued in the US. The SEC’s lawsuit against Heart, filed last summer, was brought in the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York. The SEC alleges Heart raised more than $1 billion by selling unregistered securities. He is accused of using at least $12.1 million of investor funds for personal luxury purchases. Making his own pitch for dismissal, Heart said the court doesn’t have jurisdiction to hear the case. The SEC didn’t allege he has US offices or bank accounts or that he visited the US. Rather, the complaint points to an undetermined number of US users, as well as YouTube videos and other social media posts. “When do US courts have the ability to hear disputes involving these kinds of borderless transactions?” said Jonathan Schmalfeld, a Polsinelli attorney focused on blockchain and other technologies. “Or in this case, would the more appropriate court, whether it’s a government agency or private individuals or anybody else, be Helsinki?” Additionally, Heart said there weren’t the kinds of US securities transactions that would give the SEC authority. The SEC’s complaint merely points to an “unidentified resident of Brooklyn” and other unspecified US investors as having sent crypto assets to a blockchain address associated with PulseChain, Heart said. Citing one anonymous person in Brooklyn sending funds “is pretty stark in comparison to how usually you would analyze whether the SEC has jurisdiction over a securities matter,” Schmalfeld said. The case is Securities and Exchange Commission v. Schueler , E.D.N.Y., No. 23-cv-05749. Bloomberg Law provides trusted coverage of current events enhanced with legal analysis.

Crypto users, including tens of thousands who have come to Heart’s defense, are raising concerns about the SEC naming Hex and a blockchain protocol as defendants in the suit, and the implications it could have down the road. In a filing last month, they argued those are technological innovations that can’t be sued.
Legal scholars agree the SEC’s approach appears new.

“This is a case of technology moving faster than the law,” said Michele Neitz, a professor at the University of San Francisco School of Law and the founder of the Blockchain Law for Social Good Center.
Financial regulators have increasingly set their sights on decentralized finance, or DeFi.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought enforcement actions in September against three DeFi firms and signaled more may be coming. The SEC is also investigating Uniswap, the creator of the largest DeFi trading platform on Ethereum, for securities law violations.

The nature of the technology poses tricky questions for regulators. The SEC alleges Hex, which trades at a fraction of 1 cent, is both a security and an entity. Heart and crypto users dispute both interpretations.

“So much of it is the fact that it could be a security, it could be a currency, and then it could be an entity, that makes it confusing and hard to get your arms around,” said Carliss Chatman, a Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law professor who teaches business and commercial law.

The SEC has also named as defendants, along with Heart and Hex, the PulseChain blockchain network and PulseX, a decentralized finance platform. The SEC alleges Hex and the other software are “unincorporated alter-ego entities” of Heart.
Suing computer software is “bizarre,” and the SEC’s legal theories are “novel and unsupported,” PulseChain users said in a filing last month.

“You can’t sue the sidewalk, or a piece of software,” users said in the brief , authored by Jenner & Block LLP partner Kayvan Sadeghi and Nick Morgan, a former SEC attorney and founder of the Investor Choice Advocates Network.

The SEC’s reasons for including the token and network as defendants are unclear. But users fear it’s an attempt to effectively shut down PulseChain and Hex, which have amassed a significant following.

Some blockchain attorneys say the agency’s approach could open the door to developers being held liable for the computer software they write. The SEC’s investigation of Uniswap has triggered similar concerns.

Allowing the SEC to proceed with the case would create a “cloud of uncertainty about what conduct may or may not ultimately be deemed to violate the federal securities laws (and what inanimate technology might somehow be deemed liable for any violation),” the users’ brief said.
The SEC isn’t the first regulator to advance what critics have called novel, and concerning, arguments in this area.

The CFTC in 2022 won a ruling that a so-called decentralized autonomous organization, the Ooki DAO, could be sued as an unincorporated association. DAOs are blockchain-based groups controlled by their members.
The CFTC had served the DAO with notice of the suit by posting a copy of the complaint in an online chat box and help forum, which various crypto groups argued was improper.

In another case, a judge allowed crypto users to sue a related DAO as a general partnership. The ruling put thousands of members of the group at risk of being held personally responsible in the suit, which the parties later settled.

These types of cases underscore lingering uncertainties about how the new technologies fit into traditional legal concepts, and the extent of potential legal risk for DeFi participants, attorneys say.

“I think people starting crypto and DeFi were hoping that you’d have even greater protection because there’d be no entity at all,” said Stephen Rutenberg of Polsinelli PC, who focuses on cryptocurrency and blockchain technology.
“But the nightmare scenario,” Rutenberg said, “is you lose even the corporate protection and you become basically a partnership where everyone is responsible for everything.”
Another question in the case is whether Heart can be sued in the US.

The SEC’s lawsuit against Heart, filed last summer, was brought in the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York. The SEC alleges Heart raised more than $1 billion by selling unregistered securities. He is accused of using at least $12.1 million of investor funds for personal luxury purchases.
Making his own pitch for dismissal, Heart said the court doesn’t have jurisdiction to hear the case.

The SEC didn’t allege he has US offices or bank accounts or that he visited the US. Rather, the complaint points to an undetermined number of US users, as well as YouTube videos and other social media posts.

“When do US courts have the ability to hear disputes involving these kinds of borderless transactions?” said Jonathan Schmalfeld, a Polsinelli attorney focused on blockchain and other technologies. “Or in this case, would the more appropriate court, whether it’s a government agency or private individuals or anybody else, be Helsinki?”
Additionally, Heart said there weren’t the kinds of US securities transactions that would give the SEC authority.

The SEC’s complaint merely points to an “unidentified resident of Brooklyn” and other unspecified US investors as having sent crypto assets to a blockchain address associated with PulseChain, Heart said.
Citing one anonymous person in Brooklyn sending funds “is pretty stark in comparison to how usually you would analyze whether the SEC has jurisdiction over a securities matter,” Schmalfeld said.
The case is Securities and Exchange Commission v. Schueler , E.D.N.Y., No. 23-cv-05749.

sources.title: Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade - CNBC
passages: Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022.
Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout , protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.
The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade.

The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets.
Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus.

On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
"Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds?

For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC.
"Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage."
Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence.
Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019.
BitGo Holdings , founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions.
"Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk.

Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.

Here the question is different: who gains when the market decides that guarding keys is harder, and more valuable, than moving coins? Binance experienced a security incident on October 29, 2026, involving unauthorized withdrawals from hot wallets. The exchange put the value of the affected assets at roughly $6.3 billion. The attack touched wallets on 10 blockchain networks, according to reporting that cites Binance’s own investigation. That spread matters, and we return to it below. On November 3, Teng told CNBC that Binance had replenished 98% of the $6.34 billion in affected assets. One day later, in its November 4 update, Binance said about $2.85 billion in digital assets had been frozen or intercepted. The exchange added that the figure remained subject to reconciliation and to swings in market prices. Those two numbers answer different questions, and mixing them up is the most common error in coverage so far. Four items stay unconfirmed. First, the claim that this is the largest theft in digital-asset history. Outlets have used that framing, but no audited ledger backs it. Second, the link to North Korea, which has circulated in reports but lacks independent confirmation in the material we reviewed. Third, the $4.7 billion in net customer withdrawals reported after withdrawals resumed. Fourth, the $6.3 billion loss estimate and the $3 billion frozen estimate, which are unaudited disclosures. Two gaps stand out. The 98% and 95% replenishment figures sit three points apart, which on a $6.34 billion base equals roughly $190 million. And the $2.85 billion frozen figure sits about $150 million below the $3 billion estimate CNBC used. Neither gap looks alarming alone. Together they show that the recovery story is still being written. TRM Labs said the attackers compromised Binance’s signing infrastructure, the machinery that authorizes transactions. That finding explains why the damage crossed so many chains at once. A flaw in one smart contract would hit one network. A compromise of the system that produces valid signatures hits every network the exchange touches. Binance’s initial investigation pointed to a different starting point. It indicated an attacker may have compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop and then reached a service container used to submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. We covered that path in our earlier piece on the reported attack chain behind the $6.3 billion loss . The two accounts fit together. A laptop is the door, the service container is the hallway, and the signing layer is the vault. The Financial Express summarized the speed in its headline, saying the exchange lost about $6 billion in 20 minutes. Speed is the point for custody design. A control that needs a human to notice, decide and act cannot beat a sweep that finishes in the time of a coffee break. Controls have to fire automatically, and they have to live outside any system an attacker already holds. CNBC framed the breach as a turning point for how investors value crypto companies. Much of crypto’s progress this year, the outlet noted, has come from firms moving beyond reliance on trading volume and fees toward infrastructure that links digital assets to traditional finance. The Binance incident adds cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience to that list of things investors now price. CNBC also drew a line between this event and the FTX collapse of late 2022. The Binance breach, it argued, was neither an indictment of crypto itself nor a case of leadership-driven fraud. Management moved to contain the fallout and committed company resources to cover losses. That distinction explains why the story reads as an infrastructure trade and not a panic. The thesis runs like this. Winners in the next phase may not be the firms with the most users, the biggest volume or the most assets under custody. They may be the firms that can prove they protect assets under extreme duress. CNBC also cited Morgan Stanley in pointing to the separation of custody from execution as the more consequential structural shift, and it noted that the stress could drive consolidation as companies buy capabilities and chase scale. BusinessDay in Nigeria reached a similar reading from a different market. Its coverage said the breach exposes vulnerabilities in crypto custody , which suggests the message is travelling well beyond US trading desks. For emerging markets that lean heavily on exchanges as the entry point to crypto, the lesson lands harder, because few local alternatives exist. My read is that the market is repricing one specific risk: the operational path between a key and a transaction. Holding assets used to mean guarding private keys. After October 29, it means guarding the software, the people and the approval policies that decide when a key may sign. The industry response showed how much of crypto’s safety net sits with a few centralized actors. Tether, Circle, Ripple and other entities moved to freeze or restrict access to roughly $3 billion in stolen assets, according to CNBC. Reports put Tether’s share at nearly $1.57 billion and Circle’s at more than $800 million. Those two firms alone account for about $2.37 billion, which is close to 80% of the $3 billion estimate. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance. Binance said it worked with crypto custodian BitGo to freeze some of the stolen funds. Both details matter for the custody trade, because they show custody firms acting as active defenders in an incident, not merely as vaults waiting for deposits. Names also spread quickly on social media during the first days. We tracked which companies were said to be exposed and found that, as of our earlier reporting, three firms were named but none was confirmed hit . That caution still applies. Coinbase, Circle and BitGo appear in this story as responders, not victims. Customer behavior adds another layer. Reports cited net withdrawals of $4.7 billion after withdrawals resumed, a figure we label unconfirmed. Our earlier look at the reported outflows explains why that number needs care. If the figure holds up, it would show that customers hedge by moving assets to places they trust more, which feeds directly into the custody story. We searched for hard evidence of a price reaction in listed custody and infrastructure names and found none we could verify. No reliable, specific equity move for Coinbase, BitGo or similar firms surfaced in the material we reviewed, so this article does not offer one. Any outlet that quotes a precise percentage should show its source and time stamp. What the record does show is a change in argument. CNBC’s piece says the breach could place a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to hold and protect digital assets. It lists several firms with custody operations, including Coinbase, Circle, Ripple and BitGo, and it says smaller players face a tougher time funding cybersecurity and compliance. It also suggests demand could rise for specialized custodians with established asset-protection track records. The ratings are our qualitative analysis, not published scores. Binance’s case sits in the first row. Hot wallets exist to be fast, which means the signing path stays online and reachable. TRM Labs’ finding that the signing infrastructure itself fell shows why the weak point was the path and not a single key. Issuant also contrasts the survivors with Japan’s DMM Bitcoin, which lost about $305 million and did not recover the same way. The lesson it draws is that the deciding variable is rarely the attacker’s sophistication. It is the balance sheet and the architecture standing behind the assets. A firm that can absorb a loss of this size survives. A thinner one can fail from a much smaller hit. Industry data adds scale. Issuant cites Chainalysis figures saying private key compromises caused 43.8% of stolen crypto in 2024, and that total theft reached $3.4 billion in 2025. Set against that, one October 2026 event at $6.3 billion would exceed the entire 2025 total by roughly 85%. We present that comparison as arithmetic on reported figures, since the Binance number itself remains unaudited. FTX is the other reference point. That 2022 collapse involved leadership conduct. The Binance event, as CNBC stressed, did not. For custody buyers, the difference is large: fraud is a governance question, while a signing-layer breach is an engineering question that better controls can narrow. Public statements since the incident have been short. We reproduce the ones below word for word from our verified quote file and attach the source for each. Changpeng Zhao, the Binance founder, told Yahoo Finance: “There’s no 100% security.” The remark, published in a Yahoo Finance interview , sets the tone for the custody debate. If perfect protection is impossible, the buying question shifts from who is safe to who limits damage and recovers fastest. In the same interview, Zhao said: “When you run a platform, especially a crypto platform, the possibility is always there.” That framing treats breach risk as a permanent operating cost. It echoes the argument for layered custody, where no single failure empties the vault. Zhao also told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi: “AI is just making hacking so much easier now.” The comment, relayed by 24/7 Wall St., points to a trend defenders should plan for. We have no verified evidence about how AI figured in this specific attack, so we read the remark as Zhao’s view of the threat environment and not as a finding about the incident. Binance’s initial investigation pointed at a DevOps engineer’s laptop. Engineers with production access are high-value targets, so their devices need the same scrutiny as servers. Limit standing access, isolate build and deploy tooling from finance systems and review who can reach service containers that touch wallets. The $2.85 billion that Binance reported frozen or intercepted came from fast coordination with issuers, custodians and other exchanges. Firms that already have named contacts at stablecoin issuers and custody providers act in minutes. Firms that start a call list mid-incident lose the window. Write the playbook, test it and keep the contacts current. Regulators will watch the same points. Our report on security coverage across ransomware, breaches and compliance shows how often the same operational gaps recur across sectors, from crypto to retail systems. Custody is one more place where basic controls decide the outcome. Binance reported a security incident on October 29, 2026, involving unauthorized withdrawals from hot wallets. The affected assets were valued at about $6.3 billion across 10 blockchain networks, according to reporting that cites Binance’s investigation.

The breach did not break one custody model. It stressed the weakest link in each. The table compares the five models people use most, with the failure point the Binance incident puts in focus. The ratings are our qualitative analysis, not published scores.

Binance’s case sits in the first row. Hot wallets exist to be fast, which means the signing path stays online and reachable. TRM Labs’ finding that the signing infrastructure itself fell shows why the weak point was the path and not a single key.

Issuant also contrasts the survivors with Japan’s DMM Bitcoin, which lost about $305 million and did not recover the same way. The lesson it draws is that the deciding variable is rarely the attacker’s sophistication. It is the balance sheet and the architecture standing behind the assets. A firm that can absorb a loss of this size survives. A thinner one can fail from a much smaller hit.

Industry data adds scale. Issuant cites Chainalysis figures saying private key compromises caused 43.8% of stolen crypto in 2024, and that total theft reached $3.4 billion in 2025. Set against that, one October 2026 event at $6.3 billion would exceed the entire 2025 total by roughly 85%. We present that comparison as arithmetic on reported figures, since the Binance number itself remains unaudited.

FTX is the other reference point. That 2022 collapse involved leadership conduct. The Binance event, as CNBC stressed, did not. For custody buyers, the difference is large: fraud is a governance question, while a signing-layer breach is an engineering question that better controls can narrow.
Public statements since the incident have been short. We reproduce the ones below word for word from our verified quote file and attach the source for each.

Changpeng Zhao, the Binance founder, told Yahoo Finance: “There’s no 100% security.” The remark, published in a Yahoo Finance interview , sets the tone for the custody debate. If perfect protection is impossible, the buying question shifts from who is safe to who limits damage and recovers fastest.

In the same interview, Zhao said: “When you run a platform, especially a crypto platform, the possibility is always there.” That framing treats breach risk as a permanent operating cost. It echoes the argument for layered custody, where no single failure empties the vault.

Zhao also told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi: “AI is just making hacking so much easier now.” The comment, relayed by 24/7 Wall St., points to a trend defenders should plan for. We have no verified evidence about how AI figured in this specific attack, so we read the remark as Zhao’s view of the threat environment and not as a finding about the incident.

Binance’s initial investigation pointed at a DevOps engineer’s laptop. Engineers with production access are high-value targets, so their devices need the same scrutiny as servers. Limit standing access, isolate build and deploy tooling from finance systems and review who can reach service containers that touch wallets.

The $2.85 billion that Binance reported frozen or intercepted came from fast coordination with issuers, custodians and other exchanges. Firms that already have named contacts at stablecoin issuers and custody providers act in minutes. Firms that start a call list mid-incident lose the window. Write the playbook, test it and keep the contacts current.

Regulators will watch the same points. Our report on security coverage across ransomware, breaches and compliance shows how often the same operational gaps recur across sectors, from crypto to retail systems. Custody is one more place where basic controls decide the outcome.
