extraction.body: Search queries are growing at their fastest rate in five years, Google parent Alphabet said in its earnings report last week. However, Google’s Search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent year over year in the third quarter, down from roughly 17 percent in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, growth in paid clicks — clicks on ads that generate revenue for Google — slowed from 13 percent to 8 percent. That’s still substantial growth, but not the direction investors were hoping for from a company planning to spend about $200 billion this year on infrastructure, largely to support AI. Alphabet shares have fallen about 14 percent since it reported earnings last week, as investors question the costs and returns of the company’s AI ambitions. Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said currency effects were the biggest driver of the revenue-growth slowdown, alongside changes in spending by advertisers in particular industries. But Google’s AI makeover also contributed to the slowdown: AI Mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at a lower rate than traditional searches, Schindler says. He added that Google feels good about its trajectory and that its “ad experiments have shown promising results.” It remains unclear whether that reflects a deliberate rollout of ads, as Google says, or a more fundamental problem with advertising in AI search. YOY growth for search revenue vs. paid clicks in Q1-3 in 2026 “This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades,” Nate Elliott, an eMarketer principal analyst covering AI and advertising, tells The Verge. AI is changing how people find information — and whether they click on the ads that fund Google’s business. What Google’s core Search business looks like increasingly depends on what you ask. In many cases, AI Overviews add generated summaries to search results; electing AI Mode turns searching into a conversation. But someone searching for Nikes can still get familiar shopping listings and text ads, says Andy Taylor, vice president of research at digital advertising agency Tinuiti. Google’s argument is that AI is expanding the business. Schindler says most AI Mode queries are “incremental” — additional questions rather than replacements for existing searches. Many are also “upper-funnel,” meaning people are researching potential purchases before they know what they want. The company sees those searches as opportunities to sell more ads over time. Google is currently expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode, including internationally and across multiple turns of US AI Mode conversations. It has also floated bringing ads to its standalone Gemini app, saying formats developed for AI Mode could carry over, but hasn’t announced when. The thing is, Google, as well as competitors like OpenAI, are still figuring out how to make ads work in AI — both delivering results for advertisers and avoiding alienating the people using their AI tools. For now, advertisers are still getting results from Google. Tinuiti’s same-store advertisers increased their Google paid search spending 14 percent year over year in the third quarter while maintaining their return-on-ad-spend targets. “We’re still seeing a good return, and we’re not seeing performance take a hit,” Taylor says. The catch is that advertisers can’t isolate how Google’s AI ads are doing. Google doesn’t let them separately target that inventory or break out its performance, Taylor says. Steady overall returns could mean AI ad traffic is still too small to noticeably affect the results, or that it performs similarly to existing inventory. That leaves an important question unanswered: How much will AI add to Google’s advertising business, and how much could it replace? Additional queries could bring in new revenue even if each earns less than a traditional search. The risk is that AI Mode also draws people away from searches that Google monetizes more effectively. Google’s claim that most AI Mode queries are additional doesn’t tell us how much revenue it could lose from the searches AI Mode replaces. “If people are clicking through less often,” Elliott says, “that is a challenge that they need to figure out.” The promise of conversational advertising is that people share much more about their needs than they would in a few keywords. “It’s not a slam dunk that it’s going to turn into more effective advertising,” Elliott says. An early study of ChatGPT ads suggests richer conversations don’t automatically translate into more retail sales. An October working paper found that US visits from ChatGPT ads generated 64 percent less revenue for retailers per session than visits from Google Search ads: $0.89 versus $2.45. The working paper measures retailers’ sales rather than platform revenue, and its findings about ChatGPT don’t establish how Google’s own AI ads perform. Taylor cautions that those comparisons depend on what people are searching for.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling Alphabet's Q2 report puts precise numbers on the overall Search business while Google's claims about clicks to the web stay round and aggregate. Here's what that gap looks like. Alphabet shared its Q2 earnings this week, showing that Google Search & Other revenue increased by 17% year over year to reach $63.27 billion. For all the details, check out our earnings brief , including how the growth rate has slowed from 19% in Q1, marking the first slowdown after four quarters of accelerating growth. The numbers also leave out part of the story. Alphabet provides a detailed breakdown of Search business earnings in its securities filing, while Google describes what the web gets back in broad assurances. Both perspectives are now part of every quarter, and the distance between them is the story. The revenue aspect of Search offers everything you’d hope for from a data source. Alphabet provided clear numbers, comparisons year-over-year, and consistent definitions across quarters, making it straightforward to follow the progress. The trajectory is checkable: Search & Other growth went from 10% in Q1 2025 to 12%, then 15%, 17%, and reaching 19% in Q1 2026 , before easing back to 17% this quarter. In its earnings release, CEO Sundar Pichai connected these results to AI, saying the company’s “popular AI features are driving Search query growth.” Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler pointed out strengths across different industries, with retail leading the way, followed by finance, technology, media, and entertainment, and credited the Gemini integration within Google’s advertising systems. However, Google didn’t specify the exact contribution of each vertical. The spending side got the same precise treatment. Roger Montti covered this , including the capital expenditures that led to negative free cash flow for the quarter. That said, none of this detailed financial data addresses the most important question for businesses: the number of clicks to websites. Neither the Q4 2025 nor Q1 2026 reports we covered offered this information. Google’s broader claims about outbound traffic come from other sources like blog posts, interviews, and social media updates from its executives. Google’s public statements about website traffic can be grouped into three categories. By organizing them this way, we see what kind of data each one would need to be testable. The first group includes usage claims. In April, Pichai mentioned that “queries are at an all-time high” and repeated the query-growth link in this week’s release. In July, Nick Fox, senior vice president of Knowledge and Information, noted that Search reached its highest usage on record during a World Cup match. These claims highlight superlatives without providing specific counts. Having more queries does not mean more clicks leaving Google. The second group involves volume claims. Fox shared in a July LinkedIn post that AI features in Search send billions of clicks to websites weekly. He also mentioned the previous daily figure: “Actually, as we’ve shared before, we continue to send billions of clicks to the web every day through Search.” However, both numbers only specify “billions,” without exact figures. Since one is daily and the other weekly, it’s unclear how the AI-related click count compares to overall clicks or what portion of Search traffic comes from AI surfaces. The third group focuses on quality claims. Liz Reid, Google’s head of Search, stated that AI Overviews mainly remove “bounce clicks,” visits where users quickly find a fact and leave. In an August 2025 blog post , Reid mentioned that the total organic click volume has been “relatively stable” year-over-year, with an increase in average click quality. She also explained that Google is directing slightly more “quality clicks” to websites than a year earlier. Reid defines quality clicks as visits where users don’t swiftly return to the results page. The post also challenged third-party reports of sharp traffic drops, attributing them to flawed methods and isolated cases. These statements are directional comparisons without a published baseline or measurement. Overall, all three categories lack precise counts, consistent definitions over time, splits between traditional results, AI Overviews, and AI Mode, and site-level click reporting for AI features. Our review of Google’s blog posts and executive statements before mid-July, as covered in our Fox analysis, shows no breakdown of click figures by AI features. As of publication, that hasn’t changed. Search Console’s generative AI reports , accessible to some websites, show impressions without clicks , including details by page, country, and device type, but no click-through rates. Compare this to the revenue reports Alphabet filed this month. One side provides a detailed time series, while the other offers three types of assurance. While independent data can help fill in some gaps, each source measures different things and doesn’t fully replace Google’s overall data. Since Google has challenged outside measurements, it’s helpful to understand the limitations of each dataset. Click-through rate (CTR) on results pages with AI Overviews provides the clearest insight. Seer Interactive’s analysis found that organic CTR for queries with AI Overviews dropped from 1.76% in 2024 to just 0.61% in 2025. Similarly, Pew Research Center’s data shows users clicked results 8% of the time when AI Overviews appeared, compared to 15% without them. Both sets of data are specific to the queries and panels they examined. Seer notes AI Overview queries tend to be informational, which naturally have lower CTRs. Looking at position-level CTR across all queries offers a different perspective. Advanced Web Ranking’s Q1 data indicates that CTRs improved for the top five desktop positions but declined for the top mobile position. However, since this data doesn’t specifically isolate AI Overview queries, it can’t definitively support or challenge the bounce-clicks explanation. Another perspective is assistant referrals. SE Ranking’s data shows that referral traffic from Gemini increased after the Gemini 3 releases. Keep in mind, this measures a different product than clicks from AI Overviews or AI Mode within Search. Finally, there’s downstream behavior. A Similarweb report found that brands recommended by ChatGPT answers were 2.5 times more likely to receive a site visit within a week. Of that traffic, 55.9% came from branded searches. This suggests AI recommendations can lead to visits through indirect routes, although it doesn’t directly test Google’s claims about clicks from AI features within Search. Each analysis captures a different part of the traffic picture. None reproduces Google’s aggregate outbound-click claims. Together, these outside data points show that while there is some click pressure on specific surfaces that Google’s assurances don’t fully address, there are also indirect benefits elsewhere. This makes it challenging to draw a straightforward conclusion about a loss. Ultimately, no single dataset can capture the full picture. Google’s claims refer to overall clicks across Search and AI features, but every outside measurement focuses on a specific panel, keyword set, or referral path. The two can’t be reconciled with what’s publicly available. The Q2 numbers don’t settle the click debate, and you shouldn’t expect any earnings report to. They show us something a bit narrower: Search revenue can go up without revealing whether organic visits increased or decreased. The quarter added another piece of evidence to one side of that question but doesn’t add clarity to the other. That’s the practical challenge with the overall claims. Billions of weekly clicks provide important market context, but they don’t tell you if your pages gained or lost visitors because both your site’s performance and the overall market can be true at the same time. A single figure that describes everyone doesn’t really describe anyone. Your own data is the closest thing to a checkable click number for your site. Tools like Search Console and analytics give you a clear picture of your traffic, even if they can’t always pinpoint which AI feature affected it. If you notice impressions are increasing while clicks are dropping on informational queries, that pattern is consistent with what Seer found with AI Overview queries. Broader CTR data remains mixed across devices and query types. For publishers, the key indicators to watch are how referral shares from search change over time, and how branded versus non-branded traffic compares. The pattern from Similarweb suggests that AI recommendations might lead to branded search visits rather than direct referrals, so seeing a decline in referrals alongside growth in branded searches can tell a different story than a simple drop. When clients ask if Google’s reassurances should influence their strategies, a good answer is that the reassurances can’t be tested, but your own data can. Decisions should be based on the verifiable information you have. This quarter’s gap isn’t between Google’s claims and independent data. It’s between two different disclosure standards within the same company, with only one set of numbers that everyone can verify. To bridge this gap, we need some specific details: click and CTR data in Search Console’s generative AI reports, a published methodology behind the aggregate claims, and detailed breakdowns by surface. As of now, these haven’t been shared. Still, Alphabet’s upcoming quarterly report will offer a snapshot of revenue, regardless of these missing details. The earnings reports from the past three quarters haven’t included AI-feature traffic data, and Google hasn’t suggested it will include this information in the future. Follow on YouTube. Matt G. The spending side got the same precise treatment. Roger Montti covered this , including the capital expenditures that led to negative free cash flow for the quarter.

That said, none of this detailed financial data addresses the most important question for businesses: the number of clicks to websites. Neither the Q4 2025 nor Q1 2026 reports we covered offered this information. Google’s broader claims about outbound traffic come from other sources like blog posts, interviews, and social media updates from its executives.
Google’s public statements about website traffic can be grouped into three categories. By organizing them this way, we see what kind of data each one would need to be testable.

The first group includes usage claims. In April, Pichai mentioned that “queries are at an all-time high” and repeated the query-growth link in this week’s release. In July, Nick Fox, senior vice president of Knowledge and Information, noted that Search reached its highest usage on record during a World Cup match. These claims highlight superlatives without providing specific counts. Having more queries does not mean more clicks leaving Google.

The second group involves volume claims. Fox shared in a July LinkedIn post that AI features in Search send billions of clicks to websites weekly. He also mentioned the previous daily figure: “Actually, as we’ve shared before, we continue to send billions of clicks to the web every day through Search.” However, both numbers only specify “billions,” without exact figures. Since one is daily and the other weekly, it’s unclear how the AI-related click count compares to overall clicks or what portion of Search traffic comes from AI surfaces.

The third group focuses on quality claims. Liz Reid, Google’s head of Search, stated that AI Overviews mainly remove “bounce clicks,” visits where users quickly find a fact and leave. In an August 2025 blog post , Reid mentioned that the total organic click volume has been “relatively stable” year-over-year, with an increase in average click quality. She also explained that Google is directing slightly more “quality clicks” to websites than a year earlier. Reid defines quality clicks as visits where users don’t swiftly return to the results page. The post also challenged third-party reports of sharp traffic drops, attributing them to flawed methods and isolated cases. These statements are directional comparisons without a published baseline or measurement.

Overall, all three categories lack precise counts, consistent definitions over time, splits between traditional results, AI Overviews, and AI Mode, and site-level click reporting for AI features. Our review of Google’s blog posts and executive statements before mid-July, as covered in our Fox analysis, shows no breakdown of click figures by AI features. As of publication, that hasn’t changed. Search Console’s generative AI reports , accessible to some websites, show impressions without clicks , including details by page, country, and device type, but no click-through rates.
Compare this to the revenue reports Alphabet filed this month. One side provides a detailed time series, while the other offers three types of assurance.

While independent data can help fill in some gaps, each source measures different things and doesn’t fully replace Google’s overall data. Since Google has challenged outside measurements, it’s helpful to understand the limitations of each dataset.

Click-through rate (CTR) on results pages with AI Overviews provides the clearest insight. Seer Interactive’s analysis found that organic CTR for queries with AI Overviews dropped from 1.76% in 2024 to just 0.61% in 2025. Similarly, Pew Research Center’s data shows users clicked results 8% of the time when AI Overviews appeared, compared to 15% without them. Both sets of data are specific to the queries and panels they examined. Seer notes AI Overview queries tend to be informational, which naturally have lower CTRs.

Looking at position-level CTR across all queries offers a different perspective. Advanced Web Ranking’s Q1 data indicates that CTRs improved for the top five desktop positions but declined for the top mobile position. However, since this data doesn’t specifically isolate AI Overview queries, it can’t definitively support or challenge the bounce-clicks explanation.

Another perspective is assistant referrals. SE Ranking’s data shows that referral traffic from Gemini increased after the Gemini 3 releases. Keep in mind, this measures a different product than clicks from AI Overviews or AI Mode within Search.

Finally, there’s downstream behavior. A Similarweb report found that brands recommended by ChatGPT answers were 2.5 times more likely to receive a site visit within a week. Of that traffic, 55.9% came from branded searches. This suggests AI recommendations can lead to visits through indirect routes, although it doesn’t directly test Google’s claims about clicks from AI features within Search.
Each analysis captures a different part of the traffic picture. None reproduces Google’s aggregate outbound-click claims.

Together, these outside data points show that while there is some click pressure on specific surfaces that Google’s assurances don’t fully address, there are also indirect benefits elsewhere. This makes it challenging to draw a straightforward conclusion about a loss. Ultimately, no single dataset can capture the full picture. Google’s claims refer to overall clicks across Search and AI features, but every outside measurement focuses on a specific panel, keyword set, or referral path. The two can’t be reconciled with what’s publicly available.

The Q2 numbers don’t settle the click debate, and you shouldn’t expect any earnings report to. They show us something a bit narrower: Search revenue can go up without revealing whether organic visits increased or decreased. The quarter added another piece of evidence to one side of that question but doesn’t add clarity to the other.

That’s the practical challenge with the overall claims. Billions of weekly clicks provide important market context, but they don’t tell you if your pages gained or lost visitors because both your site’s performance and the overall market can be true at the same time. A single figure that describes everyone doesn’t really describe anyone.

Your own data is the closest thing to a checkable click number for your site. Tools like Search Console and analytics give you a clear picture of your traffic, even if they can’t always pinpoint which AI feature affected it. If you notice impressions are increasing while clicks are dropping on informational queries, that pattern is consistent with what Seer found with AI Overview queries. Broader CTR data remains mixed across devices and query types.

For publishers, the key indicators to watch are how referral shares from search change over time, and how branded versus non-branded traffic compares. The pattern from Similarweb suggests that AI recommendations might lead to branded search visits rather than direct referrals, so seeing a decline in referrals alongside growth in branded searches can tell a different story than a simple drop.

When clients ask if Google’s reassurances should influence their strategies, a good answer is that the reassurances can’t be tested, but your own data can. Decisions should be based on the verifiable information you have.
This quarter’s gap isn’t between Google’s claims and independent data. It’s between two different disclosure standards within the same company, with only one set of numbers that everyone can verify.

To bridge this gap, we need some specific details: click and CTR data in Search Console’s generative AI reports, a published methodology behind the aggregate claims, and detailed breakdowns by surface. As of now, these haven’t been shared.

Still, Alphabet’s upcoming quarterly report will offer a snapshot of revenue, regardless of these missing details. The earnings reports from the past three quarters haven’t included AI-feature traffic data, and Google hasn’t suggested it will include this information in the future.

sources.title: Bitcoin slips as Democratic sweep bets threaten crypto agenda - The Business Times
passages: BITCOIN edged lower as bets on a possible Democratic sweep of Congress gained traction , adding political uncertainty to a market already struggling with fragile investor appetite.
For now, Bitcoin trading offers limited utility as a gauge of broader market sentiment.
Crypto has been grappling with the fallout from a US$6.3 billion hack of Binance last week and diminished retail enthusiasm amid the artificial intelligence boom.
Those pressures make it harder to separate the macro-driven market moves from industry-specific issues already weighing on digital assets.
The original cryptocurrency slipped as much as 1.6 per cent in Asia on Wednesday (Nov 4) and was trading around US$76,600 as of 10.30 am in Singapore.
The modest move followed declines in US stock futures and the dollar, while Treasuries gained, reflecting expectations that Democratic control of Congress could lead to gridlock in Washington.
For crypto investors, the immediate concern is that a Democratic takeover could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital-asset firms.
More than US$1 billion flowed out of US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Friday and Monday while investors sought greater downside protection in options markets ahead of the US elections.

The modest move followed declines in US stock futures and the dollar, while Treasuries gained, reflecting expectations that Democratic control of Congress could lead to gridlock in Washington. “Sentiment is cautious, but this isn’t capitulation,” said Rachael Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets. “Options show investors hedging the positions they already hold, and they expect any election volatility to be short-lived.” For crypto investors, the immediate concern is that a Democratic takeover could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital-asset firms. The broader macroeconomic implications are less clear: Political stalemate could limit further fiscal stimulus and weigh on speculative assets, though lower Treasury yields could eventually provide support by easing financial conditions. For now, Bitcoin trading offers limited utility as a gauge of broader market sentiment. Crypto has been grappling with the fallout from a US$6.3 billion hack of Binance last week and diminished retail enthusiasm amid the artificial intelligence boom. Those pressures make it harder to separate the macro-driven market moves from industry-specific issues already weighing on digital assets. “Overall sentiment in crypto is near-term moderate fear and long-term uncertainty,” said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital. “Near-term fear because it is still tracking overall risk assets, and with the tech selloff and potentially a restart to the war in the Middle East that is causing some downward pressure.” Democrats had been widely expected to take control of the House of Representatives, with a chance of also taking the Senate, putting them at odds with President Donald Trump’s Republican White House. The Trump family’s financial gains from its crypto ventures became a contentious issue this year, helping derail a regulatory bill seen as critical to the industry. “With the Clarity Act already stalled in the Senate, a change in committee control would most likely mean renegotiation rather than a quick revival, and markets had largely priced that in,” Lucas said. Bitcoin is down roughly 6 per cent from the high last Thursday, before the Binance hack. More than US$1 billion flowed out of US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Friday and Monday while investors sought greater downside protection in options markets ahead of the US elections. BITCOIN edged lower as bets on a possible Democratic sweep of Congress gained traction , adding political uncertainty to a market already struggling with fragile investor appetite.

The original cryptocurrency slipped as much as 1.6 per cent in Asia on Wednesday (Nov 4) and was trading around US$76,600 as of 10.30 am in Singapore. The modest move followed declines in US stock futures and the dollar, while Treasuries gained, reflecting expectations that Democratic control of Congress could lead to gridlock in Washington.

“Sentiment is cautious, but this isn’t capitulation,” said Rachael Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets. “Options show investors hedging the positions they already hold, and they expect any election volatility to be short-lived.”
For crypto investors, the immediate concern is that a Democratic takeover could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital-asset firms.

The broader macroeconomic implications are less clear: Political stalemate could limit further fiscal stimulus and weigh on speculative assets, though lower Treasury yields could eventually provide support by easing financial conditions.

For now, Bitcoin trading offers limited utility as a gauge of broader market sentiment. Crypto has been grappling with the fallout from a US$6.3 billion hack of Binance last week and diminished retail enthusiasm amid the artificial intelligence boom. Those pressures make it harder to separate the macro-driven market moves from industry-specific issues already weighing on digital assets.

“Overall sentiment in crypto is near-term moderate fear and long-term uncertainty,” said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital. “Near-term fear because it is still tracking overall risk assets, and with the tech selloff and potentially a restart to the war in the Middle East that is causing some downward pressure.”
Democrats had been widely expected to take control of the House of Representatives, with a chance of also taking the Senate, putting them at odds with President Donald Trump’s Republican White House.
The Trump family’s financial gains from its crypto ventures became a contentious issue this year, helping derail a regulatory bill seen as critical to the industry.

“With the Clarity Act already stalled in the Senate, a change in committee control would most likely mean renegotiation rather than a quick revival, and markets had largely priced that in,” Lucas said.
Bitcoin is down roughly 6 per cent from the high last Thursday, before the Binance hack.

sources.title: What GPT‑5 means for IT teams, devs, and the future of AI at work - Help Net Security
passages: Max Sinclair , CEO of Azoma, told Help Net Security: “GPT‑5 represents a fundamental shift in commerce technology.
We’re looking at AI that doesn’t just process transactions, it builds genuine customer relationships through memory and context that spans months, even years of interactions.
Your customers won’t need to repeat themselves.
The system learns their size, style, and seasonal habits, delivering relationship commerce at scale.
The multimodal piece is also really interesting.
Customers will be able to interact with ChatGPT via image, voice or video, much like an in store experience.
It will essentially eliminate the friction between physical and digital retail environments.”
IT teams and developers can expect faster, smarter automation and more flexible AI use.

Whether it’s helping a developer debug code or helping a customer find the right product based on long-term preferences, GPT‑5 is designed to work more like a capable assistant and less like a basic chatbot.
Another big change is how GPT‑5 handles safety.
Older versions often refused to answer certain questions outright.
Instead of shutting down the conversation, it tries to respond with context while staying within safety rules.
For professionals who work with AI daily, this means fewer dead ends and more productive interactions.
GPT‑5 also comes with a much bigger memory window.
It can now remember and work with up to 256,000 tokens of text in a single session.
This allows it to stay focused over long conversations or when reviewing long documents, which can be especially helpful for tasks like coding, documentation, or analyzing business reports.
Unlike previous versions, GPT‑5 uses a new approach behind the scenes.
If the task is more complex, it switches to a deeper reasoning engine.
Users can also prompt it to “think step by step” to trigger more thoughtful answers.
For developers, GPT‑5 brings new tools like code generation, reasoning toggles, and the ability to fine-tune how verbose or concise it is.
It also supports a feature called free-form function calling, which helps automate more complex workflows without rigid API structures.
OpenAI has released GPT‑5, the newest version of its large language model.
It’s now available to developers and ChatGPT users, and it brings some real changes to how AI can be used in business and IT environments.

GPT‑5 (with thinking) performs better than OpenAI o3 with 50-80% less output tokens across capabilities, including visual reasoning, agentic coding, and graduate-level scientific problem solving (Source: Open AI)
“Here’s what excites me most – GPT‑5’s autonomous reasoning capabilities.
We will see many start-ups and existing vendors reinventing customer experiences based off this new technology,” Sinclair added.
There are several versions of GPT‑5 available.
A standard version offers full capability, while smaller versions offer faster performance or lower cost.
These models can be accessed through OpenAI’s API, GitHub Copilot, and tools like ChatGPT Enterprise.

extraction.body: For years, detection has served as the foundation of every cybersecurity strategy. And that’s not changing. But as AI continues to accelerate attacks, the gap between seeing an attacker’s latest move and understanding what they’re likely to do next is getting tougher to close. Agentic AI is a primary perp behind this shift. In the last year alone, AI has shown us that attackers can use it to execute workflows, adapt to changing conditions, and even spawn other agents to handle subtasks. All this at speeds that make human response times look, well , undeniably human. Exploits that recently took them days or weeks to execute will take just a minute by 2027 . Now, add in bad actors' second-favorite advantage, highly interconnected environments , and you’ve got one worrisome landscape. As attackers chain tactics across endpoints, networks, cloud environments, and data repositories, they move from one control point to the next. And persistent attackers take plenty of opportunities to keep trying, adapting until something works. Block one path, and AI helps them find another. Disrupt one technique, they pivot—all within minutes. By the time analysts sort through telemetry from multiple domains to understand what’s happened, the attacker may already be two moves ahead. But what if your teams could see four steps ahead of their attacker? Here’s how that works. Before you can predict an attacker’s next move, you need to understand the moves they’ve already made. While that may sound like a line out of The Art of War , the key to an attacker’s next move is often hidden within their previous move. That’s because modern, sophisticated attacks rarely stay in one place. In a single chain of events, an attacker can establish access through an endpoint, move laterally across the network, abuse credentials, and access sensitive data. Most security controls only see a piece of that, which leaves analysts to pick up the pieces and manually stitch together answers. And this comes at a high cost of defender’s time and energy —two resources at critically low levels in most SOCs. To go from behavioral datapoints to behavioral intelligence, security teams need to start connecting the dots. When you correlate activity across multiple vectors, the attack starts to look less like a collection of isolated events and more like what it actually is: a coordinated sequence of moves. Scattered behavioral data turns into invaluable intelligence that can help defenders understand what’s happening in their environment, and what might come next. Native telemetry correlation brings signals across every domain to help security teams get a clear view of how individual events connect across an attack chain. Instead of investigating isolated alerts, analysts can start with the bigger picture: What is this activity telling us about the attack? Consider a phishing email that delivers a beaconing agent. The attacker then begins listing network shares and creates a remote scheduled task. With cross-domain correlation, all these signals are brought together to unveil the attacker’s strategy. Now your team knows exactly what’s going on and why. That’s step one and two, complete. Everything has a pattern. By analyzing thousands of real-world attack chains, AI can learn the playbook attackers repeatedly use to move from one stage to another. Instead of manually correlating fragments across disconnected tools, defenders can let AI solve the next move problem and focus on what’s most likely to happen next. But prediction is only useful when defenders can understand what’s happening. AI-generated incident summaries can turn complex security activity into clear, plain-language explanations. Analysts get a clearer picture of what happened, why it matters, and where to go next without having to stitch together every alert and event themselves. With a clearer view of where an attacker is headed, teams can raise the proper defenses, cut the right paths, and potentially save their organization billions. Because when analysts are able to see the patterns behind the noise, they can finally get ahead of the attack. That’s the unique, exclusive power behind Incident Prediction, a predictive AI capability engineered to uncover patterns and transform them into foresight. Trained on over 500,000 real-world attack chains analyzed by Symantec and Carbon Black Threat Hunters, Incident Prediction leverages AI-powered behavioral analysis and probability scoring to identify the likely next steps in an active attack. Instead of waiting for the next stage of an attack to happen, defenders can anticipate and automatically disrupt the chain before attackers reach the point of impact—and before data can be encrypted, stolen, or exfiltrated. For attacks that deliberately hide behind legitimate tools, like living off the land (LOTL) attacks, seeing the sequence can be the difference between suspecting an LOTL attack and stopping one. With Incident Prediction, defenders can identify high confidence attack sequences in 80% of real-world incidents , giving analysts the context and confidence to determine exactly where attention—and intervention—would make the biggest impact. And when the threat calls for it, protective policies can be enforced before damage occurs, then automatically reverted to baseline once the threat is neutralized. If you’re thinking that’s cool, Incident Prediction is merely one example of what becomes possible when AI actually delivers what the assistance and protection defenders want. Seeing four moves ahead is a pretty wicked advantage. They’re putting AI to work at every turn. Defenders should do the same. That means looking beyond the hype and finding the areas where AI can actually help security teams grow faster, sharper, and frankly, a little less overwhelmed. From predicting an attacker’s next move to cutting through alert fatigue to correlating signals across domains and reducing hours of investigation to minutes, AI is changing what’s possible in the SOC. A new eBook, 8 Ways AI is Easing Stress on the SOC , takes a closer look at the ways AI is already transforming cybersecurity. No baseless promises. No sci-fi scenarios. Just eight practical ways AI is delivering real defensive value today. Ready to see predictive AI at work? Watch How to Predict Bad Actor Moves With AI for an exclusive look at Incident Prediction, part of Symantec CBX, and how security teams can use AI to disrupt attacks earlier in the sequence. Or reach out to your in-region partner to schedule a 1:1 demo . Shanleigh bridges the gap between product and storytelling. With almost a decade of experience, she's helped launch industry-first innovations and amplified iconic industry brands.

coreStoryFacts.text: Max Sinclair , CEO of Azoma, told Help Net Security: “GPT‑5 represents a fundamental shift in commerce technology.
We’re looking at AI that doesn’t just process transactions, it builds genuine customer relationships through memory and context that spans months, even years of interactions.
Your customers won’t need to repeat themselves.
The system learns their size, style, and seasonal habits, delivering relationship commerce at scale.
The multimodal piece is also really interesting.
Customers will be able to interact with ChatGPT via image, voice or video, much like an in store experience.
It will essentially eliminate the friction between physical and digital retail environments.”
IT teams and developers can expect faster, smarter automation and more flexible AI use.

Whether it’s helping a developer debug code or helping a customer find the right product based on long-term preferences, GPT‑5 is designed to work more like a capable assistant and less like a basic chatbot.
Another big change is how GPT‑5 handles safety.
Older versions often refused to answer certain questions outright.
Instead of shutting down the conversation, it tries to respond with context while staying within safety rules.
For professionals who work with AI daily, this means fewer dead ends and more productive interactions.
GPT‑5 also comes with a much bigger memory window.
It can now remember and work with up to 256,000 tokens of text in a single session.
Unlike previous versions, GPT‑5 uses a new approach behind the scenes.
Users can also prompt it to “think step by step” to trigger more thoughtful answers.
For developers, GPT‑5 brings new tools like code generation, reasoning toggles, and the ability to fine-tune how verbose or concise it is.
OpenAI has released GPT‑5, the newest version of its large language model.

GPT‑5 (with thinking) performs better than OpenAI o3 with 50-80% less output tokens across capabilities, including visual reasoning, agentic coding, and graduate-level scientific problem solving (Source: Open AI)
“Here’s what excites me most – GPT‑5’s autonomous reasoning capabilities.
We will see many start-ups and existing vendors reinventing customer experiences based off this new technology,” Sinclair added.
There are several versions of GPT‑5 available.
These models can be accessed through OpenAI’s API, GitHub Copilot, and tools like ChatGPT Enterprise.

extraction.body: For years, detection has served as the foundation of every cybersecurity strategy. And that’s not changing. But as AI continues to accelerate attacks, the gap between seeing an attacker’s latest move and understanding what they’re likely to do next is getting tougher to close. Agentic AI is a primary perp behind this shift. In the last year alone, AI has shown us that attackers can use it to execute workflows, adapt to changing conditions, and even spawn other agents to handle subtasks. All this at speeds that make human response times look, well , undeniably human. Exploits that recently took them days or weeks to execute will take just a minute by 2027 . Now, add in bad actors' second-favorite advantage, highly interconnected environments , and you’ve got one worrisome landscape. As attackers chain tactics across endpoints, networks, cloud environments, and data repositories, they move from one control point to the next. And persistent attackers take plenty of opportunities to keep trying, adapting until something works. Block one path, and AI helps them find another. Disrupt one technique, they pivot—all within minutes. By the time analysts sort through telemetry from multiple domains to understand what’s happened, the attacker may already be two moves ahead. But what if your teams could see four steps ahead of their attacker? Here’s how that works. Before you can predict an attacker’s next move, you need to understand the moves they’ve already made. While that may sound like a line out of The Art of War , the key to an attacker’s next move is often hidden within their previous move. That’s because modern, sophisticated attacks rarely stay in one place. In a single chain of events, an attacker can establish access through an endpoint, move laterally across the network, abuse credentials, and access sensitive data. Most security controls only see a piece of that, which leaves analysts to pick up the pieces and manually stitch together answers. And this comes at a high cost of defender’s time and energy —two resources at critically low levels in most SOCs. To go from behavioral datapoints to behavioral intelligence, security teams need to start connecting the dots. When you correlate activity across multiple vectors, the attack starts to look less like a collection of isolated events and more like what it actually is: a coordinated sequence of moves. Scattered behavioral data turns into invaluable intelligence that can help defenders understand what’s happening in their environment, and what might come next. Native telemetry correlation brings signals across every domain to help security teams get a clear view of how individual events connect across an attack chain. Instead of investigating isolated alerts, analysts can start with the bigger picture: What is this activity telling us about the attack? Consider a phishing email that delivers a beaconing agent. The attacker then begins listing network shares and creates a remote scheduled task. With cross-domain correlation, all these signals are brought together to unveil the attacker’s strategy. Now your team knows exactly what’s going on and why. That’s step one and two, complete. Everything has a pattern. By analyzing thousands of real-world attack chains, AI can learn the playbook attackers repeatedly use to move from one stage to another. Instead of manually correlating fragments across disconnected tools, defenders can let AI solve the next move problem and focus on what’s most likely to happen next. But prediction is only useful when defenders can understand what’s happening. AI-generated incident summaries can turn complex security activity into clear, plain-language explanations. Analysts get a clearer picture of what happened, why it matters, and where to go next without having to stitch together every alert and event themselves. With a clearer view of where an attacker is headed, teams can raise the proper defenses, cut the right paths, and potentially save their organization billions. Because when analysts are able to see the patterns behind the noise, they can finally get ahead of the attack. That’s the unique, exclusive power behind Incident Prediction, a predictive AI capability engineered to uncover patterns and transform them into foresight. Trained on over 500,000 real-world attack chains analyzed by Symantec and Carbon Black Threat Hunters, Incident Prediction leverages AI-powered behavioral analysis and probability scoring to identify the likely next steps in an active attack. Instead of waiting for the next stage of an attack to happen, defenders can anticipate and automatically disrupt the chain before attackers reach the point of impact—and before data can be encrypted, stolen, or exfiltrated. This article is an automated aggregation of coverage from news outlets. Our editorials offer in-depth analysis curated by the NewsCord team.
Greenland's parliament ratified a trilateral security accord with the United States and Denmark. The 16-0 vote with seven abstentions formalized expanded U.S. military presence.

Greenland’s parliament ratified a trilateral security agreement with the United States and Denmark on Tuesday, clearing the way for two new U.S. military bases on the Arctic island and for Trump’s “Golden Dome” missile defence system.
Agreement includes missile defence 'Golden Dome' deployment

The agreement was signed in September by U.S. President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Greenlandic lawmakers voted 16-0 for the agreement, with seven abstentions, and the deal was described as strengthening security in the Arctic and North Atlantic while keeping Greenland under Danish control.
Mute Egede framed the ratification as a step forward for the self-governing island, writing, “The road to this point has been a difficult one for us as a people.”
The agreement’s entry into force was tied to Denmark and Greenland completing “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland.”
Opposition party members questioned the deal’s economic value even as the agreement advanced, with Reuters describing that some lawmakers raised concerns about what the arrangement would be worth.

Pele Broberg, chair of the pro-independence Naleraq party, said, “We are looking for a better agreement that we can benefit from when we become an independent state. But no economic benefit has been gained from the agreement.”
DW reported that Greenland’s Foreign Minister Mute Egede told lawmakers, “We must accept that peace and stability are no longer something we can take for granted,” shortly before the vote in Nuuk.

The agreement was presented as alleviating pressure after Trump’s repeated threats to take control of the self-governing Danish territory, and it was also described as easing tensions over calls for Greenland to become part of the United States.
The trilateral deal was also framed as allowing the United States to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base in northwest Greenland.
The agreement’s immediate political impact was that Greenlandic approval paved the way for further Danish consideration, with Danish lawmakers set to debate the deal later this month.
ABC News reported that the White House had no immediate comment on the vote, while the State Department said it “marks another major victory for American national security.”

In Ilulissat, Nukaaka Lund-Mathaeussen hoped the approval meant the Trump administration “got what they wanted,” and she added, “Hopefully after this we won’t be getting underhanded threats from the American government.”

Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of Avannaata Municipality, said he was not convinced Greenlanders would see advantages, arguing, “It’s a good deal for Denmark, NATO. Not a good deal for us,” and adding, “Zero.”

The agreement also specified that, as Washington expands its military presence, it would award contracts for goods and services related to setting up, maintaining or dismantling such bases “to Greenlandic sources to the maximum extent possible.”

But we have stood firm on our fundamental principles, chosen dialogue and taken responsibility for our country’s interests,” he wrote in a ⁠post on Facebook. “This is about all of us. The Greenland we love. ⁠About our security. And about our ⁠right to shape our own future,” he said. Located between Europe and North America, Greenland is the world’s largest island, with a population of 57,000 people. Trump’s refusal last year to rule out a military invasion had caused fear among Greenlanders, the majority of whom rejected US control, according to opinion polls. The trilateral deal paves the way for more US bases on Greenland. It also allows the US to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base, a remote US military installation in northwest Greenland. Under its terms, Greenland will remain under Danish control – but the agreement would still apply if the island eventually chooses independence. The deal stipulates it will only “enter into force” once the “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed”. Danish lawmakers are set to debate it later this month, while no approval is required from the US Senate.

extraction.body: European Union lawmakers gave final approval to the 27-nation bloc’s artificial intelligence law Wednesday, putting the world-leading rules on track to take effect later this year. Lawmakers in the European Parliament voted overwhelmingly in favor of the Artificial Intelligence Act, five years after regulations were first proposed. The AI Act is expected to act as a global signpost for other governments grappling with how to regulate the fast-developing technology. “The AI Act has nudged the future of AI in a human-centric direction, in a direction where humans are in control of the technology and where it — the technology — helps us leverage new discoveries, economic growth, societal progress and unlock human potential,” Dragos Tudorache, a Romanian lawmaker who was a co-leader of the Parliament negotiations on the draft law, said before the vote. Big tech companies generally have supported the need to regulate AI while lobbying to ensure any rules work in their favor. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman caused a minor stir last year when he suggested the ChatGPT maker could pull out of Europe if it can’t comply with the AI Act — before backtracking to say there were no plans to leave. Here’s a look at the world’s first comprehensive set of AI rules: Like many EU regulations, the AI Act was initially intended to act as consumer safety legislation, taking a “risk-based approach” to products or services that use artificial intelligence. The vast majority of AI systems are expected to be low risk, such as content recommendation systems or spam filters. Other banned uses include police scanning faces in public using AI-powered remote “biometric identification” systems, except for serious crimes like kidnapping or terrorism. They added provisions for so-called generative AI models, the technology underpinning AI chatbot systems that can produce unique and seemingly lifelike responses, images and more. Developers of general purpose AI models — from European startups to OpenAI and Google — will have to provide a detailed summary of the text, pictures, video and other data on the internet that is used to train the systems as well as follow EU copyright law. There’s extra scrutiny for the biggest and most powerful AI models that pose “systemic risks,” which include OpenAI’s GPT4 — its most advanced system — and Google’s Gemini. The EU says it’s worried that these powerful AI systems could “cause serious accidents or be misused for far-reaching cyberattacks.” They also fear generative AI could spread “harmful biases” across many applications, affecting many people. Brussels first suggested AI regulations in 2019, taking a familiar global role in ratcheting up scrutiny of emerging industries, while other governments scramble to keep up. In the U.S., President Joe Biden signed a sweeping executive order on AI in October that’s expected to be backed up by legislation and global agreements. In the meantime, lawmakers in at least seven U.S. states are working on their own AI legislation. Chinese President Xi Jinping has proposed his Global AI Governance Initiative for fair and safe use of AI, and authorities have issued « interim measures » for managing generative AI, which applies to text, pictures, audio, video and other content generated for people inside China. Other countries, from Brazil to Japan, as well as global groupings like the United Nations and Group of Seven industrialized nations, are moving to draw up AI guardrails. The AI Act is expected to officially become law by May or June, after a few final formalities, including a blessing from EU member countries. Provisions will start taking effect in stages, with countries required to ban prohibited AI systems six months after the rules enter the lawbooks. Rules for general purpose AI systems like chatbots will start applying a year after the law takes effect. When it comes to enforcement, each EU country will set up their own AI watchdog, where citizens can file a complaint if they think they’ve been the victim of a violation of the rules. Meanwhile, Brussels will create an AI Office tasked with enforcing and supervising the law for general purpose AI systems. Violations of the AI Act could draw fines of up to 35 million euros ($38 million), or 7% of a company’s global revenue. This isn’t Brussels’ last word on AI rules, said Italian lawmaker Brando Benifei, co-leader of Parliament’s work on the law. More AI-related legislation could be ahead after summer elections, including in areas like AI in the workplace that the new law partly covers, he said.

passages: That changed when the European Union introduced the AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive law governing the use of artificial intelligence.
sources.body: That changed when the European Union introduced the AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive law governing the use of artificial intelligence.

extraction.body: Artificial intelligence is transforming the way we live, work, and interact, often faster than governments or citizens can keep up. For years, this powerful technology developed in a near-legal vacuum, raising hopes of innovation but also fears of abuse. That changed when the European Union introduced the AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive law governing the use of artificial intelligence. More than a legal milestone, the Act is Europe’s declaration that technology must serve society, not the other way around. Just as the EU’s landmark data protection rules reshaped global privacy standards, this bold new framework is set to influence how AI is built and deployed far beyond Europe’s borders. Brussels has spent years wrestling with a simple but urgent question: how do you regulate a technology that changes faster than politics? The European Commission launched its proposal in 2021, setting off a long process of debate and negotiation. After intense lobbying and compromise, the European Parliament approved the final text in March 2024, and EU governments in the Council gave their backing two months later. On August 1, the AI Act officially entered into force, marking a global first. 1 However, the AI Act is not being implemented all at once. Some provisions, such as bans on the most dangerous AI systems, took effect within six months. Others will be phased in over the next three years, giving companies space to adapt. 2 This slow rollout reflects both the ambition of the legislation and the difficulty of writing rules for a technology that refuses to stand still. The core of the AI Act is its risk-based approach. Instead of treating all algorithms the same, the EU categorized AI systems. “Unacceptable risk” systems are banned completely. This includes social scoring, where people are judged by automated systems, and unauthorized real-time biometric surveillance. “High-risk” systems, such as AI used in healthcare, policing, or hiring, are allowed only under strict conditions. They must meet standards for transparency, oversight, and safety testing. “Limited risk” systems, like deepfakes, must inform users that they are interacting with AI. “Minimal risk” tools, such as spam filters, face little regulation. 3 A recent addition to the AI Act is its emphasis on general-purpose AI (GPAI). These are large, adaptable systems like ChatGPT that can write text, answer questions, or generate code. Unlike AI designed for a single task, foundation models can be built into many different products and services, from chatbots to medical tools. That versatility makes them powerful but also unpredictable, which is why the EU decided they deserve their own set of rules. From August 2025, GPAI providers will face strict transparency obligations. They must share technical documentation with regulators and with companies that rely on their models, publish a summary of the data used for training, and adopt policies to respect copyright law. These measures are meant to lift the lid on systems that are often treated as “black boxes,” giving both officials and the public a clearer picture of how they work and what fuels them. 4 For models considered a systemic risk, meaning they are so large or widely used that failures could have serious consequences, the rules go further. Developers must run safety tests, report serious incidents, and put strong cybersecurity protections in place. 5 By carving out these additional safeguards, the EU is signalling that foundation models are not just another type of AI but the engines of the digital future. The aim is to make them accountable without cutting off the innovation they promise. The scope of the AI Act is intentionally broad. It does not just cover European tech companies but also any foreign business whose AI systems are used inside the EU. A U.S. startup offering AI-driven hiring software in Berlin, or a Chinese company selling facial-recognition tools in Paris, would both have to play by Europe’s rules. Just as the EU’s data protection law (GDPR) set the global benchmark for privacy, the AI Act is expected to export European standards around the world. 6 There are, however, a few exceptions. According to Recital 24 of the AI Act, AI built for military or national security purposes is excluded, as is research still in the lab. But once an AI system makes the leap from experimentation to the marketplace, the law applies. The idea is simple: innovation should thrive in early stages, but once AI enters people’s daily lives, it must be subject to safeguards that protect society. Regulating artificial intelligence is no small task, so the EU has set up new institutions to keep watch. At the centre is the European AI Office, a body within the European Commission that will monitor compliance and step in when powerful general-purpose models step out of line. National authorities in each member state will also play a role, coordinated to make sure the rules are applied consistently across the Union. To avoid leaving these decisions to politicians and lawyers alone, the framework also brings in outside voices. An independent panel of scientists will provide technical expertise, while an advisory forum will give civil society groups and industry representatives a seat at the table. The aim is to strike a balance: rules that are rigorous enough to keep people safe, but also legitimate and inclusive enough to earn public trust. 7 The AI Act comes with teeth. Companies caught using banned systems can be fined up to €35 million or seven percent of their global revenue. Even lesser violations carry fines of up to €15 million or three percent of revenue, as stipulated in Article 99 of the AI Act. These numbers are not symbolic. They echo the strict enforcement of the EU’s data protection law, GDPR, where regulators showed they were willing to take on some of the world’s biggest companies. Few expect the AI Act to be any different. But big penalties are only part of the story. The law has also sparked debate about whether strict regulation will stifle innovation. Critics warn that compliance costs could hit startups hardest, leaving them unable to compete with large tech firms that have the resources to cope. Even some European leaders share these concerns. 8 Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has called parts of the law confusing and burdensome, suggesting that the EU may be undermining its own competitiveness. 9 Supporters counter that clear rules are the key to building public trust. If citizens feel protected, they argue, they will be more willing to accept AI in sensitive areas like healthcare or finance. For them, the AI Act is not an obstacle to innovation but the foundation of an ethical and sustainable digital economy. 10 The clash of views reveals a familiar European challenge: how to regulate boldly without slowing growth in a global race. While the political debate continues, industries are already adjusting. In fashion, AI tools that recommend outfits or run virtual fitting rooms now need human oversight and transparency. In media, generative systems must be labeled or watermarked, reshaping how audiences consume images and video. Even American companies are rethinking their practices, updating documentation and audit processes to avoid trouble with European regulators. Just as GDPR became the world’s privacy benchmark, the AI Act is already pushing firms worldwide to design safer, more transparent AI. The stakes extend far beyond Europe. In the United States, the government has issued executive orders and voluntary guidelines, but no binding law. China has drawn up its own rules, shaped by its political priorities. This patchwork approach has left the global AI landscape divided. Against this backdrop, Europe is positioning itself as the champion of trustworthy AI. Whether other powers will follow its lead remains uncertain, but the EU has already made one point clear: artificial intelligence will not remain a lawless frontier. The AI Act is both pioneering and imperfect. It is pioneering because Europe has chosen to write rules for artificial intelligence before the technology has fully matured. It is imperfect because no law can anticipate every risk, every breakthrough, or every misuse that may still emerge. What matters is that Europe has acted. By putting forward the world’s first comprehensive framework, the EU hopes to protect its citizens while shaping the terms of the global debate. The gamble is clear: that democratic societies can harness technological power without sacrificing rights or trust. Whether other nations follow Europe’s lead or strike out on their own path, one thing is certain. passages: Artificial intelligence is transforming the way we live, work, and interact, often faster than governments or citizens can keep up. For years, this powerful technology developed in a near-legal vacuum, raising hopes of innovation but also fears of abuse. That changed when the European Union introduced the AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive law governing the use of artificial intelligence. More than a legal milestone, the Act is Europe’s declaration that technology must serve society, not the other way around. Just as the EU’s landmark data protection rules reshaped global privacy standards, this bold new framework is set to influence how AI is built and deployed far beyond Europe’s borders.

Brussels has spent years wrestling with a simple but urgent question: how do you regulate a technology that changes faster than politics? The European Commission launched its proposal in 2021, setting off a long process of debate and negotiation. After intense lobbying and compromise, the European Parliament approved the final text in March 2024, and EU governments in the Council gave their backing two months later. On August 1, the AI Act officially entered into force, marking a global first. 1

However, the AI Act is not being implemented all at once. Some provisions, such as bans on the most dangerous AI systems, took effect within six months. Others will be phased in over the next three years, giving companies space to adapt. 2 This slow rollout reflects both the ambition of the legislation and the difficulty of writing rules for a technology that refuses to stand still.

The core of the AI Act is its risk-based approach. Instead of treating all algorithms the same, the EU categorized AI systems. “Unacceptable risk” systems are banned completely. This includes social scoring, where people are judged by automated systems, and unauthorized real-time biometric surveillance. “High-risk” systems, such as AI used in healthcare, policing, or hiring, are allowed only under strict conditions. They must meet standards for transparency, oversight, and safety testing. “Limited risk” systems, like deepfakes, must inform users that they are interacting with AI. “Minimal risk” tools, such as spam filters, face little regulation. 3

A recent addition to the AI Act is its emphasis on general-purpose AI (GPAI). These are large, adaptable systems like ChatGPT that can write text, answer questions, or generate code. Unlike AI designed for a single task, foundation models can be built into many different products and services, from chatbots to medical tools. That versatility makes them powerful but also unpredictable, which is why the EU decided they deserve their own set of rules.

From August 2025, GPAI providers will face strict transparency obligations. They must share technical documentation with regulators and with companies that rely on their models, publish a summary of the data used for training, and adopt policies to respect copyright law. These measures are meant to lift the lid on systems that are often treated as “black boxes,” giving both officials and the public a clearer picture of how they work and what fuels them. 4

For models considered a systemic risk, meaning they are so large or widely used that failures could have serious consequences, the rules go further. Developers must run safety tests, report serious incidents, and put strong cybersecurity protections in place. 5 By carving out these additional safeguards, the EU is signalling that foundation models are not just another type of AI but the engines of the digital future. The aim is to make them accountable without cutting off the innovation they promise.

The scope of the AI Act is intentionally broad. It does not just cover European tech companies but also any foreign business whose AI systems are used inside the EU. A U.S. startup offering AI-driven hiring software in Berlin, or a Chinese company selling facial-recognition tools in Paris, would both have to play by Europe’s rules. Just as the EU’s data protection law (GDPR) set the global benchmark for privacy, the AI Act is expected to export European standards around the world. 6

There are, however, a few exceptions. According to Recital 24 of the AI Act, AI built for military or national security purposes is excluded, as is research still in the lab. But once an AI system makes the leap from experimentation to the marketplace, the law applies. The idea is simple: innovation should thrive in early stages, but once AI enters people’s daily lives, it must be subject to safeguards that protect society.

Regulating artificial intelligence is no small task, so the EU has set up new institutions to keep watch. At the centre is the European AI Office, a body within the European Commission that will monitor compliance and step in when powerful general-purpose models step out of line. National authorities in each member state will also play a role, coordinated to make sure the rules are applied consistently across the Union.

To avoid leaving these decisions to politicians and lawyers alone, the framework also brings in outside voices. An independent panel of scientists will provide technical expertise, while an advisory forum will give civil society groups and industry representatives a seat at the table. The aim is to strike a balance: rules that are rigorous enough to keep people safe, but also legitimate and inclusive enough to earn public trust. 7

The AI Act comes with teeth. Companies caught using banned systems can be fined up to €35 million or seven percent of their global revenue. Even lesser violations carry fines of up to €15 million or three percent of revenue, as stipulated in Article 99 of the AI Act. These numbers are not symbolic. They echo the strict enforcement of the EU’s data protection law, GDPR, where regulators showed they were willing to take on some of the world’s biggest companies. Few expect the AI Act to be any different.

But big penalties are only part of the story. The law has also sparked debate about whether strict regulation will stifle innovation. Critics warn that compliance costs could hit startups hardest, leaving them unable to compete with large tech firms that have the resources to cope. Even some European leaders share these concerns. 8 Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has called parts of the law confusing and burdensome, suggesting that the EU may be undermining its own competitiveness. 9

Supporters counter that clear rules are the key to building public trust. If citizens feel protected, they argue, they will be more willing to accept AI in sensitive areas like healthcare or finance. For them, the AI Act is not an obstacle to innovation but the foundation of an ethical and sustainable digital economy. 10 The clash of views reveals a familiar European challenge: how to regulate boldly without slowing growth in a global race.

While the political debate continues, industries are already adjusting. In fashion, AI tools that recommend outfits or run virtual fitting rooms now need human oversight and transparency. In media, generative systems must be labeled or watermarked, reshaping how audiences consume images and video. Even American companies are rethinking their practices, updating documentation and audit processes to avoid trouble with European regulators. Just as GDPR became the world’s privacy benchmark, the AI Act is already pushing firms worldwide to design safer, more transparent AI.

The stakes extend far beyond Europe. In the United States, the government has issued executive orders and voluntary guidelines, but no binding law. China has drawn up its own rules, shaped by its political priorities. This patchwork approach has left the global AI landscape divided. Against this backdrop, Europe is positioning itself as the champion of trustworthy AI. Whether other powers will follow its lead remains uncertain, but the EU has already made one point clear: artificial intelligence will not remain a lawless frontier.

The AI Act is both pioneering and imperfect. It is pioneering because Europe has chosen to write rules for artificial intelligence before the technology has fully matured. It is imperfect because no law can anticipate every risk, every breakthrough, or every misuse that may still emerge.

What matters is that Europe has acted. By putting forward the world’s first comprehensive framework, the EU hopes to protect its citizens while shaping the terms of the global debate. Whether other nations follow Europe’s lead or strike out on their own path, one thing is certain. Artificial intelligence will no longer develop in a vacuum, and the rules written in Brussels will be impossible to ignore.

extraction.body: European Union lawmakers gave final approval to the 27-nation bloc’s artificial intelligence law Wednesday, putting the world-leading rules on track to take effect later this year. Lawmakers in the European Parliament voted overwhelmingly in favor of the Artificial Intelligence Act, five years after regulations were first proposed. The AI Act is expected to act as a global signpost for other governments grappling with how to regulate the fast-developing technology. “The AI Act has nudged the future of AI in a human-centric direction, in a direction where humans are in control of the technology and where it — the technology — helps us leverage new discoveries, economic growth, societal progress and unlock human potential,” Dragos Tudorache, a Romanian lawmaker who was a co-leader of the Parliament negotiations on the draft law, said before the vote. Big tech companies generally have supported the need to regulate AI while lobbying to ensure any rules work in their favor. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman caused a minor stir last year when he suggested the ChatGPT maker could pull out of Europe if it can’t comply with the AI Act — before backtracking to say there were no plans to leave. Here’s a look at the world’s first comprehensive set of AI rules: Like many EU regulations, the AI Act was initially intended to act as consumer safety legislation, taking a “risk-based approach” to products or services that use artificial intelligence. The vast majority of AI systems are expected to be low risk, such as content recommendation systems or spam filters. Other banned uses include police scanning faces in public using AI-powered remote “biometric identification” systems, except for serious crimes like kidnapping or terrorism. They added provisions for so-called generative AI models, the technology underpinning AI chatbot systems that can produce unique and seemingly lifelike responses, images and more. Developers of general purpose AI models — from European startups to OpenAI and Google — will have to provide a detailed summary of the text, pictures, video and other data on the internet that is used to train the systems as well as follow EU copyright law. There’s extra scrutiny for the biggest and most powerful AI models that pose “systemic risks,” which include OpenAI’s GPT4 — its most advanced system — and Google’s Gemini. The EU says it’s worried that these powerful AI systems could “cause serious accidents or be misused for far-reaching cyberattacks.” They also fear generative AI could spread “harmful biases” across many applications, affecting many people. Brussels first suggested AI regulations in 2019, taking a familiar global role in ratcheting up scrutiny of emerging industries, while other governments scramble to keep up. In the U.S., President Joe Biden signed a sweeping executive order on AI in October that’s expected to be backed up by legislation and global agreements. In the meantime, lawmakers in at least seven U.S. states are working on their own AI legislation. Chinese President Xi Jinping has proposed his Global AI Governance Initiative for fair and safe use of AI, and authorities have issued « interim measures » for managing generative AI, which applies to text, pictures, audio, video and other content generated for people inside China. Other countries, from Brazil to Japan, as well as global groupings like the United Nations and Group of Seven industrialized nations, are moving to draw up AI guardrails. The AI Act is expected to officially become law by May or June, after a few final formalities, including a blessing from EU member countries. Provisions will start taking effect in stages, with countries required to ban prohibited AI systems six months after the rules enter the lawbooks. Rules for general purpose AI systems like chatbots will start applying a year after the law takes effect. When it comes to enforcement, each EU country will set up their own AI watchdog, where citizens can file a complaint if they think they’ve been the victim of a violation of the rules. Meanwhile, Brussels will create an AI Office tasked with enforcing and supervising the law for general purpose AI systems. Violations of the AI Act could draw fines of up to 35 million euros ($38 million), or 7% of a company’s global revenue. This isn’t Brussels’ last word on AI rules, said Italian lawmaker Brando Benifei, co-leader of Parliament’s work on the law. More AI-related legislation could be ahead after summer elections, including in areas like AI in the workplace that the new law partly covers, he said.
