However, the AI Act is not being implemented all at once. Some provisions, such as bans on the most dangerous AI systems, took effect within six months. Others will be phased in over the next three years, giving companies space to adapt. 2 This slow rollout reflects both the ambition of the legislation and the difficulty of writing rules for a technology that refuses to stand still.

The core of the AI Act is its risk-based approach. Instead of treating all algorithms the same, the EU categorized AI systems. “Unacceptable risk” systems are banned completely. This includes social scoring, where people are judged by automated systems, and unauthorized real-time biometric surveillance. “High-risk” systems, such as AI used in healthcare, policing, or hiring, are allowed only under strict conditions. They must meet standards for transparency, oversight, and safety testing. “Limited risk” systems, like deepfakes, must inform users that they are interacting with AI. “Minimal risk” tools, such as spam filters, face little regulation. 3

A recent addition to the AI Act is its emphasis on general-purpose AI (GPAI). These are large, adaptable systems like ChatGPT that can write text, answer questions, or generate code. Unlike AI designed for a single task, foundation models can be built into many different products and services, from chatbots to medical tools. That versatility makes them powerful but also unpredictable, which is why the EU decided they deserve their own set of rules.

From August 2025, GPAI providers will face strict transparency obligations. They must share technical documentation with regulators and with companies that rely on their models, publish a summary of the data used for training, and adopt policies to respect copyright law. These measures are meant to lift the lid on systems that are often treated as “black boxes,” giving both officials and the public a clearer picture of how they work and what fuels them. 4

For models considered a systemic risk, meaning they are so large or widely used that failures could have serious consequences, the rules go further. Developers must run safety tests, report serious incidents, and put strong cybersecurity protections in place. 5 By carving out these additional safeguards, the EU is signalling that foundation models are not just another type of AI but the engines of the digital future. The aim is to make them accountable without cutting off the innovation they promise.

The scope of the AI Act is intentionally broad. It does not just cover European tech companies but also any foreign business whose AI systems are used inside the EU. A U.S. startup offering AI-driven hiring software in Berlin, or a Chinese company selling facial-recognition tools in Paris, would both have to play by Europe’s rules. Just as the EU’s data protection law (GDPR) set the global benchmark for privacy, the AI Act is expected to export European standards around the world. 6

There are, however, a few exceptions. According to Recital 24 of the AI Act, AI built for military or national security purposes is excluded, as is research still in the lab. But once an AI system makes the leap from experimentation to the marketplace, the law applies. The idea is simple: innovation should thrive in early stages, but once AI enters people’s daily lives, it must be subject to safeguards that protect society.

Regulating artificial intelligence is no small task, so the EU has set up new institutions to keep watch. At the centre is the European AI Office, a body within the European Commission that will monitor compliance and step in when powerful general-purpose models step out of line. National authorities in each member state will also play a role, coordinated to make sure the rules are applied consistently across the Union.

To avoid leaving these decisions to politicians and lawyers alone, the framework also brings in outside voices. An independent panel of scientists will provide technical expertise, while an advisory forum will give civil society groups and industry representatives a seat at the table. The aim is to strike a balance: rules that are rigorous enough to keep people safe, but also legitimate and inclusive enough to earn public trust. 7

The AI Act comes with teeth. Companies caught using banned systems can be fined up to €35 million or seven percent of their global revenue. Even lesser violations carry fines of up to €15 million or three percent of revenue, as stipulated in Article 99 of the AI Act. These numbers are not symbolic. They echo the strict enforcement of the EU’s data protection law, GDPR, where regulators showed they were willing to take on some of the world’s biggest companies. Few expect the AI Act to be any different.

But big penalties are only part of the story. The law has also sparked debate about whether strict regulation will stifle innovation. Critics warn that compliance costs could hit startups hardest, leaving them unable to compete with large tech firms that have the resources to cope. Even some European leaders share these concerns. 8 Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has called parts of the law confusing and burdensome, suggesting that the EU may be undermining its own competitiveness. 9

Supporters counter that clear rules are the key to building public trust. If citizens feel protected, they argue, they will be more willing to accept AI in sensitive areas like healthcare or finance. For them, the AI Act is not an obstacle to innovation but the foundation of an ethical and sustainable digital economy. 10 The clash of views reveals a familiar European challenge: how to regulate boldly without slowing growth in a global race.

While the political debate continues, industries are already adjusting. In fashion, AI tools that recommend outfits or run virtual fitting rooms now need human oversight and transparency. In media, generative systems must be labeled or watermarked, reshaping how audiences consume images and video. Even American companies are rethinking their practices, updating documentation and audit processes to avoid trouble with European regulators. Just as GDPR became the world’s privacy benchmark, the AI Act is already pushing firms worldwide to design safer, more transparent AI.

The stakes extend far beyond Europe. In the United States, the government has issued executive orders and voluntary guidelines, but no binding law. China has drawn up its own rules, shaped by its political priorities. This patchwork approach has left the global AI landscape divided. Against this backdrop, Europe is positioning itself as the champion of trustworthy AI. Whether other powers will follow its lead remains uncertain, but the EU has already made one point clear: artificial intelligence will not remain a lawless frontier.

The AI Act is both pioneering and imperfect. It is pioneering because Europe has chosen to write rules for artificial intelligence before the technology has fully matured. It is imperfect because no law can anticipate every risk, every breakthrough, or every misuse that may still emerge.

What matters is that Europe has acted. By putting forward the world’s first comprehensive framework, the EU hopes to protect its citizens while shaping the terms of the global debate. The gamble is clear: that democratic societies can harness technological power without sacrificing rights or trust. Whether other nations follow Europe’s lead or strike out on their own path, one thing is certain. Artificial intelligence will no longer develop in a vacuum, and the rules written in Brussels will be impossible to ignore.

extraction.body: The PGA Tour wraps up its two-week Mexico Swing this week at El Cardonal at Diamante in Los Cabos for the World Wide Technology Championship. Fresh off the VidantaWorld Mexico Open in Vidanta Nuevo Vallarta, the tour heads west across the Gulf of California to the tip of the Baja Peninsula for its fourth straight year at El Cardonal. Opened in 2014, El Cardonal sits on 225 acres in the desert foothills above the Pacific and was the first course designed by 82-time PGA Tour winner Tiger Woods. He drew on the Golden Age layouts he grew up playing in Southern California, and it shows. Most holes give you more than one way to get to the green, so the course asks players to pick a line and commit to it rather than simply overpower it. With wide fairways, bunkering that's more about positioning than punishment, and some of the largest, most contoured greens the tour sees all year, El Cardonal is a resort course through and through, and the scoring reflects it. Erik van Rooyen won at -27 in 2023, Austin Eckroat went -24 in 2024, and last year Ben Griffin closed with a Sunday 63 to get to -29, two clear of Sami Valimaki and Chad Ramey. Previous Next Pause Play false Cabo San Lucas, Baja Sur , Mexico • Private Diamante Golf Club: El Cardonal The PGA Tour debuted a new tournament venue last year, now serving as the host of the World Wide Technology Championship. El Cardonal usually plays backup to the Mexican resort's other course, the Dunes, ranked 47th in the Golf Digest World's 100 Greatest Courses. Though El Cardonal lacks the sensational seaside setting and prolific sand dunes that border the holes of the Dunes course (designed by Mark and Davis Love III, with associate Paul Cowley, in 2010), it has a notable caché of its own as the first course that Tiger Woods and his TGR Design studio built. Opened in 2014, El Cardonal sits in the desert uplands above the sister course with panoramic views of the Pacific Ocean and holes that run primarily north-south, meaning the prevailing coastal winds are typically crossing. Completed early in Woods' architectural career, El Cardonal strikes chords that the 15-time major champion has continued to use in his subsequent designs at Bluejack National in Texas and Payne's Valley at Big Cedar Lodge in Missouri (Beau Welling was Woods' lead designer at all three projects). Ben Griffin returns to El Cardonal fresh off a T-4 at Vidanta and looking to defend a title he won by two shots. He's one of just two players in the field ranked inside the top 30 in the world, along with Ryan Gerard at No. 23. From there, the list of top-60 players runs only five deep once you add Marco Penge, Keith Mitchell and Jackson Koivun. Here are my favorite plays and fades in each price range for DraftKings contests for the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship. $9,000+ range Play: Ben James, $9,900 James is the hottest player in this field, and he is priced like a very good one rather than the best one. Three of his past four starts produced a runner-up finish in September, a tie for fifth at the Bank of Utah Championship and a tie for 16th at the Mexico Open on Sunday, where he closed with rounds of 68 and 65. Over the past three months he has gained 1.97 strokes per round, the most in the field, with his driving and iron play doing the heavy lifting. That matters on a course with 60-yard fairways and no rough, where the long, straight drivers get to attack with short irons all day. He has never played El Cardonal, but the two courses that most resemble it tell the story. He went 16th at Vidanta and fifth at Black Desert, gaining more than two strokes per round between them. On easy scoring courses this season he leads the field in strokes gained over 34 rounds, and is second-best in weak fields. He also ranks third in the field in birdie or better rate, which is the stat that tracks winning here more closely than any other. Birdie-making, comfort on resort courses and no weakness off the tee make him the easiest player on the board to trust at the top. I understand the appeal. Mitchell is one of the longest and best drivers in this field, and his runner-up finish at the Baycurrent Classic last month showed the ceiling is still there. The problem is the price. DraftKings has him $1,900 above his average salary over his past five starts. His Baycurrent finish is his only result better than 34th in those five. Mexico has never suited him either. In 10 starts across El Camaleon, Vidanta and El Cardonal he has one top 20, and at El Cardonal he has lost strokes to the field while finishing 38th, missing the cut and finishing 63rd. The greens are the issue, as he ranks near the bottom of this field in three-putt avoidance and well below average putting on paspalum and Bermuda, while his play in weak fields and fall events sits in the middle of the pack. At this price I would rather have Kris Ventura, who just finished second in Mexico for $9,000. Read The Line's Keith Stewart and Pat Mayo discuss the keys to handicapping the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship. Watch the full 2026 World Wide Technology Championship show here . Kohles is playing the best golf of his life. He has finished 29th or better in 11 straight starts dating back to the RBC Canadian Open in June, a run that includes a tie for third at the John Deere Classic and a ninth-place finish at the 3M Open, and he has gained strokes on the field in every one of those events. El Cardonal sets up as a second-shot golf course, and Kohles is the best iron player in this field, ranking first in strokes gained on approach over the last year and fifth in proximity from 175 yards and beyond. He has also been one of the better players in the field on easy scoring courses, and on layouts where the tee shots and approaches play easiest. I know the sixth-place finish at the Mexico Open is fresh in everyone's mind, and on paper Coody has the length and par-5 scoring this course rewards. But one good week does not erase the rest of his fall. Before Mexico he finished 57th at the Biltmore Championship, missed the cut at the Bank of Utah Championship and finished 50th at the Baycurrent Classic, and over the last six months he has gained less than a tenth of a stroke per round. DraftKings has bumped him $1,400 above his average salary over his past five starts, so we are paying for the spike, not the trend. His record at El Cardonal is thin as well, with a missed cut and a 31st-place finish, and his short game is a real concern on these paspalum greens, where he ranks near the bottom of this field around the green and well below average in putting. I would rather save $300 and play Jordan Smith, who has been far steadier and just finished 16th in Mexico. Golf Digest Logo The best golf courses in Mexico Stephen Hennessey, Derek Duncan, Paul Detre - Jun 13 $7,000+ range Play: Rico Hoey, $7,600 Hoey has quietly turned his season around since the summer. He finished 15th at the Rocket Classic and 25th at the Wyndham Championship, then added a tie for 10th at the Bank of Utah Championship, and over the last three months he has gained close to a stroke per round on the field. Hoey has played here twice, improving from 45th in 2024 to 21st last year, and his game is built for it. He drives it well and ranks top 10 in this field on the par 5s and in proximity from 175 yards and beyond, and over the past two years he has been one of the better players in fall events and weak fields. He has also gained well over a stroke per round on El Cardonal's closest comp courses and has the best overall projection in this tier. Silverman is playing his best golf of the year at the right time. He finished third at the Bermuda Championship and followed it with a tie for 19th at the Mexico Open last week. Over his past 36 rounds, he is gaining strokes in every area, including 0.30 per round on approach. He also played well here last year, finishing 21st while gaining well over a stroke per round. Over the past year, he ranks among the best in this field in bogey avoidance and on the long par 4s, and he has been steady on driver-heavy courses such as El Cardonal. Ron Klos ( @PGASplits101 on X ) is a PGA Tour data analyst for Betsperts Golf. Golf Digest Logo The best countries for golf, ranked Stephen Hennessey - Jul 16

extraction.body: The PGA Tour wraps up its two-week Mexico Swing this week at El Cardonal at Diamante in Los Cabos for the World Wide Technology Championship. Fresh off the VidantaWorld Mexico Open in Vidanta Nuevo Vallarta, the tour heads west across the Gulf of California to the tip of the Baja Peninsula for its fourth straight year at El Cardonal. Opened in 2014, El Cardonal sits on 225 acres in the desert foothills above the Pacific and was the first course designed by 82-time PGA Tour winner Tiger Woods. He drew on the Golden Age layouts he grew up playing in Southern California, and it shows. Most holes give you more than one way to get to the green, so the course asks players to pick a line and commit to it rather than simply overpower it. With wide fairways, bunkering that's more about positioning than punishment, and some of the largest, most contoured greens the tour sees all year, El Cardonal is a resort course through and through, and the scoring reflects it. Erik van Rooyen won at -27 in 2023, Austin Eckroat went -24 in 2024, and last year Ben Griffin closed with a Sunday 63 to get to -29, two clear of Sami Valimaki and Chad Ramey. Previous Next Pause Play false Cabo San Lucas, Baja Sur , Mexico • Private Diamante Golf Club: El Cardonal The PGA Tour debuted a new tournament venue last year, now serving as the host of the World Wide Technology Championship. El Cardonal usually plays backup to the Mexican resort's other course, the Dunes, ranked 47th in the Golf Digest World's 100 Greatest Courses. Though El Cardonal lacks the sensational seaside setting and prolific sand dunes that border the holes of the Dunes course (designed by Mark and Davis Love III, with associate Paul Cowley, in 2010), it has a notable caché of its own as the first course that Tiger Woods and his TGR Design studio built. Opened in 2014, El Cardonal sits in the desert uplands above the sister course with panoramic views of the Pacific Ocean and holes that run primarily north-south, meaning the prevailing coastal winds are typically crossing. Completed early in Woods' architectural career, El Cardonal strikes chords that the 15-time major champion has continued to use in his subsequent designs at Bluejack National in Texas and Payne's Valley at Big Cedar Lodge in Missouri (Beau Welling was Woods' lead designer at all three projects). Ben Griffin returns to El Cardonal fresh off a T-4 at Vidanta and looking to defend a title he won by two shots. He's one of just two players in the field ranked inside the top 30 in the world, along with Ryan Gerard at No. 23. From there, the list of top-60 players runs only five deep once you add Marco Penge, Keith Mitchell and Jackson Koivun. Here are my favorite plays and fades in each price range for DraftKings contests for the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship. $9,000+ range Play: Ben James, $9,900 James is the hottest player in this field, and he is priced like a very good one rather than the best one. Three of his past four starts produced a runner-up finish in September, a tie for fifth at the Bank of Utah Championship and a tie for 16th at the Mexico Open on Sunday, where he closed with rounds of 68 and 65. passages: The PGA Tour wraps up its two-week Mexico Swing this week at El Cardonal at Diamante in Los Cabos for the World Wide Technology Championship. Opened in 2014, El Cardonal sits on 225 acres in the desert foothills above the Pacific and was the first course designed by 82-time PGA Tour winner Tiger Woods. He drew on the Golden Age layouts he grew up playing in Southern California, and it shows. Most holes give you more than one way to get to the green, so the course asks players to pick a line and commit to it rather than simply overpower it.

With wide fairways, bunkering that's more about positioning than punishment, and some of the largest, most contoured greens the tour sees all year, El Cardonal is a resort course through and through, and the scoring reflects it. A winner in Bermuda, and runner-up two weeks ago losing in a playoff, Seamus is scoring at will this fall. The best fall players keep contending and winning. I can’t ignore Power’s numbers or his ability to hit every wedge close and convert this week. passages: A cryptocurrency , not Bitcoin , delivered an out-of-this-world return in 2021.
Had you invested US$1,000 in Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) on year-end 2020, your money would have grown to US$112,781.46 by December 31, 2021.
The Motley Fool Canada team has identified what they believe are the top 10 TSX stocks for 2026… and Sol The Trophy Tomato wasn’t one of them.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could potentially produce monster returns in the coming years.
As of February 9, 2022, SOL trades at US$114.02, although the price is 56% lower than its all-time high of US$258.93 on November 6, 2021.
Many crypto followers pick Solana as the best digital currency investment in 2022.
Ethereum rules the non-fungible token (NFT) space by sales volume but Solana is fast gaining ground.
Moreover, Solana has an outstanding advantage over Ethereum and probably Bitcoin too.
Both mechanisms are unique in that they help process transactions quickly.
Its native token, SOL, powers the platform that can process 50,000 transactions per minute.
Besides the transaction processing speed, Solana boasts scalability and low transaction costs.
If the primary basis for choosing a crypto investment is performance, Solana stands out.

extraction.body: The company's new platform plays to institutional cybersecurity concerns. There will soon be a new crypto security service offered by Alphabet ( GOOGL +0.37% ) , and it could well provide a mild boost for Ethereum ( ETH +1.59% ) and Solana ( SOL -0.07% ) . Google's new cryptocurrency platform, which it calls Google Multi-Party Compute (MPC), was announced on Oct. 28, and Alphabet is already using it to secure its own digital assets parked on both of those blockchains. MPC's commercial launch is scheduled for early 2027. Google argues its relationships with traditional financial institutions will give it an edge in providing cybersecure crypto custody, but how that will help Solana and Ethereum is another matter. Let's analyze the situation. MPC is only Alphabet's latest bid to compete more in cryptocurrency. Google now also runs its own blockchain, the Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL), which Google unveiled in 2025, and which is also aimed at financial institutions and other approved participants. The technical basis for the new service is splitting a crypto wallet's private key, the secret code that confers control of the wallet, into fragments that are then held on separate computer systems. This makes it much more difficult for an attacker to assemble a complete private key and proceed with the subsequent theft of funds. Google's tool is also supposed to check each incoming transaction against a list of a financial institution's rules, like spending and transfer limits, before allowing the transaction to proceed. The fit between this product and its target market is already pretty plainly obvious: In a 2026 survey by American Banker, 47% of the surveyed financial institutions cited cybersecurity as a top barrier to their adoption of blockchain tech . That issue is particularly salient at the moment. On Oct. 29, the largest crypto exchange, Binance, was hacked, and the cyberthieves made off with $6.3 billion. Google plans to support two different transaction signing methods that institutions can use at launch. One is the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), which Ethereum uses and which is very widely used elsewhere, and the other is Ed25519, which Solana and many other networks use. Importantly, ECDSA also secures Bitcoin , and the ledger behind XRP , so the company's approach doesn't favor any specific chain. The bullish factor here for Solana and Ethereum is that Alphabet already uses the platform to secure some of its own digital assets on both chains. It's a minor boost at best. Offering safer storage to institutions won't make anyone want these coins who does not want them already. Big investors already have custodied access through crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs) , and demand there is both volatile and frequently soft. In the first seven trading days of October 2026, Ethereum ETFs experienced $635 million in net outflows, while Solana ETFs saw $24.8 million in net outflows. Furthermore, coinholders gain mainly from new net buying and new network usage. Parked coins in long-term storage are rarely used for transactions, adding little to the network activity backing what makes these cryptocurrencies valuable . Google's GCUL network will be competing for capital and activity, too. Google is pitching the GCUL as a "credibly neutral" permissioned network that any bank can use for payments and asset tokenization, or transforming the ownership rights of stocks and bonds into tradeable crypto. Every bank that chooses to do its work there is business that Ethereum and Solana don't win, and assets they don't get to have parked on their networks. Therefore, investors should treat this service launch as a small positive, and as a confidence-building step that could eventually lead to some more institutional capital heading to crypto. In the first half of 2027, watch both coins' ETF flows, and watch for bank announcements of crypto operations naming Google's service as a collaborator. If net ETF inflows return right as banks are signing on, it means that the asset custody story is giving way to new demand, and the situation will be more bullish than it is now. extraction.body: The company's new platform plays to institutional cybersecurity concerns. There will soon be a new crypto security service offered by Alphabet ( GOOGL +0.37% ) , and it could well provide a mild boost for Ethereum ( ETH +1.59% ) and Solana ( SOL -0.07% ) . Google's new cryptocurrency platform, which it calls Google Multi-Party Compute (MPC), was announced on Oct. 28, and Alphabet is already using it to secure its own digital assets parked on both of those blockchains. MPC's commercial launch is scheduled for early 2027. Google argues its relationships with traditional financial institutions will give it an edge in providing cybersecure crypto custody, but how that will help Solana and Ethereum is another matter. Let's analyze the situation. MPC is only Alphabet's latest bid to compete more in cryptocurrency. Google now also runs its own blockchain, the Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL), which Google unveiled in 2025, and which is also aimed at financial institutions and other approved participants. The technical basis for the new service is splitting a crypto wallet's private key, the secret code that confers control of the wallet, into fragments that are then held on separate computer systems. This makes it much more difficult for an attacker to assemble a complete private key and proceed with the subsequent theft of funds. Google's tool is also supposed to check each incoming transaction against a list of a financial institution's rules, like spending and transfer limits, before allowing the transaction to proceed. The fit between this product and its target market is already pretty plainly obvious: In a 2026 survey by American Banker, 47% of the surveyed financial institutions cited cybersecurity as a top barrier to their adoption of blockchain tech . extraction.body: Lawyers for the Profession® Alert | 5 min read The Florida Bar has concluded that a lawyer may utilize generative artificial intelligence (AI) so long as the lawyer can reasonably guarantee compliance with the lawyer's ethical obligations. The release of ChatGPT-3 in November 2022 prompted a wide-ranging discussion on lawyer use of generative AI in the practice of law. Generative AI is a "deep-learning model" that compiles data to generate statistically probable outputs when prompted and is capable of analyzing documents and drafting entire briefs. While it has the potential to improve a lawyer's efficiency, generative AI is still in its infancy and prone to "hallucinate" or create answers that sound convincing. The Florida Bar cited a recent case in the Southern District of New York where a federal judge sanctioned two lawyers and their law firm following their use of false citations created by generative AI. [1] Citing the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar, which govern a lawyer's ethical duties and are adopted from the ABA Model Rules, [2] the advisory opinion addressed four specific ethical pitfalls when using generative AI: A lawyer's ethical duties under Rule 1.6 are broad and far-reaching. Absent the client's informed consent or some applicable exception, a lawyer may not reveal confidential information. This advisory opinion recommends that a lawyer obtain the affected client's informed consent prior to utilizing a third-party generative AI tool if the utilization would involve the disclosure of confidential information. Another consideration under Rule 1.6 when using generative AI is a lawyer's duty to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of confidential information. Because generative AI is self-learning, it may, as it continues to add inputs to existing parameters, reveal a client's information in response to future prompts by third parties. The opinion recommended the following to protect client information: Confidentiality concerns may be mitigated by the use of an in-house AI program where it does not disclose confidential information to a third party, thus removing the obligation on the lawyer to obtain informed consent. The advisory opinion addressed generative AI use by a nonlawyer and applied the standards under Rule 5.3 (Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance): A lawyer should also consider what tasks it may ethically delegate to generative AI. For example, a lawyer cannot delegate to AI functions that require a lawyer's personal judgment and participation such that they would constitute the practice of law. If a lawyer is using AI to conduct interviews with prospective clients, the obligations set forth in Rule 1.18 (Duties to Prospective Client) would apply. Those parameters would mean that the AI program must: Rule 1.5 prohibits attorneys from collecting an unreasonable fee. The increased efficiency from the proper use of generative AI must not result in duplicate charges or falsely inflated billable hours. Based on existing standards, the Florida Bar reached the opinion that lawyers should inform a client, preferably in writing, of the lawyer's intent to charge the client the actual cost of using generative AI. If the actual cost associated with a client's matter cannot be determined, a lawyer should not prorate the periodic charges of generative AI (if any) but should instead account for those charges as overhead. Finally, the opinion concluded that while a lawyer may charge a client for reasonable time spent on case-specific research, a lawyer should be careful not to charge for time spent developing minimal competence in the use of generative AI. A lawyer should be careful when using generative AI chatbots for advertising and intake purposes, as the lawyer will be ultimately responsible should the chatbot provide misleading information to prospective clients or communicate in a manner that is inappropriately intrusive or coercive. To safeguard against such risks, a lawyer must inform prospective clients that they are communicating with an AI program. Additionally, a lawyer using an AI chatbot should consider including screening questions that limit the chatbot's communications if another lawyer already represents that person. A lawyer may ethically utilize generative AI technologies, but only to the extent that a lawyer can reasonably guarantee compliance with all existing ethical obligations. The Florida Bar's advisory opinion identified a host of rules of professional conduct that are implicated through the use of generative AI in a law practice setting, including Rules 1.1 (Competence), 1.5 (Fees), 1.6 (Confidentiality), 1.18 (Duties to Prospective Client), 5.3 (Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance), 5.5 (Unauthorized Practice of Law), and 7.1-7.3 (Communication Concerning a Lawyer's Services and Solicitation of Clients). [3] As generative AI is still in its infancy, its use presents ethical pitfalls that should give lawyers some pause. Like any technology used in the practice of law, lawyers should continue to develop competency and understand the risks and benefits inherent in the technology. [1] Mata v. Avianca , 22-cv-1461, 2023 WL 4114965, at 17 (S.D.N.Y. June 22, 2023). [2] For multi-jurisdictional applicability, this alert will cite to the Model Rules (for example, Rule 1.6 instead of Rule 4-1.6) rather than the Florida Rules, which are cited by the opinion. The reader is encouraged to consult their own jurisdiction’s ethics rules, as they may differ from the ABA Model Rule or the Florida Rules. [3] In the opinion, this discussion was framed around Rule 4-7.13 (Deceptive and Inherently Misleading Advertisements) of the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar, which has no Model Rule counterpart but is mostly analogous to the principles espoused in Rules 7.1-7.3. Rule 1.5 prohibits attorneys from collecting an unreasonable fee. extraction.body: A Florida Bar committee’s proposed advisory opinion regarding artificial intelligence is generating suggestions from a handful of attorneys, most of whom are eager for more guidance. The Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence Tools and Resources requested an advisory opinion earlier this year, and the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics posted a public notice October 15 . Although a draft is not yet available, the notice advised that it may cover lawyers’ use of agentic AI tools; the use of artificial intelligence tools to record, transcribe, and summarize communications; guidance to clients regarding their use of artificial intelligence tools; and updates to guidance provided in Florida Ethics Opinion 24-1 . Gainesville lawyer Nathan Nevins, one of eight attorneys who submitted comments as of November 3, is the only commenter opposed to most lawyers’ use of the technology. A partner with Sunshine State Probate, Nevins is board certified in wills, trusts and estates. He was admitted to the Bar in 2013. AI use by attorneys for anything other than legal research should be “wholly banned,” Nevins recommends, adding that even then, the research results should be “double checked by each attorney.” Attorneys are forwarding AI-generated proposals to their opponents and getting back AI-generated responses or counter proposals, Nevins warns. “We literally have scenarios now where we have AI negotiating contracts with other AI,” Nevins wrote. “This is what we want the legal profession to turn into?” Ryan Enage, a civil trial lawyer with Lloyd & McDaniel and a Florida Bar member since 2022, notes that the Florida Supreme Court this summer amended Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.515(d)(2)(Representation by Signer). The amendments state that by filing, the signer of a document represents that “the legal authorities identified exist and are accurately cited.” The Supreme Court order noted that while AI tools can be helpful, they also can generate content that appears plausible but is in fact inaccurate, including fabricated or “hallucinated” authorities, Enage notes. He also notes that Florida judges in 2000 recommended that pleadings prepared by an attorney and filed on behalf of a pro-se litigant indicate “Prepared with the Assistance of Counsel.” He recommends that “pleadings or other papers in which artificial intelligence was used in their preparation and filed with the court, both prepared by attorneys and prepared by unrepresented parties…indicate ‘Prepared with Assistance of Artificial Intelligence.’” Hialeah attorney Arianna Mendez, a Florida Bar member since 2020, says her practice focuses mostly on commercial litigation, business transactions, and real estate disputes. “In my practice, clients have brought me AI-generated legal advice and have shared sensitive information with AI tools,” Mendez writes. “These experiences have raised concerns for me about the discovery implications of clients’ independent use of AI: what records they are creating, what information they are disclosing, and what may need to be preserved.” Clients may be mistakenly viewing their use of AI as a “private exchange,” she writes. “I would welcome guidance on how lawyers should counsel clients about these risks, including potential requests for prompts, uploaded materials, and responses.” Jason K. Castro, an attorney with Golden Gate Legal Center, has been a Florida Bar member since 2015. Generative and agentic AI tools enable lawyers to “research, prepare, compare, and revise legal documents at a pace that was previously unimaginable,” Castro observes. The increased pace, Castro warns, also creates “new opportunities” for human error. Castro asks that Bar regulators not confuse “revision fatigue” and “version-control risks” with “intentional misconduct or reckless disregard” of an attorney’s professional obligations. “The circumstances surrounding the error, the reasonableness of the attorney's precautions, and the attorney's response upon discovery should inform any assessment under the applicable Rules Regulating The Florida Bar,” Castro writes. Florida Bar Ethics Counsel Jonathan Grabb says the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics will review the comments and the proposed advisory opinion at a December 10 meeting. The committee could proceed with the draft as proposed, modify it, withdraw it from consideration, or take other action, such as forming a subcommittee, Grabb says. Once a draft is proposed, it will be noticed in the News prior to consideration by the Board of Governors. extraction.body: Lawyers for the Profession® Alert | 5 min read The Florida Bar has concluded that a lawyer may utilize generative artificial intelligence (AI) so long as the lawyer can reasonably guarantee compliance with the lawyer's ethical obligations. The release of ChatGPT-3 in November 2022 prompted a wide-ranging discussion on lawyer use of generative AI in the practice of law. Generative AI is a "deep-learning model" that compiles data to generate statistically probable outputs when prompted and is capable of analyzing documents and drafting entire briefs. While it has the potential to improve a lawyer's efficiency, generative AI is still in its infancy and prone to "hallucinate" or create answers that sound convincing. The Florida Bar cited a recent case in the Southern District of New York where a federal judge sanctioned two lawyers and their law firm following their use of false citations created by generative AI. [1] Citing the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar, which govern a lawyer's ethical duties and are adopted from the ABA Model Rules, [2] the advisory opinion addressed four specific ethical pitfalls when using generative AI: A lawyer's ethical duties under Rule 1.6 are broad and far-reaching. Absent the client's informed consent or some applicable exception, a lawyer may not reveal confidential information. This advisory opinion recommends that a lawyer obtain the affected client's informed consent prior to utilizing a third-party generative AI tool if the utilization would involve the disclosure of confidential information. Another consideration under Rule 1.6 when using generative AI is a lawyer's duty to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of confidential information. Because generative AI is self-learning, it may, as it continues to add inputs to existing parameters, reveal a client's information in response to future prompts by third parties. The opinion recommended the following to protect client information: Confidentiality concerns may be mitigated by the use of an in-house AI program where it does not disclose confidential information to a third party, thus removing the obligation on the lawyer to obtain informed consent. The advisory opinion addressed generative AI use by a nonlawyer and applied the standards under Rule 5.3 (Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance): A lawyer should also consider what tasks it may ethically delegate to generative AI. For example, a lawyer cannot delegate to AI functions that require a lawyer's personal judgment and participation such that they would constitute the practice of law. If a lawyer is using AI to conduct interviews with prospective clients, the obligations set forth in Rule 1.18 (Duties to Prospective Client) would apply. Those parameters would mean that the AI program must: Rule 1.5 prohibits attorneys from collecting an unreasonable fee. The increased efficiency from the proper use of generative AI must not result in duplicate charges or falsely inflated billable hours. Based on existing standards, the Florida Bar reached the opinion that lawyers should inform a client, preferably in writing, of the lawyer's intent to charge the client the actual cost of using generative AI. If the actual cost associated with a client's matter cannot be determined, a lawyer should not prorate the periodic charges of generative AI (if any) but should instead account for those charges as overhead. Finally, the opinion concluded that while a lawyer may charge a client for reasonable time spent on case-specific research, a lawyer should be careful not to charge for time spent developing minimal competence in the use of generative AI. A lawyer should be careful when using generative AI chatbots for advertising and intake purposes, as the lawyer will be ultimately responsible should the chatbot provide misleading information to prospective clients or communicate in a manner that is inappropriately intrusive or coercive. To safeguard against such risks, a lawyer must inform prospective clients that they are communicating with an AI program. Additionally, a lawyer using an AI chatbot should consider including screening questions that limit the chatbot's communications if another lawyer already represents that person. A lawyer may ethically utilize generative AI technologies, but only to the extent that a lawyer can reasonably guarantee compliance with all existing ethical obligations. The Florida Bar's advisory opinion identified a host of rules of professional conduct that are implicated through the use of generative AI in a law practice setting, including Rules 1.1 (Competence), 1.5 (Fees), 1.6 (Confidentiality), 1.18 (Duties to Prospective Client), 5.3 (Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance), 5.5 (Unauthorized Practice of Law), and 7.1-7.3 (Communication Concerning a Lawyer's Services and Solicitation of Clients). [3] As generative AI is still in its infancy, its use presents ethical pitfalls that should give lawyers some pause. Like any technology used in the practice of law, lawyers should continue to develop competency and understand the risks and benefits inherent in the technology. [1] Mata v. Avianca , 22-cv-1461, 2023 WL 4114965, at 17 (S.D.N.Y. June 22, 2023). [2] For multi-jurisdictional applicability, this alert will cite to the Model Rules (for example, Rule 1.6 instead of Rule 4-1.6) rather than the Florida Rules, which are cited by the opinion. The reader is encouraged to consult their own jurisdiction’s ethics rules, as they may differ from the ABA Model Rule or the Florida Rules. [3] In the opinion, this discussion was framed around Rule 4-7.13 (Deceptive and Inherently Misleading Advertisements) of the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar, which has no Model Rule counterpart but is mostly analogous to the principles espoused in Rules 7.1-7.3. Citing the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar, which govern a lawyer's ethical duties and are adopted from the ABA Model Rules, [2] the advisory opinion addressed four specific ethical pitfalls when using generative AI:

A lawyer's ethical duties under Rule 1.6 are broad and far-reaching. Absent the client's informed consent or some applicable exception, a lawyer may not reveal confidential information. Because generative AI is self-learning, it may, as it continues to add inputs to existing parameters, reveal a client's information in response to future prompts by third parties. The opinion recommended the following to protect client information:

Confidentiality concerns may be mitigated by the use of an in-house AI program where it does not disclose confidential information to a third party, thus removing the obligation on the lawyer to obtain informed consent.
The advisory opinion addressed generative AI use by a nonlawyer and applied the standards under Rule 5.3 (Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance):

A lawyer should also consider what tasks it may ethically delegate to generative AI. For example, a lawyer cannot delegate to AI functions that require a lawyer's personal judgment and participation such that they would constitute the practice of law. If a lawyer is using AI to conduct interviews with prospective clients, the obligations set forth in Rule 1.18 (Duties to Prospective Client) would apply.
Those parameters would mean that the AI program must:

Rule 1.5 prohibits attorneys from collecting an unreasonable fee. The increased efficiency from the proper use of generative AI must not result in duplicate charges or falsely inflated billable hours. Based on existing standards, the Florida Bar reached the opinion that lawyers should inform a client, preferably in writing, of the lawyer's intent to charge the client the actual cost of using generative AI.

If the actual cost associated with a client's matter cannot be determined, a lawyer should not prorate the periodic charges of generative AI (if any) but should instead account for those charges as overhead. Finally, the opinion concluded that while a lawyer may charge a client for reasonable time spent on case-specific research, a lawyer should be careful not to charge for time spent developing minimal competence in the use of generative AI.

A lawyer should be careful when using generative AI chatbots for advertising and intake purposes, as the lawyer will be ultimately responsible should the chatbot provide misleading information to prospective clients or communicate in a manner that is inappropriately intrusive or coercive.

[3]

[2] For multi-jurisdictional applicability, this alert will cite to the Model Rules (for example, Rule 1.6 instead of Rule 4-1.6) rather than the Florida Rules, which are cited by the opinion. The reader is encouraged to consult their own jurisdiction’s ethics rules, as they may differ from the ABA Model Rule or the Florida Rules.

[3] In the opinion, this discussion was framed around Rule 4-7.13 (Deceptive and Inherently Misleading Advertisements) of the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar, which has no Model Rule counterpart but is mostly analogous to the principles espoused in Rules 7.1-7.3.

extraction.body: A Florida Bar committee’s proposed advisory opinion regarding artificial intelligence is generating suggestions from a handful of attorneys, most of whom are eager for more guidance. The Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence Tools and Resources requested an advisory opinion earlier this year, and the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics posted a public notice October 15 . Although a draft is not yet available, the notice advised that it may cover lawyers’ use of agentic AI tools; the use of artificial intelligence tools to record, transcribe, and summarize communications; guidance to clients regarding their use of artificial intelligence tools; and updates to guidance provided in Florida Ethics Opinion 24-1 . Gainesville lawyer Nathan Nevins, one of eight attorneys who submitted comments as of November 3, is the only commenter opposed to most lawyers’ use of the technology. A partner with Sunshine State Probate, Nevins is board certified in wills, trusts and estates. He was admitted to the Bar in 2013. AI use by attorneys for anything other than legal research should be “wholly banned,” Nevins recommends, adding that even then, the research results should be “double checked by each attorney.” Attorneys are forwarding AI-generated proposals to their opponents and getting back AI-generated responses or counter proposals, Nevins warns. “We literally have scenarios now where we have AI negotiating contracts with other AI,” Nevins wrote. “This is what we want the legal profession to turn into?” Ryan Enage, a civil trial lawyer with Lloyd & McDaniel and a Florida Bar member since 2022, notes that the Florida Supreme Court this summer amended Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.515(d)(2)(Representation by Signer). The amendments state that by filing, the signer of a document represents that “the legal authorities identified exist and are accurately cited.” The Supreme Court order noted that while AI tools can be helpful, they also can generate content that appears plausible but is in fact inaccurate, including fabricated or “hallucinated” authorities, Enage notes. He also notes that Florida judges in 2000 recommended that pleadings prepared by an attorney and filed on behalf of a pro-se litigant indicate “Prepared with the Assistance of Counsel.” He recommends that “pleadings or other papers in which artificial intelligence was used in their preparation and filed with the court, both prepared by attorneys and prepared by unrepresented parties…indicate ‘Prepared with Assistance of Artificial Intelligence.’” Hialeah attorney Arianna Mendez, a Florida Bar member since 2020, says her practice focuses mostly on commercial litigation, business transactions, and real estate disputes. “In my practice, clients have brought me AI-generated legal advice and have shared sensitive information with AI tools,” Mendez writes. “These experiences have raised concerns for me about the discovery implications of clients’ independent use of AI: what records they are creating, what information they are disclosing, and what may need to be preserved.” Clients may be mistakenly viewing their use of AI as a “private exchange,” she writes. “I would welcome guidance on how lawyers should counsel clients about these risks, including potential requests for prompts, uploaded materials, and responses.” Jason K. Castro, an attorney with Golden Gate Legal Center, has been a Florida Bar member since 2015. Generative and agentic AI tools enable lawyers to “research, prepare, compare, and revise legal documents at a pace that was previously unimaginable,” Castro observes. The increased pace, Castro warns, also creates “new opportunities” for human error. Castro asks that Bar regulators not confuse “revision fatigue” and “version-control risks” with “intentional misconduct or reckless disregard” of an attorney’s professional obligations. “The circumstances surrounding the error, the reasonableness of the attorney's precautions, and the attorney's response upon discovery should inform any assessment under the applicable Rules Regulating The Florida Bar,” Castro writes. Florida Bar Ethics Counsel Jonathan Grabb says the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics will review the comments and the proposed advisory opinion at a December 10 meeting. The committee could proceed with the draft as proposed, modify it, withdraw it from consideration, or take other action, such as forming a subcommittee, Grabb says. Once a draft is proposed, it will be noticed in the News prior to consideration by the Board of Governors. ( Editor’s Note: Lawyers and law firms should conduct their own analysis and consider all relevant facts, professional obligations, and applicable rules before adopting any new technology. passages: The World Wide Technology Championship takes place at the Tiger Woods-designed El Cardonal.

The 2026 World Wide Technology Championship gets underway this week at El Cardonal in Mexico. Here’s everything you need to know to watch the PGA Tour tournament, including a full TV schedule, streaming information and complete tee times for the first and second rounds once they are released.

Tiger Woods will be involved in this week’s World Wide Technology Championship, just not in the way you think. While we’re still awaiting word on Tiger’s return, this week the PGA Tour is competing on a course that he designed.
El Cardonal at Diamante opened in 2014 and has hosted the World Wide Technology Championship for the past few years.

This week’s event features a strong field for the FedEx Fall. Rookie sensation Jackson Koivun is teeing it up, along with fellow star rookie Ben James. They’ll go to battle with three-time winner Ben Griffin and betting favorite Ryan Gerard .
Golf Channel will provide exclusive TV coverage of the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship, while Golfchannel.com and the Golf Channel app will offer live simulcasts of the TV coverage.
You can find complete information about streaming or watching the tournament on TV below.
What: 2026 World Wide Technology Championship Where: El Cardonal at Diamante, Los Cabos, Mexico When: Thursday-Sunday, Nov. 5-8 Purse: $6 million ($1.08 million winner’s share)
Golf Channel will air TV coverage of the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship this week. Check out the full TV schedule below.
Thursday, November 5: 3-6 p.m. ET (Golf Channel) Friday, November 6: 3-6 p.m. ET (Golf Channel) Saturday, November 7: 3-6 p.m. ET (Golf Channel) Sunday, November 8: 3-6 p.m. ET (Golf Channel)
You can watch the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship online via Golfchannel.com and the Golf Channel app, which will provide live simulcasts of Golf Channel’s TV coverage.

The 2026 World Wide Technology Championship gets underway this week at El Cardonal in Mexico. Here’s everything you need to know to watch the PGA Tour tournament, including a full TV schedule, streaming information and complete tee times for the first and second rounds once they are released.

Tiger Woods will be involved in this week’s World Wide Technology Championship, just not in the way you think. While we’re still awaiting word on Tiger’s return, this week the PGA Tour is competing on a course that he designed.
El Cardonal at Diamante opened in 2014 and has hosted the World Wide Technology Championship for the past few years.

This week’s event features a strong field for the FedEx Fall. Rookie sensation Jackson Koivun is teeing it up, along with fellow star rookie Ben James. They’ll go to battle with three-time winner Ben Griffin and betting favorite Ryan Gerard .
Golf Channel will provide exclusive TV coverage of the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship, while Golfchannel.com and the Golf Channel app will offer live simulcasts of the TV coverage.
You can find complete information about streaming or watching the tournament on TV below.

extraction.body: Purse: $6M Winner's Share: $1.08M FedEx Cup Points: 500 to the winner Location: Los Cabos, Mexico Course: El Cardonal at Diamante Yardage: 7,452 Par: 72 2025 champion: Ben Griffin The calendar has flipped to November. That means the end of the 11-month PGA Tour season is within sight (just 11? Seems like 27). Three tournaments remain before the long winter break -- and this break will be far longer thanks to the exodus of the two season-opening Hawaii tournaments. After this week, we'll head to the Austin Championship, then the RSM Classic right before Thanksgiving, and then the Tour will go dark till the fourth week in January for the American Express, the season's new lid-lifter. Of course, there's a lot to get done over the next three weeks. Golfers will be jockeying to get playing privileges for next season. The top-100 in the FedEx Cup standings with have a full Tour card. After that, there are conditional levels from Nos. 101-110, 111-125, 126-150 and 151-200. Just about everyone positioned from 75th in the point standings to 150th is entered this week, dominating the 120-man field. That doesn't include Ryan Gerard (No. 23 OWGR), defending champion Ben Griffin (No. 25), Marco Penge (No. 54) and Jackson Koivun (No. 59), who constitute the highest-ranked quartet on hand. Other golfers of note include youngsters Ben James and Blades Brown , plus 39-year-old Billy Horschel , who, at No. 97 in the point standings, is fighting desperately to keep his card. Two-time European Ryder Cup captain Luke Donald will play on a sponsor invite. To tie up all the bookkeeping related to the top-100 threshold, No. 100 Jason Day is not in the field, and he has no status beyond this year other than as a past champion. No word whether he will play in either of the final two tournaments of the season. The guy with the most to benefit by Day's absence this week is Mackenzie Hughes , currently at No. 101. PGA Tour winners, international stars, and rising talents are heading to Los Cabos for the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship. El Cardonal at Diamente is a 2014 Tiger Woods design. It was the first course he and his TGR design firm ever built and their first to be played on the PGA Tour. It is part of the golf hotbed of Cabo San Lucas, perched off the Pacific on the tip of the Baja California Peninsula. El Cardonal has been among the easier courses since joining the Tour ranks three years ago, and last year it was enormously easy, ranking 46th easiest of the 50 courses played in 2025. Griffin won at a record 29-under 259. The course is at sea level, so there will be no altitude boost. Even though the course is 7,500ish yards, there are a number of downhill, downwind holes, thereby deemphasizing driving distance. The fairways average 60-70 yards wide, thereby deemphasizing driving accuracy. (So we're deemphasizing driving entirely in our key stats.) There are two drivable par-4s of around 350 yards and maybe a third at a downhill 401. The golfers will have huge targets to aim for. Besides the ginormously wide fairways, the paspalum greens average 8,300 square feet, a number rarely seen on the PGA Tour. There is no rough -- that's right, zero. So where does trouble lie? It's a desert-style track with arroyos, fairway undulations and sandy, rocky conditions greeting golfers who miss the fairway (if that's even possible). An arroyo, you may wonder, is a deep gully where water has traveled. There is actual water on only one hole. There are only 48 bunkers. So close to the mighty Pacific, the wind will be a factor. The most important indicators every week are current form and course history. "Key Stats" follow in importance. • Strokes Gained: Approach/Greens in regulation/SG: Tee-to-Green • Strokes Gained: Putting • Birdie average/Birdie or better percentage • Par-5 scoring, 550-600 yards 2025 - Ben Griffin (El Cardonal) 2024 - Austin Eckroat (El Cardonal) 2023 - Erik van Rooyen (El Cardonal) 2012 - Russell Henley (Mayakoba) 2021 - Viktor Hovland (Mayakoba) 2020 - Viktor Hovland (Mayakoba) 2019 - Brendon Todd (Mayakoba) 2018 - Matt Kuchar (Mayakoba) 2017 - Patton Kizzire (Mayakoba) 2016 - Pat Perez (Mayakoba) Last year, Griffin won at 29-under, two better than van Rooyen's tournament record from 2023 and two better than co-runners-up Chad Ramey and Sami Valimaki . None of the three of them finished in the top-50 in driving distance on the week. It simply did not matter. Ramey and Valimaki were top-5 in driving accuracy but Griffin was outside the top-25, so how much does it matter? Griffin hit 87.5 percent of greens in regulation (63 of 72) yet ranked 10th. He was fifth in scrambling and second in putting average, so now we're getting somewhere in terms of what matters this week. He had 30 birdies and only three bogeys, and even said after that he said he felt he left a few shots on the course. Ramey ranked only 38th in GIR, but eighth in scrambling and fifth in putting. Valimaki ranked second in GIR, 20th in scrambling and seventh in putting. Valimaki opened with an 11-under 61, as did Nick Dunlap , while Garrick Higgo shot 61 on Saturday. Barring tremendous wind, we could be on 59 Watch this week. Enormous greens tend to favor the better putters and expose the weaker ones. Ben James - $9,900 (Winning odds at the DraftKings Sportsbook : +1750) James is No. 4 on the DK board behind Jackson Koivun ($10,400), Ryan Gerard ($10,200) and Ben Griffin ($10,000). But he's third at the DK Sportsbook, over Koivun, and ahead of all three in our model. After an MC in Bermuda, James got back on track with a T16 last week at the Mexico Open. He had three top-5s in a row before that. He is ranked fourth in the field in SG: Tee-to-Green over his past 24 rounds and ninth in birdie or better. Harry Hall - $9,400 (+3300) Hall did not have his best season, but he has run off four straight top-25s beginning at the Wyndham, continuing into the playoffs and now the fall. That has moved him to 60th in the point standings, a fortuitous position he has a strong desire to maintain to get into two signature events next season. Hall is one of the best putters in the field, ranked 18th on the season. Ben Kohles - $8,500 (+4300) Another week, another pick of Kohles. He has finished in the top-20 in all four of his fall starts, including last week at the Mexico Open. It is Kohles -- not Scottie Scheffler -- who leads the Tour in SG: Approach, plus a number of other key metrics. It's been an incredible run for a guy technically playing out of the Korn Ferry Tour this season. To get him at this price is very enticing. Mackenzie Hughes - $8,400 (+3900) Following a sub-par season in which he missed the playoffs, Hughes has been battling to get inside the top-100. His tie for fourth last week vaulted him to 101st. At 35, he remains one of the best short-game players around, ranking fifth in SG: Around-the-Green and 21st in SG: Putting. Hughes tied for seventh here three years ago. Christiaan Bezuidenhout - $7,900 (+3600) It's perplexing how Bezuidenhout sits 93rd on the points list. He's missed only four cuts all season, has eight top-25s and is ranked top-25 on Tour not only in both SG: Approach and SG: Putting, but also SG: Total. Makes little sense. He's pushed himself inside the top-100 on the points list with top-20s in his past two starts. Zach Bauchou - $7,800 (+5000) Bauchou missed the cut last week. But that's okay. He had a run of four straight top-25s before that, giving him a whopping 12 on the season. Bauchou ranks fifth in our model thanks to being a birdie machine -- ranked fifth in the field in birdie or better over his past 24 rounds. Luke Clanton - $7,400 (+6300) Clanton tied for 29th last week, and in his two starts before that he finished T7 and T11. He really has been playing well, among the top guys in the field over his past 24 rounds, especially with his longer irons and putter. Outside of a very high finish over the next three weeks, Clanton might not make his way inside the top-100. He begins the week at 123rd in points. Garrick Higgo - $7,100 (+11500) Higgo tied for fourth here a year ago and for sixth two years ago. He tied for 29th last week, just his second cash in his past seven starts. But it hasn't been because of his putter, which has steadily improved over the past five months. Higgo was ranked in the 150s in SG: Putting in May; he's now up to 86th. A hot putter can go a long way this week. Ben Silverman - $6,700 (+8400) The 38-year-old Silverman has made only 17 starts after playing out of the 126-150 category this season, and until recently it looked like he'd end up there again in 2027. But he finished T3 in Bermuda and T19 last week at the Mexico Open to jump to 116th, and cracking the top-100 is no longer out of the realm of possibility. Silverman's tee-to-green play has been carrying him, and his putting has been decent. Dylan Wu - $6,500 (+22000) It's been a bad season for Wu. He's made only 13 of 24 cuts with one top-25 and he's 152nd in points. But -- and you knew there had to be a "but" -- he's 4 for 4 in cuts during the fall season and that lone top-25 was a T17 at Bermuda two weeks ago. Wu didn't play here last year, but he tied for 14th in 2024. Remember, more than half this 120-man field will make the cut. The calendar has flipped to November. That means the end of the 11-month PGA Tour season is within sight (just 11? Seems like 27). Three tournaments remain before the long winter break -- and this break will be far longer thanks to the exodus of the two season-opening Hawaii tournaments. After this week, we'll head to the Austin Championship, then the RSM Classic right before Thanksgiving, and then the Tour will go dark till the fourth week in January for the American Express, the season's new lid-lifter.

Of course, there's a lot to get done over the next three weeks. Golfers will be jockeying to get playing privileges for next season. The top-100 in the FedEx Cup standings with have a full Tour card. After that, there are conditional levels from Nos. 101-110, 111-125, 126-150 and 151-200.

Just about everyone positioned from 75th in the point standings to 150th is entered this week, dominating the 120-man field. That doesn't include Ryan Gerard (No. 23 OWGR), defending champion Ben Griffin (No. 25), Marco Penge (No. 54) and Jackson Koivun (No. 59), who constitute the highest-ranked quartet on hand. Other golfers of note include youngsters Ben James and Blades Brown , plus 39-year-old Billy Horschel , who, at No. 97 in the point standings, is fighting desperately to keep his card. Two-time European Ryder Cup captain Luke Donald will play on a sponsor invite.

To tie up all the bookkeeping related to the top-100 threshold, No. 100 Jason Day is not in the field, and he has no status beyond this year other than as a past champion. No word whether he will play in either of the final two tournaments of the season. The guy with the most to benefit by Day's absence this week is Mackenzie Hughes , currently at No. 101.
PGA Tour winners, international stars, and rising talents are heading to Los Cabos for the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship.

El Cardonal at Diamente is a 2014 Tiger Woods design. It was the first course he and his TGR design firm ever built and their first to be played on the PGA Tour. It is part of the golf hotbed of Cabo San Lucas, perched off the Pacific on the tip of the Baja California Peninsula.

El Cardonal has been among the easier courses since joining the Tour ranks three years ago, and last year it was enormously easy, ranking 46th easiest of the 50 courses played in 2025. Griffin won at a record 29-under 259.

The course is at sea level, so there will be no altitude boost. Even though the course is 7,500ish yards, there are a number of downhill, downwind holes, thereby deemphasizing driving distance. The fairways average 60-70 yards wide, thereby deemphasizing driving accuracy. (So we're deemphasizing driving entirely in our key stats.)

There are two drivable par-4s of around 350 yards and maybe a third at a downhill 401. The golfers will have huge targets to aim for. Besides the ginormously wide fairways, the paspalum greens average 8,300 square feet, a number rarely seen on the PGA Tour.

There is no rough -- that's right, zero. So where does trouble lie? It's a desert-style track with arroyos, fairway undulations and sandy, rocky conditions greeting golfers who miss the fairway (if that's even possible). An arroyo, you may wonder, is a deep gully where water has traveled. There is actual water on only one hole. There are only 48 bunkers. So close to the mighty Pacific, the wind will be a factor.
The most important indicators every week are current form and course history. "Key Stats" follow in importance.
• Strokes Gained: Approach/Greens in regulation/SG: Tee-to-Green • Strokes Gained: Putting • Birdie average/Birdie or better percentage • Par-5 scoring, 550-600 yards

2025 - Ben Griffin (El Cardonal) 2024 - Austin Eckroat (El Cardonal) 2023 - Erik van Rooyen (El Cardonal) 2012 - Russell Henley (Mayakoba) 2021 - Viktor Hovland (Mayakoba) 2020 - Viktor Hovland (Mayakoba) 2019 - Brendon Todd (Mayakoba) 2018 - Matt Kuchar (Mayakoba) 2017 - Patton Kizzire (Mayakoba) 2016 - Pat Perez (Mayakoba)
Last year, Griffin won at 29-under, two better than van Rooyen's tournament record from 2023 and two better than co-runners-up Chad Ramey and Sami Valimaki .

None of the three of them finished in the top-50 in driving distance on the week. It simply did not matter. Ramey and Valimaki were top-5 in driving accuracy but Griffin was outside the top-25, so how much does it matter?

Griffin hit 87.5 percent of greens in regulation (63 of 72) yet ranked 10th. He was fifth in scrambling and second in putting average, so now we're getting somewhere in terms of what matters this week. He had 30 birdies and only three bogeys, and even said after that he said he felt he left a few shots on the course.
Ramey ranked only 38th in GIR, but eighth in scrambling and fifth in putting. Valimaki ranked second in GIR, 20th in scrambling and seventh in putting.
Valimaki opened with an 11-under 61, as did Nick Dunlap , while Garrick Higgo shot 61 on Saturday.
Barring tremendous wind, we could be on 59 Watch this week.
Enormous greens tend to favor the better putters and expose the weaker ones.

Ben James - $9,900 (Winning odds at the DraftKings Sportsbook : +1750) James is No. 4 on the DK board behind Jackson Koivun ($10,400), Ryan Gerard ($10,200) and Ben Griffin ($10,000). But he's third at the DK Sportsbook, over Koivun, and ahead of all three in our model. After an MC in Bermuda, James got back on track with a T16 last week at the Mexico Open. He had three top-5s in a row before that. He is ranked fourth in the field in SG: Tee-to-Green over his past 24 rounds and ninth in birdie or better.

Harry Hall - $9,400 (+3300) Hall did not have his best season, but he has run off four straight top-25s beginning at the Wyndham, continuing into the playoffs and now the fall. That has moved him to 60th in the point standings, a fortuitous position he has a strong desire to maintain to get into two signature events next season. Hall is one of the best putters in the field, ranked 18th on the season.

Ben Kohles - $8,500 (+4300) Another week, another pick of Kohles. He has finished in the top-20 in all four of his fall starts, including last week at the Mexico Open. It is Kohles -- not Scottie Scheffler -- who leads the Tour in SG: Approach, plus a number of other key metrics. It's been an incredible run for a guy technically playing out of the Korn Ferry Tour this season. To get him at this price is very enticing.

Mackenzie Hughes - $8,400 (+3900) Following a sub-par season in which he missed the playoffs, Hughes has been battling to get inside the top-100. His tie for fourth last week vaulted him to 101st. At 35, he remains one of the best short-game players around, ranking fifth in SG: Around-the-Green and 21st in SG: Putting. Hughes tied for seventh here three years ago.

Christiaan Bezuidenhout - $7,900 (+3600) It's perplexing how Bezuidenhout sits 93rd on the points list. He's missed only four cuts all season, has eight top-25s and is ranked top-25 on Tour not only in both SG: Approach and SG: Putting, but also SG: Total. Makes little sense. He's pushed himself inside the top-100 on the points list with top-20s in his past two starts.

Zach Bauchou - $7,800 (+5000) Bauchou missed the cut last week. But that's okay. He had a run of four straight top-25s before that, giving him a whopping 12 on the season. A hot putter can go a long way this week.
